abstract: In this paper, we wish to analyze the convergence behavior of a number of neuronal plasticity models. Recent neurophysiological research suggests that the neuronal behavior is adaptive. In particular, memory stored within a neuron is associated with the synaptic weights which are varied or adjusted to achieve learning. A number of adaptive neuronal models have been proposed in the literature. Three specific models will be analyzed in this paper, specifically the Hebb model, the Sutton-Barto model, and the most recent trace model. In this paper we will examine the conditions for convergence, the position of conver(cid:173) gence and the rate at convergence, of these models as they applied to classical conditioning. Simulation results are also presented to verify the analysis.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes how three neuronal plasticity models behave as learning proceeds: the Hebb model, the Sutton–Barto model, and a trace model. It treats changes in synaptic weights as the mechanism through which a neuron learns and stores memory. The models are examined in the setting of classical conditioning.

The analysis separates three questions about convergence. First, under what conditions does learning settle? Second, what values does it settle toward? Third, how quickly does it approach those values? These questions distinguish the existence of a stable learning outcome from the nature of that outcome and the time needed to reach it.

The authors also present simulations to verify the mathematical analysis. This pairing makes the paper an investigation of learning dynamics, with computed behavior used to check the theoretical account. Its value is a common set of questions for understanding several adaptive models: whether their adjustments stabilize, where they lead, and how their convergence unfolds when applied to conditioning.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes convergence conditions, limiting values, and convergence rates for three synaptic learning models in classical conditioning.

title: Mathematical Analysis of Learning Behavior of Neuronal Models

abstract: Recently, many modifications to the McCulloch/Pitts model have been proposed where both learning and forgetting occur. Given that the network never saturates (ceases to function effectively due to an overload of information), the learning updates can con(cid:173) tinue indefinitely. For these networks, we need to introduce performance measmes in addi(cid:173) tion to the information capacity to evaluate the different networks. We mathematically define quantities such as the plasticity of a network, the efficacy of an information vector, and the probability of network saturation. From these quantities we analytically compare different networks.

For these networks, we need to introduce performance measmes in addi(cid:173) tion to the information capacity to evaluate the different networks. paragraphs: Associative memories that continually learn and forget raise evaluation questions beyond how much information they can store at once. The paper considers modifications of the McCulloch/Pitts model with both processes. If such a network avoids saturation, learning updates can continue indefinitely, making its behavior over continuing use central to its assessment.

Saturation here means an overload of information that prevents the memory from functioning effectively. Because learning and forgetting change what the network retains, a single information-capacity measure is insufficient to compare these systems. The authors introduce mathematical quantities for network plasticity, the efficacy of an information vector, and the probability of saturation.

These quantities provide additional ways to characterize a memory and support analytical comparisons between different networks. The approach matters because ongoing learning requires attention to adaptation, the usefulness of stored information, and the risk of overload together. The paper’s contribution is a more suitable evaluation framework for memories whose contents keep changing, with continued updating explicitly dependent on avoiding saturation.
summary.tldr: The paper defines measures beyond storage capacity to compare associative memories that continually learn and forget.

title: Performance Measures for Associative Memories that Learn and Forget

abstract: The firing patterns of populations of cells in the cat visual cor(cid:173) tex can exhibit oscillatory responses in the range of 35 - 85 Hz. Furthermore, groups of neurons many mm's apart can be highly synchronized as long as the cells have similar orientation tuning. We investigate two basic network architectures that incorporate ei(cid:173) ther nearest-neighbor or global feedback interactions and conclude that non-local feedback plays a fundamental role in the initial syn(cid:173) chronization and dynamic stability of the oscillations.

paragraphs: Populations of neurons in the cat visual cortex can respond with oscillations between 35 and 85 Hz. Groups separated by many millimeters can also synchronize strongly when their orientation preferences are similar. This paper investigates what kind of network interaction could account for coordinated oscillations across that spatial separation.

The authors examine two basic architectures. One uses interactions between nearest neighbors, while the other includes global feedback. Comparing these arrangements focuses attention on the reach of the connections: coordination could depend on interactions confined to nearby cells or on feedback that connects activity across a broader network.

The analysis concludes that non-local feedback plays a fundamental role in both establishing synchronization and keeping the oscillations dynamically stable. These are distinct aspects of collective activity: the network must first coordinate its rhythms and then sustain that coordination. The result gives broader feedback connections a central place in explaining synchronized visual-cortical activity, linking the spatial structure of network interactions to their behavior over time.
summary.tldr: Comparing local and global interactions identifies non-local feedback as central to synchronizing and stabilizing visual-cortical oscillations.

title: Collective Oscillations in the Visual Cortex

These provide both a partial description of the stress pattern itself and a prediction of its learnability, without invoking abstract theoretical constructs such as metrical feet. paragraphs: This paper uses neural learning experiments to study linguistic stress: the patterns determining which syllables receive emphasis. Its question concerns not only how to describe these patterns, but also how easy they are to learn. The authors position measured learning behavior as an empirical alternative to arguments based on logically deducing linguistic parameter settings from an initial state.

The experiments train perceptrons on data from nineteen human languages. From these experiments, the authors develop a characterization using six parameters. These parameters serve two purposes: they partially describe a language’s stress pattern and predict its learnability. The characterization does not require theoretical structures such as metrical feet, which appear in traditional analyses.

The contribution is therefore a link between descriptive linguistic categories and the behavior of a learning system. A useful description should capture aspects of the patterns while also helping explain differences in learning difficulty. The work demonstrates how machine learning experiments can inform linguistic analysis, with the learnability conclusions grounded in the perceptron experiments described.
summary.tldr: Perceptron experiments on nineteen languages yield six parameters that describe stress patterns and predict their learnability.

title: A Connectionist Learning Approach to Analyzing Linguistic Stress

abstract: We proposed a model of Time Warping Invariant Neural Networks (TWINN) to handle the time warped continuous signals. Although TWINN is a simple modifica(cid:173) tion of well known recurrent neural network, analysis has shown that TWINN com(cid:173) pletely removes time warping and is able to handle difficult classification problem. It is also shown that TWINN has certain advantages over the current available sequential processing schemes: Dynamic Programming(DP)[I], Hidden Markov Model((cid:173) HMM)[2], Time Delayed Neural Networks(TDNN) [3] and Neural Network Finite Automata(NNFA)[4]. We also analyzed the time continuity employed in TWINN and pointed out that this kind of structure can memorize longer input history compared with Neural Net(cid:173) work Finite Automata (NNFA). This may help to understand the well accepted fact that for learning grammatical reference with NNF A one had to start with very short strings in training set. The numerical example we used is a trajectory classification problem. This problem, making a feature of variable sampling rates, having internal states, continu(cid:173) ous dynamics, heavily time-warped data and deformed phase space trajectories, is shown to be difficult to other schemes. With TWINN this problem has been learned in 100 iterations. For benchmark we also trained the exact same problem with TDNN and completely failed as expected.

paragraphs: The same continuous trajectory can be sampled or performed at different speeds, making a fixed temporal representation unreliable. Time Warping Invariant Neural Networks modify a recurrent architecture to remove that variation. The paper studies how continuous-time structure changes both invariance and memory of earlier inputs.

The analysis argues that TWINN can eliminate time warping in the considered formulation and retain longer input history than the compared neural-network finite automaton. The authors relate this memory property to difficulties encountered when training finite-automaton models on long strings. The architecture therefore addresses sequence representation as well as timing variability.

A trajectory-classification example combines variable sampling rates, internal state, continuous dynamics, and distorted paths. TWINN learns the task in 100 iterations, while the tested time-delay network fails. The contribution demonstrates how an architectural treatment of temporal continuity can handle a difficult timing-sensitive problem, with the comparative result tied to that constructed example.
summary.tldr: TWINN modifies recurrent processing to handle time-warped continuous trajectories and succeeds on a difficult trajectory-classification example.

title: Time Warping Invariant Neural Networks

abstract: This paper introduces a new recognition-based segmentation ap(cid:173) proach to recognizing on-line cursive handwriting from a database of 10,000 English words. The original input stream of z, y pen coor(cid:173) dinates is encoded as a sequence of uniform stroke descriptions that are processed by six feed-forward neural-networks, each designed to recognize letters of different sizes. Words are then recognized by performing best-first search over the space of all possible segmen(cid:173) tations. Results demonstrate that the method is effective at both writer dependent recognition (1.7% to 15.5% error rate) and writer independent recognition (5.2% to 31.1% error rate).

The original input stream of z, y pen coor(cid:173) dinates is encoded as a sequence of uniform stroke descriptions that are processed by six feed-forward neural-networks, each designed to recognize letters of different sizes. Words are then recognized by performing best-first search over the space of all possible segmen(cid:173) tations. paragraphs: The paper tackles cursive handwriting by using recognition to help decide where letters begin and end. Joined writing admits multiple possible segmentations, so the system considers letter recognition and word segmentation together. It operates on online handwriting, where the input is a stream of pen coordinates.

The coordinate stream is converted into a sequence of uniform stroke descriptions. Six feed-forward neural networks process these descriptions, with different networks intended to recognize letters of different sizes. A best-first search then explores possible segmentations to recognize the word. This makes the choice of segmentation depend on the recognition process rather than fixing all boundaries in advance.

The study uses a database of 10,000 English words. Reported error rates range from 1.7% to 15.5% for writer-dependent recognition and from 5.2% to 31.1% for writer-independent recognition. These findings demonstrate the method in both settings while showing different reported ranges. The central contribution is the combination of stroke encoding, multiple letter recognizers, and search over alternative word segmentations.
summary.tldr: Six neural letter recognizers and best-first search jointly segment and recognize online cursive words.

title: Recognition-based Segmentation of On-Line Cursive Handwriting

abstract: We describe an analog VLSI implementation of the ARTI algorithm (Carpenter, 1987). A prototype chip has been fabricated in a standard low cost 1.5~m double-metal single-poly CMOS process. It has a die area of lcm2 and is mounted in a 12O-pins PGA package. The chip realizes a modified version of the original ARTI architecture. Such modification has been shown to preserve all computational properties of the original algorithm (Serrano, 1994a), while being more appropriate for VLSI realizations. The chip implements an ARTI network with 100 F 1 nodes and 18 F2 nodes. It can therefore cluster 100 binary pixels input patterns into up to 18 different categories. Modular expansibility of the system is possible by assembling an NxM array of chips without any extra interfacing circuitry, resulting in an F 1 layer with l00xN nodes, and an F2 layer with 18xM nodes. Pattern classification is performed in less than 1.8~s, which means an equivalent computing power of 2.2x109 connections and connection-updates per second. Although internally the chip is analog in nature, it interfaces to the outside world through digital signals, thus having a true asynchrounous digital behavior. Experimental chip test results are available, which have been obtained through test equipments for digital chips.

paragraphs: This paper presents a fabricated analog chip implementing a modified ART1 clustering network. The modification makes the architecture more suitable for integrated circuitry while preserving the original algorithm's computational properties. The contribution includes working hardware and experimental chip tests, bringing the clustering procedure into a physical implementation.

A single chip contains 100 input-layer nodes and 18 category-layer nodes, allowing it to cluster patterns of 100 binary pixels into as many as 18 categories. The design also supports expansion through an array of chips without additional interfacing circuitry. Increasing one array dimension enlarges the input layer, while increasing the other expands the category layer.

Although the internal computation is analog, the chip communicates with external equipment using digital signals and behaves asynchronously. That interface allows testing with equipment intended for digital chips. The abstract reports an equivalent processing rate of 2.2 billion connections and connection updates per second. Together, the implementation and expansion scheme show how specialized neural hardware can combine analog computation with digital system integration.
summary.tldr: A fabricated ART1 clustering chip combines analog computation, digital interfaces, and modular expansion for rapid binary-pattern classification.

title: A Real Time Clustering CMOS Neural Engine

abstract: We present a hypothesis about how the cerebellum could partici(cid:173) pate in regulating movement in the presence of significant feedback delays without resorting to a forward model of the motor plant. We show how a simplified cerebellar model can learn to control end(cid:173) point positioning of a nonlinear spring-mass system with realistic delays in both afferent and efferent pathways. The model's opera(cid:173) tion involves prediction, but instead of predicting sensory input, it directly regulates movement by reacting in an anticipatory fashion to input patterns that include delayed sensory feedback.
originalAbstract: We present a hypothesis about how the cerebellum could partici(cid:173) pate in regulating movement in the presence of significant feedback delays without resorting to a forward model of the motor plant. We show how a simplified cerebellar model can learn to control end(cid:173) point positioning of a nonlinear spring-mass system with realistic delays in both afferent and efferent pathways. The model's opera(cid:173) tion involves prediction, but instead of predicting sensory input, it directly regulates movement by reacting in an anticipatory fashion to input patterns that include delayed sensory feedback.

paragraphs: Movement control becomes difficult when sensory feedback arrives late and motor commands also take time to act. This paper proposes a hypothesis about how the cerebellum could help regulate movement despite both delays. The central idea is that a controller can learn to act in anticipation of what will happen without explicitly forecasting the sensory input it will receive.

The authors demonstrate the idea with a simplified cerebellar model controlling the endpoint position of a nonlinear spring–mass system. The setup includes realistic delays in the pathways carrying sensory information and outgoing commands. The model learns to regulate movement using input patterns that include the delayed feedback.

Prediction therefore appears in the controller's responses: it reacts early enough to influence subsequent movement. This differs from building a forward model of the controlled system to predict future sensory observations. The result supports an alternative computational account of cerebellar involvement in delayed control, demonstrated through learned positioning in the simplified mechanical system.
summary.tldr: A simplified cerebellar model learns anticipatory movement control despite feedback delays without explicitly predicting future sensory input.

title: A Predictive Switching Model of Cerebellar Movement Control

abstract: Up-propagation is an algorithm for inverting and learning neural network generative models Sensory input is processed by inverting a model that generates patterns from hidden variables using topdown connections The inversion process is iterative utilizing a negative feedback loop that depends on an error signal propagated by bottomup connections The error signal is also used to learn the generative model from examples The algorithm is benchmarked against principal component analysis in experiments on images of handwritten digits.
originalAbstract: Up-propagation is an algorithm for inverting and learning neural network generative models Sensory input is processed by inverting a model that generates patterns from hidden variables using topdown connections The inversion process is iterative utilizing a negative feedback loop that depends on an error signal propagated by bottomup connections The error signal is also used to learn the generative model from examples The algorithm is benchmarked against principal component analysis in experiments on images of handwritten digits.

paragraphs: This paper introduces up-propagation, an algorithm for both interpreting observations with a neural generative model and learning that model from examples. The generative model uses top-down connections to produce patterns from hidden variables. Processing sensory input requires reversing that relationship: finding hidden-variable values that account for the observed pattern.

The inversion is iterative. A negative-feedback loop uses an error signal carried through bottom-up connections to revise the model's interpretation of the input. Top-down generation and bottom-up error propagation therefore work together, with the error communicating the mismatch that the ongoing inference process needs to address.

The same error signal also trains the generative model, connecting inference and learning through a shared mechanism. The authors benchmark the algorithm against principal component analysis using images of handwritten digits. That experiment places the method alongside another approach to representing image variation. The central contribution is an explicit feedback procedure that uses a generative network both to explain incoming patterns and to learn from them.
summary.tldr: Up-propagation uses bottom-up error feedback to infer hidden variables and train a top-down neural generative model.

title: Learning Generative Models with the Up Propagation Algorithm

abstract: The ARTMAP-FD neural network performs both identification (placing test patterns in classes encountered during training) and familiarity discrimination (judging whether a test pattern belongs to any of the classes encountered during training). The perfor(cid:173) mance of ARTMAP-FD is tested on radar pulse data obtained in the field, and compared to that of the nearest-neighbor-based NEN algorithm and to a k > 1 extension of NEN.
originalAbstract: The ARTMAP-FD neural network performs both identification (placing test patterns in classes encountered during training) and familiarity discrimination (judging whether a test pattern belongs to any of the classes encountered during training). The perfor(cid:173) mance of ARTMAP-FD is tested on radar pulse data obtained in the field, and compared to that of the nearest-neighbor-based NEN algorithm and to a k > 1 extension of NEN.

paragraphs: This paper examines a neural network called ARTMAP-FD on radar pulse data collected in the field. The network performs two related tasks. Identification assigns a test pattern to a class encountered during training. Familiarity discrimination asks whether the pattern belongs to any of the classes represented in that training experience.

The distinction changes what a successful recognition system must decide. Naming a familiar class addresses which known category fits a pattern; judging familiarity addresses whether the known categories cover it at all. By including both tasks, the paper treats recognition as involving both a class assignment and a judgment about the applicability of the learned class set.

The evaluation compares ARTMAP-FD with NEN, a nearest-neighbor-based algorithm, and with an extension of NEN that uses a value of k greater than one. The stated contribution is an empirical examination of these methods on field radar data. The supplied abstract establishes the tasks and comparison being studied, without specifying a winning method or a numerical performance outcome.
summary.tldr: ARTMAP-FD is evaluated on field radar pulses for both class identification and deciding whether a pulse belongs to any learned class.

title: Familiarity Discrimination of Radar Pulses

abstract: A flexible pattern-matching analog classifier is presented in con- junction with a robust image representation algorithm called Prin- cipal Axes Projection (PAP). In the circuit, the functional form of matching is configurable in terms of the peak position, the peak height and the sharpness of the similarity evaluation. The test chip was fabri- cated in a 0.6-m m CMOS technology and successfully applied to hand-written pattern recognition and medical radiograph analysis using PAP as a feature extraction pre-processing step for robust image coding. The separation and classification of overlapping patterns is also ex- perimentally demonstrated.
originalAbstract: A flexible pattern-matching analog classifier is presented in con- junction with a robust image representation algorithm called Prin- cipal Axes Projection (PAP). In the circuit, the functional form of matching is configurable in terms of the peak position, the peak height and the sharpness of the similarity evaluation. The test chip was fabri- cated in a 0.6-m m CMOS technology and successfully applied to hand-written pattern recognition and medical radiograph analysis using PAP as a feature extraction pre-processing step for robust image coding. The separation and classification of overlapping patterns is also ex- perimentally demonstrated.

paragraphs: The paper presents an analog circuit for flexible pattern matching, paired with an image representation method called Principal Axes Projection, or PAP. The system combines a preprocessing stage that extracts image features with a hardware stage that evaluates similarity. This connects the way an image is encoded to the circuit that classifies its resulting representation.

The matching response can be configured through its peak position, peak height, and sharpness. These controls change where the similarity response is strongest, how strong that response is, and how narrowly it is concentrated. That flexibility is central to the proposed soft-matching classifier because the form of the similarity evaluation is adjustable.

The authors fabricated a test chip and successfully applied it to handwritten pattern recognition and medical radiograph analysis, using PAP for robust image coding. They also experimentally demonstrated separation and classification of overlapping patterns. These results establish operation in physical hardware and show the combined representation-and-classification approach working in the reported image tasks.
summary.tldr: An adjustable analog similarity circuit, combined with Principal Axes Projection, demonstrates recognition of handwritten, radiographic, and overlapping patterns.

title: Analog Soft-Pattern-Matching Classifier using Floating-Gate MOS Technology

abstract: Singularities are ubiquitous in the parameter space of hierarchical models such as multilayer perceptrons. At singularities, the Fisher information matrix degenerates, and the Cramer-Rao paradigm does no more hold, implying that the classical model selection the(cid:173) ory such as AIC and MDL cannot be applied. It is important to study the relation between the generalization error and the training error at singularities. The present paper demonstrates a method of analyzing these errors both for the maximum likelihood estima(cid:173) tor and the Bayesian predictive distribution in terms of Gaussian random fields, by using simple models.

At singularities, the Fisher information matrix degenerates, and the Cramer-Rao paradigm does no more hold, implying that the classical model selection the(cid:173) ory such as AIC and MDL cannot be applied. It is important to study the relation between the generalization error and the training error at singularities. paragraphs: The paper examines singularities in the parameter spaces of hierarchical models such as multilayer perceptrons. These are points where the Fisher information matrix becomes degenerate. Because that matrix underlies standard statistical reasoning about parameter estimation, its degeneration means that the usual Cramer-Rao framework no longer applies at those points.

This creates a problem for understanding the relationship between training error and generalization error. Classical model selection theory, including the AIC and MDL approaches identified in the abstract, cannot simply be applied at these singularities. The authors therefore focus on analyzing prediction behavior in precisely the setting where the standard theoretical foundations break down.

Using simple models, the paper demonstrates an analysis based on Gaussian random fields. It treats both maximum likelihood estimators and Bayesian predictive distributions, allowing the training–generalization relationship to be studied for each. The contribution is a method for examining errors in singular models. Its significance lies in addressing statistical behavior that ordinary regular-model analysis does not cover, using simple cases to demonstrate the approach.
summary.tldr: Gaussian random fields provide a way to analyze training and generalization errors where neural model singularities invalidate standard statistical theory.

title: Geometrical Singularities in the Neuromanifold of Multilayer Perceptrons

abstract: This paper presents a neuromorphic model of two olfactory signal- processing primitives: chemotopic convergence of olfactory receptor neurons, and center on-off surround lateral inhibition in the olfactory bulb. A self-organizing model of receptor convergence onto glomeruli is used to generate a spatially organized map, an olfactory image. This map serves as input to a lattice of spiking neurons with lateral connections. The dynamics of this recurrent network transforms the initial olfactory image into a spatio-temporal pattern that evolves and stabilizes into odor- and intensity-coding attractors. The model is validated using experimental data from an array of temperature-modulated gas sensors. Our results are consistent with recent neurobiological findings on the antennal lobe of the honeybee and the locust.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a neuromorphic model of two olfactory signal- processing primitives: chemotopic convergence of olfactory receptor neurons, and center on-off surround lateral inhibition in the olfactory bulb. A self-organizing model of receptor convergence onto glomeruli is used to generate a spatially organized map, an olfactory image. This map serves as input to a lattice of spiking neurons with lateral connections. The dynamics of this recurrent network transforms the initial olfactory image into a spatio-temporal pattern that evolves and stabilizes into odor- and intensity-coding attractors. The model is validated using experimental data from an array of temperature-modulated gas sensors. Our results are consistent with recent neurobiological findings on the antennal lobe of the honeybee and the locust.

paragraphs: The paper models two stages of smell processing: organizing receptor signals into a spatial map and transforming that map through lateral inhibition. The first stage uses a self-organizing model of receptor convergence onto glomeruli. Its output is an olfactory image, a spatial arrangement of information about the chemical input.

That image enters a lattice of spiking neurons with lateral connections. Through recurrent activity, the network changes the initial spatial representation into a pattern that develops over both space and time. The activity eventually stabilizes into attractors that encode odor and intensity. Thus, the representation is shaped by the network's dynamics after the initial receptor map has been formed.

The authors validate the model using experimental measurements from temperature-modulated gas sensors. They also report that its results are consistent with neurobiological findings concerning the honeybee and locust antennal lobe. The findings support this combination of organized receptor input and recurrent inhibition as a model of chemosensory processing, with evidence from sensor data and consistency with biological observations.
summary.tldr: A self-organizing receptor map and recurrent spiking network produce stable patterns encoding odor and intensity.

title: Chemosensory Processing in a Spiking Model of the Olfactory Bulb: Chemotopic Convergence and Center Surround Inhibition

abstract: This paper presents a diffusion based probabilistic interpretation of spectral clustering and dimensionality reduction algorithms that use the eigenvectors of the normalized graph Laplacian. Given the pairwise adjacency matrix of all points, we define a diffusion distance between any two data points and show that the low dimensional representation of the data by the first few eigenvectors of the corresponding Markov matrix is optimal under a certain mean squared error criterion. Furthermore, assuming that data points are random samples from a density p(x) = e-U (x) we identify these eigenvectors as discrete approximations of eigenfunctions of a Fokker-Planck operator in a potential 2U (x) with reflecting boundary conditions. Finally, applying known results regarding the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the continuous Fokker-Planck operator, we provide a mathematical justification for the success of spectral clustering and dimensional reduction algorithms based on these first few eigenvectors. This analysis elucidates, in terms of the characteristics of diffusion processes, many empirical findings regarding spectral clustering algorithms. Keywords: Algorithms and architectures, learning theory.

abstract: The estimation of high-dimensional parametric models requires imposing some structure on the models, for instance that they be sparse, or that matrix structured parameters have low rank. A general approach for such structured parametric model estimation is to use regularized M-estimation procedures, which regularize a loss function that measures goodness of fit of the parameters to the data with some regularization function that encourages the assumed structure. In this paper, we aim to provide a unified analysis of such regularized M-estimation procedures. In particular, we report the convergence rates of such estimators in any metric norm. Using just our main theorem, we are able to rederive some of the many existing results, but also obtain a wide range of novel convergence rates results. Our analysis also identifies key properties of loss and regularization functions such as restricted strong convexity, and decomposability, that ensure the corresponding regularized M-estimators have good convergence rates.

Regularized M-estimation combines a loss measuring agreement with the data and a penalty encouraging the chosen structure. This paper develops a common framework for analyzing the accuracy of these procedures.

The main contribution is a theorem giving convergence rates measured in any metric norm. Such rates describe how estimation error changes as information accumulates. Applying the same theorem lets the authors recover existing results and derive a range of new ones, bringing analyses of different structured estimation problems into a shared mathematical framework.

The analysis highlights restricted strong convexity of the loss and decomposability of the regularizer as key properties supporting good convergence rates. These properties connect the behavior of the fitting objective with the structure encouraged by the penalty. The practical significance is analytical: researchers can examine these common conditions when studying an estimator instead of developing an entirely separate argument for every formulation.
summary.tldr: A unified theorem establishes convergence rates for structured regularized estimators and identifies loss and penalty properties that support accurate estimation.

title: A unified framework for high-dimensional analysis of $M$-estimators with decomposable regularizers

abstract: Activity of a neuron, even in the early sensory areas, is not simply a function of its local receptive field or tuning properties, but depends on global context of the stimulus, as well as the neural context. This suggests the activity of the surrounding neurons and global brain states can exert considerable influence on the activity of a neuron. In this paper we implemented an L1 regularized point process model to assess the contribution of multiple factors to the firing rate of many individual units recorded simultaneously from V1 with a 96-electrode Utah" array. We found that the spikes of surrounding neurons indeed provide strong predictions of a neuron's response, in addition to the neuron's receptive field transfer function. We also found that the same spikes could be accounted for with the local field potentials, a surrogate measure of global network states. This work shows that accounting for network fluctuations can improve estimates of single trial firing rate and stimulus-response transfer functions."

This paper examines how accounting for that context changes predictions of individual neurons' firing rates, using simultaneous recordings from V1 collected with a 96-electrode array.

The authors use an L1-regularized point-process model to assess several contributions to neural firing. The model incorporates information beyond the neuron's receptive-field response. They find that spikes from nearby neurons provide strong additional predictions of a neuron's activity. Local field potentials, used as a proxy for broader network states, can also account for those spikes.

These findings indicate that some variability in individual responses becomes more predictable when network fluctuations are included. Accounting for that context can improve estimates of firing rates on individual trials and of the relationship between stimuli and responses. The reported predictive relationships support incorporating network information without, by themselves, establishing direct causal connections between particular neurons.
summary.tldr: Including neighboring spikes or local field potentials can improve models of individual neurons' firing rates and stimulus responses.

title: Accounting for network effects in neuronal responses using L1 regularized point process models

abstract: Sparse PCA provides a linear combination of small number of features that maximizes variance across data. Although Sparse PCA has apparent advantages compared to PCA, such as better interpretability, it is generally thought to be computationally much more expensive. In this paper, we demonstrate the surprising fact that sparse PCA can be easier than PCA in practice, and that it can be reliably applied to very large data sets. This comes from a rigorous feature elimination pre-processing result, coupled with the favorable fact that features in real-life data typically have exponentially decreasing variances, which allows for many features to be eliminated. We introduce a fast block coordinate ascent algorithm with much better computational complexity than the existing first-order ones. We provide experimental results obtained on text corpora involving millions of documents and hundreds of thousands of features. These results illustrate how Sparse PCA can help organize a large corpus of text data in a user-interpretable way, providing an attractive alternative approach to topic models.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks directions of high variation that use only a small number of features. This can make the resulting components easier to interpret, but sparse PCA is commonly viewed as more computationally expensive than ordinary PCA. The paper shows that the sparse version can actually be easier in practice on large datasets.

The approach combines a rigorous feature-elimination preprocessing result with a favorable property of real data: feature variances typically decrease exponentially. That pattern allows many features to be removed before optimization. The authors also introduce a fast block coordinate ascent algorithm with substantially better computational complexity than existing first-order approaches.

Experiments use text collections with millions of documents and hundreds of thousands of features. They illustrate that sparse PCA can operate at this scale while organizing documents through components people can interpret. The result makes sparse PCA an attractive alternative to topic models for this purpose, while grounding the computational advantage in useful data structure rather than claiming that sparsity always makes optimization easier.
summary.tldr: Feature elimination and fast block coordinate ascent make sparse PCA practical for massive text collections and sometimes easier than ordinary PCA.

title: Large-Scale Sparse Principal Component Analysis with Application to Text Data

abstract: Reinforcement learning models address animal's behavioral adaptation to its changing "external" environment, and are based on the assumption that Pavlovian, habitual and goal-directed responses seek to maximize reward acquisition. Negative-feedback models of homeostatic regulation, on the other hand, are concerned with behavioral adaptation in response to the "internal" state of the animal, and assume that animals' behavioral objective is to minimize deviations of some key physiological variables from their hypothetical setpoints. Building upon the drive-reduction theory of reward, we propose a new analytical framework that integrates learning and regulatory systems, such that the two seemingly unrelated objectives of reward maximization and physiological-stability prove to be identical. The proposed theory shows behavioral adaptation to both internal and external states in a disciplined way. We further show that the proposed framework allows for a unified explanation of some behavioral phenomenon like motivational sensitivity of different associative learning mechanism, anticipatory responses, interaction among competing motivational systems, and risk aversion.

Reinforcement learning describes behavior through reward maximization, while homeostatic regulation describes it through reducing departures from physiological setpoints. The authors ask how these objectives can fit into one analytical framework.

Their approach builds on drive-reduction theory, linking reward to the reduction of physiological need. Within the proposed framework, maximizing reward and maintaining physiological stability become equivalent objectives. This provides a way to describe behavioral adaptation using both the animal's internal state and the external circumstances in which it acts.

The authors also show how this framework can jointly explain several behavioral phenomena: changes in associative learning with motivation, anticipatory responses, competition between motivational systems, and risk aversion. The contribution is a theoretical connection that gives these phenomena a shared explanation. The equivalence belongs to the proposed model, rather than establishing that every form of animal reward necessarily serves physiological regulation.
summary.tldr: A drive-reduction framework makes reward maximization and physiological stability equivalent within one theory of learning and regulation.

title: A Reinforcement Learning Theory for Homeostatic Regulation

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating Shannon's entropy H in the under-sampled regime, where the number of possible symbols may be unknown or countably infinite. Pitman-Yor processes (a generalization of Dirichlet processes) provide tractable prior distributions over the space of countably infinite discrete distributions, and have found major applications in Bayesian non-parametric statistics and machine learning. Here we show that they also provide natural priors for Bayesian entropy estimation, due to the remarkable fact that the moments of the induced posterior distribution over H can be computed analytically. We derive formulas for the posterior mean (Bayes' least squares estimate) and variance under such priors. Moreover, we show that a fixed Dirichlet or Pitman-Yor process prior implies a narrow prior on H, meaning the prior strongly determines the entropy estimate in the under-sampled regime. We derive a family of continuous mixing measures such that the resulting mixture of Pitman-Yor processes produces an approximately flat (improper) prior over H. We explore the theoretical properties of the resulting estimator, and show that it performs well on data sampled from both exponential and power-law tailed distributions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate Shannon entropy when observations are scarce relative to the possible symbols. The number of symbols may be unknown or countably infinite. In this setting, the observed sample leaves substantial uncertainty about the underlying discrete distribution, making the choice of Bayesian prior especially consequential.

The authors use Pitman–Yor processes as priors over discrete distributions and show that posterior moments of entropy can be calculated analytically. They derive both the posterior mean, which gives the least-squares Bayesian estimate, and the posterior variance. However, a fixed Dirichlet or Pitman–Yor process places entropy in a narrow prior range, allowing that prior to strongly influence estimates when data are limited.

To address this influence, the paper constructs continuous mixtures of Pitman–Yor processes that yield an approximately flat, improper prior over entropy. It investigates the resulting estimator theoretically and reports good performance on samples from distributions with exponential and power-law tails. The contribution connects tractable uncertainty calculations with a deliberate treatment of prior sensitivity.
summary.tldr: Mixtures of Pitman–Yor priors support tractable entropy estimation while addressing strong prior influence when discrete data are undersampled.

title: Bayesian estimation of discrete entropy with mixtures of stick-breaking priors

abstract: Max-product ‘belief propagation’ (BP) is a popular distributed heuristic for finding the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) assignment in a joint probability distribution represented by a Graphical Model (GM). It was recently shown that BP converges to the correct MAP assignment for a class of loopy GMs with the following common feature: the Linear Programming (LP) relaxation to the MAP problem is tight (has no integrality gap). Unfortunately, tightness of the LP relaxation does not, in general, guarantee convergence and correctness of the BP algorithm. The failure of BP in such cases motivates reverse engineering a solution – namely, given a tight LP, can we design a ‘good’ BP algorithm. In this paper, we design a BP algorithm for the Maximum Weight Matching (MWM) problem over general graphs. We prove that the algorithm converges to the correct optimum if the respective LP relaxation, which may include inequalities associated with non-intersecting odd-sized cycles, is tight. The most significant part of our approach is the introduction of a novel graph transformation designed to force convergence of BP. Our theoretical result suggests an efficient BP-based heuristic for the MWM problem, which consists of making sequential, “cutting plane”, modifications to the underlying GM. Our experiments show that this heuristic performs as well as traditional cutting-plane algorithms using LP solvers on MWM problems.

paragraphs: Max-product belief propagation is a distributed method for seeking the most probable assignment in a graphical model. A tight linear-programming relaxation can help characterize an optimization problem, but tightness alone does not generally ensure that belief propagation converges or returns the correct answer. This paper addresses that gap for maximum weight matching.

The authors introduce a graph transformation designed to make belief propagation converge. For their matching algorithm, they prove convergence to the correct optimum when the corresponding linear-programming relaxation is tight. That relaxation may include inequalities associated with non-intersecting odd-sized cycles. The guarantee therefore depends on both the proposed construction and the stated tightness condition.

The theory motivates a heuristic that repeatedly modifies the graphical model through cutting-plane steps. This connects a message-passing algorithm to a strategy for strengthening an optimization formulation. In the reported matching experiments, the heuristic performs as well as traditional cutting-plane methods using linear-programming solvers, supporting its practical promise alongside the conditional theoretical result.
summary.tldr: A graph transformation gives a belief-propagation matching algorithm a correctness guarantee when its specified linear-programming relaxation is tight.

title: A Graphical Transformation for Belief Propagation: Maximum Weight Matchings and Odd-Sized Cycles

abstract: This paper extends factorized asymptotic Bayesian (FAB) inference for latent feature models~(LFMs). FAB inference has not been applicable to models, including LFMs, without a specific condition on the Hesqsian matrix of a complete log-likelihood, which is required to derive a factorized information criterion''~(FIC). Our asymptotic analysis of the Hessian matrix of LFMs shows that FIC of LFMs has the same form as those of mixture models. FAB/LFMs have several desirable properties (e.g., automatic hidden states selection and parameter identifiability) and empirically perform better than state-of-the-art Indian Buffet processes in terms of model selection, prediction, and computational efficiency."

paragraphs: Latent feature models explain observations through hidden features, making both inference and the choice of hidden structure central concerns. This paper extends factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference, abbreviated FAB, to these models. The obstacle was a condition on the Hessian of the complete log-likelihood needed to derive the factorized information criterion, or FIC.

The authors analyze the Hessian for latent feature models asymptotically. Their analysis shows that the resulting FIC has the same form as the criteria used for mixture models. This provides the mathematical connection needed to bring latent feature models into the FAB framework despite the earlier applicability barrier.

The resulting approach has properties including automatic hidden-state selection and parameter identifiability. In the reported empirical comparisons, it performs better than state-of-the-art Indian Buffet process methods in model selection, prediction, and computational efficiency. These results support the extension on several practical dimensions: choosing hidden structure, using it for predictions, and carrying out the required computation.
summary.tldr: An asymptotic Hessian analysis extends FAB inference to latent feature models, with favorable reported results for model selection, prediction, and efficiency.

title: Factorized Asymptotic Bayesian Inference for Latent Feature Models

abstract: We study exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits (MAB) in a setting where~$k$ players collaborate in order to identify an $\epsilon$-optimal arm. Our motivation comes from recent employment of MAB algorithms in computationally intensive, large-scale applications. Our results demonstrate a non-trivial tradeoff between the number of arm pulls required by each of the players, and the amount of communication between them. In particular, our main result shows that by allowing the $k$ players to communicate \emph{only once}, they are able to learn $\sqrt{k}$ times faster than a single player. That is, distributing learning to $k$ players gives rise to a factor~$\sqrt{k}$ parallel speed-up. We complement this result with a lower bound showing this is in general the best possible. On the other extreme, we present an algorithm that achieves the ideal factor $k$ speed-up in learning performance, with communication only logarithmic in~$1/\epsilon$.

paragraphs: The paper studies several players collaborating to find a nearly best option in a multi-armed bandit problem. Each player can gather evidence by pulling arms, and the shared target is an arm within epsilon of optimal. The question is how much parallel exploration helps when communication is limited.

With k players and only one opportunity to communicate, the authors establish a square-root-of-k speedup relative to one player. A matching lower bound shows that this is generally the best possible improvement under that communication restriction. Having more players therefore does not automatically produce a proportional reduction in each player's exploration burden.

With additional communication, the paper gives an algorithm that reaches the ideal factor-k speedup. Its communication requirement grows only logarithmically with inverse epsilon. Together, the results describe a concrete tradeoff between gathering more observations locally and exchanging information across players. This matters for computationally intensive applications because distributing work and coordinating that work are separate resources, and the available coordination changes the achievable benefit of parallel learning.
summary.tldr: Collaborating bandit players achieve a square-root-of-k speedup with one communication round and a factor-k speedup with more communication.

title: Distributed Exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: In large-scale applications of undirected graphical models, such as social networks and biological networks, similar patterns occur frequently and give rise to similar parameters. In this situation, it is beneficial to group the parameters for more efficient learning. We show that even when the grouping is unknown, we can infer these parameter groups during learning via a Bayesian approach. We impose a Dirichlet process prior on the parameters. Posterior inference usually involves calculating intractable terms, and we propose two approximation algorithms, namely a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with auxiliary variables and a Gibbs sampling algorithm with stripped Beta approximation (Gibbs SBA). Simulations show that both algorithms outperform conventional maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). Gibbs SBA's performance is close to Gibbs sampling with exact likelihood calculation. Models learned with Gibbs_SBA also generalize better than the models learned by MLE on real-world Senate voting data.

paragraphs: Large network models can contain recurring patterns whose associated parameters are similar. Learning these parameters in groups can make estimation more efficient, but the useful groups may not be known beforehand. This paper develops a Bayesian approach that infers the grouping while learning an undirected graphical model, rather than requiring a separate, predetermined assignment of parameters to groups.

The method places a Dirichlet process prior on the parameters to represent their unknown grouping. Computing the resulting posterior involves intractable quantities, so the authors introduce two approximate inference algorithms. One uses Metropolis-Hastings sampling with auxiliary variables; the other uses Gibbs sampling with a stripped Beta approximation, called Gibbs SBA.

In simulations, both algorithms outperform conventional maximum likelihood estimation. Gibbs SBA also performs close to Gibbs sampling that calculates the likelihood exactly. On Senate voting data, models learned with Gibbs SBA generalize better than those learned by maximum likelihood. These findings support learning shared parameter structure alongside the model, while using approximation to make the Bayesian computation feasible.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian method discovers parameter groups in undirected graphical models and improves estimation over maximum likelihood in the reported evaluations.

title: Bayesian Estimation of Latently-grouped Parameters in Undirected Graphical Models

abstract: The beta-negative binomial process (BNBP), an integer-valued stochastic process, is employed to partition a count vector into a latent random count matrix. As the marginal probability distribution of the BNBP that governs the exchangeable random partitions of grouped data has not yet been developed, current inference for the BNBP has to truncate the number of atoms of the beta process. This paper introduces an exchangeable partition probability function to explicitly describe how the BNBP clusters the data points of each group into a random number of exchangeable partitions, which are shared across all the groups. A fully collapsed Gibbs sampler is developed for the BNBP, leading to a novel nonparametric Bayesian topic model that is distinct from existing ones, with simple implementation, fast convergence, good mixing, and state-of-the-art predictive performance.

paragraphs: The beta-negative binomial process models counts by splitting an observed count vector into an unobserved count matrix. For grouped data, this creates a way to represent memberships in shared latent components. Existing inference required truncating the beta process because the marginal distribution governing the resulting partitions had not been developed.

This paper supplies an exchangeable partition probability function that explicitly describes those partitions. Each group can divide its data among a random number of clusters, with clusters shared across groups. Exchangeability makes the partition description independent of the ordering of the data points. The new formulation gives a direct probabilistic account of how the process clusters grouped observations.

The authors use that account to develop a fully collapsed Gibbs sampler and a new nonparametric Bayesian topic model. They report simple implementation, fast convergence, good mixing, and state-of-the-art predictive performance. The contribution connects a missing mathematical description to a practical inference method: explicitly characterizing the partitions enables a different way to fit a model with shared, variable-sized latent structure.
summary.tldr: An explicit partition distribution for the beta-negative binomial process enables fully collapsed inference and a new Bayesian topic model.

title: Beta-Negative Binomial Process and Exchangeable ￼Random Partitions for Mixed-Membership Modeling

abstract: Communication remains the most significant bottleneck in the performance of distributed optimization algorithms for large-scale machine learning. In this paper, we propose a communication-efficient framework, COCOA, that uses local computation in a primal-dual setting to dramatically reduce the amount of necessary communication. We provide a strong convergence rate analysis for this class of algorithms, as well as experiments on real-world distributed datasets with implementations in Spark. In our experiments, we find that as compared to state-of-the-art mini-batch versions of SGD and SDCA algorithms, COCOA converges to the same .001-accurate solution quality on average 25× as quickly.

paragraphs: Distributing machine-learning optimization across computers creates a cost beyond the calculations themselves: the computers must communicate. This paper treats that communication as a major performance bottleneck. It introduces COCOA, a framework that uses local computation to substantially reduce the communication required during distributed optimization.

COCOA operates in a primal-dual setting, connecting the original optimization problem with its dual formulation. The key design choice is to make productive use of computation performed locally, so progress requires less information exchange across the distributed system. The authors provide a strong convergence-rate analysis for the resulting class of algorithms, giving theoretical support to the framework.

They also implement the approach in Spark and test it on real-world distributed datasets. In those experiments, COCOA reaches the same 0.001-accurate solution quality an average of 25 times faster than the compared state-of-the-art mini-batch SGD and SDCA methods. This is an experimental average for the reported comparisons. It illustrates how reducing communication can translate into substantially faster optimization while maintaining the target solution quality.
summary.tldr: COCOA uses local primal-dual computation to reduce communication and achieves a reported average 25-fold speedup in distributed experiments.

title: Communication-Efficient Distributed Dual Coordinate Ascent

abstract: We propose an original particle-based implementation of the Loopy Belief Propagation (LPB) algorithm for pairwise Markov Random Fields (MRF) on a continuous state space. The algorithm constructs adaptively efficient proposal distributions approximating the local beliefs at each note of the MRF. This is achieved by considering proposal distributions in the exponential family whose parameters are updated iterately in an Expectation Propagation (EP) framework. The proposed particle scheme provides consistent estimation of the LBP marginals as the number of particles increases. We demonstrate that it provides more accurate results than the Particle Belief Propagation (PBP) algorithm of Ihler and McAllester (2009) at a fraction of the computational cost and is additionally more robust empirically. The computational complexity of our algorithm at each iteration is quadratic in the number of particles. We also propose an accelerated implementation with sub-quadratic computational complexity which still provides consistent estimates of the loopy BP marginal distributions and performs almost as well as the original procedure.

paragraphs: This paper develops a particle-based implementation of loopy belief propagation for pairwise Markov random fields with continuous states. Its main concern is where to place particles so that they efficiently represent each node's local belief. Poorly matched proposal distributions can waste computation on particles that contribute little to that representation.

The method adapts proposals from an exponential family, repeatedly updating their parameters through expectation propagation. The resulting particle estimates are consistent for the loopy-belief-propagation marginals as the particle count increases. The target of this consistency statement matters: it concerns the marginals produced by loopy belief propagation, rather than a separate claim that those marginals always equal the model's exact marginals.

The authors report greater accuracy, lower computational cost, and better empirical robustness than an earlier particle belief-propagation algorithm. The main implementation has per-iteration cost quadratic in particle count. An accelerated version reduces this to subquadratic cost while preserving consistency for the same target marginals, and its empirical performance is nearly as good as that of the original procedure.
summary.tldr: Adaptive particle proposals improve continuous-state loopy belief propagation, with a faster variant retaining consistent estimates of its marginals.

title: Expectation Particle Belief Propagation

abstract: We present a scalable and robust Bayesian method for demand forecasting in the context of a large e-commerce platform, paying special attention to intermittent and bursty target statistics. Inference is approximated by the Newton-Raphson algorithm, reduced to linear-time Kalman smoothing, which allows us to operate on several orders of magnitude larger problems than previous related work. In a study on large real-world sales datasets, our method outperforms competing approaches on fast and medium moving items.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Bayesian forecasting method for large e-commerce inventories, with particular attention to demand that is intermittent or arrives in bursts. These patterns make forecasting more than a matter of following a smoothly changing sales level. The proposed method aims to handle such demand while remaining practical at the scale of a large platform.

Its computational contribution is an approximation to inference using Newton-Raphson updates reduced to linear-time Kalman smoothing. This reduction makes the inference procedure scalable: the authors report handling problems several orders of magnitude larger than those addressed by earlier related work. The method's practicality therefore depends on how the Bayesian calculation is organized, as well as on the forecasting approach itself.

The evaluation uses large real-world sales datasets. On fast- and medium-moving products, the method outperforms competing approaches. This is the stated empirical performance claim, even though intermittent and bursty demand motivates the broader design. Together, the computational and forecasting findings support using the approach for large inventories with varied sales patterns.
summary.tldr: A scalable Bayesian demand forecaster uses linear-time Kalman smoothing and outperforms competing approaches on fast- and medium-moving items in large sales datasets.

title: Bayesian Intermittent Demand Forecasting for Large Inventories

abstract: Many spectral unmixing methods rely on the non-negative decomposition of spectral data onto a dictionary of spectral templates. In particular, state-of-the-art music transcription systems decompose the spectrogram of the input signal onto a dictionary of representative note spectra. The typical measures of fit used to quantify the adequacy of the decomposition compare the data and template entries frequency-wise. As such, small displacements of energy from a frequency bin to another as well as variations of timber can disproportionally harm the fit. We address these issues by means of optimal transportation and propose a new measure of fit that treats the frequency distributions of energy holistically as opposed to frequency-wise. Building on the harmonic nature of sound, the new measure is invariant to shifts of energy to harmonically-related frequencies, as well as to small and local displacements of energy. Equipped with this new measure of fit, the dictionary of note templates can be considerably simplified to a set of Dirac vectors located at the target fundamental frequencies (musical pitch values). This in turns gives ground to a very fast and simple decomposition algorithm that achieves state-of-the-art performance on real musical data.

paragraphs: Music transcription can be approached by decomposing an audio spectrogram into representative note spectra. Conventional fit measures compare individual frequency entries, so small movements of energy between bins or changes in timbre can make a reasonable match appear poor. The paper changes how the observed and template spectra are compared.

Its proposed measure uses optimal transportation to treat spectral energy as a distribution across frequencies. Incorporating the harmonic structure of sound makes the measure invariant to energy shifts between harmonically related frequencies and to small local displacements. The comparison therefore accounts for relationships among frequencies rather than relying only on entry-by-entry agreement.

This measure also simplifies the note dictionary. Full spectral templates can be replaced by Dirac vectors concentrated at the target fundamental frequencies, or musical pitches. That simplification supports a fast and simple decomposition algorithm. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on real musical data, showing how a more suitable notion of spectral fit can reduce the complexity of the representation used for transcription.
summary.tldr: A transport-based spectral fit measure enables simplified note templates and fast music transcription with state-of-the-art reported performance.

title: Optimal spectral transportation with application to music transcription

abstract: Label distribution learning (LDL) is a general learning framework, which assigns to an instance a distribution over a set of labels rather than a single label or multiple labels. Current LDL methods have either restricted assumptions on the expression form of the label distribution or limitations in representation learning, e.g., to learn deep features in an end-to-end manner. This paper presents label distribution learning forests (LDLFs) - a novel label distribution learning algorithm based on differentiable decision trees, which have several advantages: 1) Decision trees have the potential to model any general form of label distributions by a mixture of leaf node predictions. 2) The learning of differentiable decision trees can be combined with representation learning. We define a distribution-based loss function for a forest, enabling all the trees to be learned jointly, and show that an update function for leaf node predictions, which guarantees a strict decrease of the loss function, can be derived by variational bounding. The effectiveness of the proposed LDLFs is verified on several LDL tasks and a computer vision application, showing significant improvements to the state-of-the-art LDL methods.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning predicts how an instance's association is spread across labels, rather than selecting just one label or a set of labels. This paper develops a forest-based approach intended to improve both the flexibility of those distributions and the ability to learn useful features alongside the predictor.

The forest uses differentiable decision trees whose predictions combine the distributions stored at their leaves. This mixture gives trees the potential to represent general distribution shapes. Differentiability also lets tree learning be combined with representation learning, addressing the difficulty of training deep features and the final distribution predictor together.

The authors define a distribution-based objective for jointly training all trees. Through variational bounding, they derive an update for leaf predictions that guarantees a strict decrease in that loss. This is a concrete optimization property of the leaf update. Evaluations across several label distribution tasks and a computer vision application report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, supporting the combination of flexible leaf mixtures and jointly learned representations.
summary.tldr: Differentiable forests jointly learn representations and label distributions, with loss-decreasing leaf updates and strong reported empirical results.

title: Label Distribution Learning Forests

abstract: In large part, rodents “see” the world through their whiskers, a powerful tactile sense enabled by a series of brain areas that form the whisker-trigeminal system. Raw sensory data arrives in the form of mechanical input to the exquisitely sensitive, actively-controllable whisker array, and is processed through a sequence of neural circuits, eventually arriving in cortical regions that communicate with decision making and memory areas. Although a long history of experimental studies has characterized many aspects of these processing stages, the computational operations of the whisker-trigeminal system remain largely unknown. In the present work, we take a goal-driven deep neural network (DNN) approach to modeling these computations. First, we construct a biophysically-realistic model of the rat whisker array. We then generate a large dataset of whisker sweeps across a wide variety of 3D objects in highly-varying poses, angles, and speeds. Next, we train DNNs from several distinct architectural families to solve a shape recognition task in this dataset. Each architectural family represents a structurally-distinct hypothesis for processing in the whisker-trigeminal system, corresponding to different ways in which spatial and temporal information can be integrated. We find that most networks perform poorly on the challenging shape recognition task, but that specific architectures from several families can achieve reasonable performance levels. Finally, we show that Representational Dissimilarity Matrices (RDMs), a tool for comparing population codes between neural systems, can separate these higher performing networks with data of a type that could plausibly be collected in a neurophysiological or imaging experiment. Our results are a proof-of-concept that DNN models of the whisker-trigeminal system are potentially within reach.

This paper explores whether neural networks trained toward a sensory goal can provide useful candidate models of those operations.

The authors construct a biophysically realistic model of a rat's whisker array and simulate sweeps across many three-dimensional objects with varied poses, angles, and speeds. They train several families of deep networks to recognize object shape from these data. Each family represents a different hypothesis about how spatial and temporal information might be combined in the biological system.

The findings offer a proof of concept for candidate computational models and a possible way to distinguish them experimentally.
summary.tldr: Simulated whisker sensing and shape-recognition networks provide a proof of concept for testable models of rodent tactile processing.

title: Toward Goal-Driven Neural Network Models for the Rodent Whisker-Trigeminal System

abstract: Approximate probabilistic inference algorithms are central to many fields. Examples include sequential Monte Carlo inference in robotics, variational inference in machine learning, and Markov chain Monte Carlo inference in statistics. A key problem faced by practitioners is measuring the accuracy of an approximate inference algorithm on a specific data set. This paper introduces the auxiliary inference divergence estimator (AIDE), an algorithm for measuring the accuracy of approximate inference algorithms. AIDE is based on the observation that inference algorithms can be treated as probabilistic models and the random variables used within the inference algorithm can be viewed as auxiliary variables. This view leads to a new estimator for the symmetric KL divergence between the approximating distributions of two inference algorithms. The paper illustrates application of AIDE to algorithms for inference in regression, hidden Markov, and Dirichlet process mixture models. The experiments show that AIDE captures the qualitative behavior of a broad class of inference algorithms and can detect failure modes of inference algorithms that are missed by standard heuristics.

paragraphs: Approximate inference methods help answer probabilistic questions when exact calculation is difficult. A practical challenge is determining how accurately a particular method behaves on the data at hand. AIDE addresses this evaluation problem by comparing the probability distributions produced by two inference algorithms, giving practitioners a way to examine their agreement more directly.

The central idea is to treat an inference algorithm itself as a probabilistic model. Its internal random choices then become auxiliary variables that can be included in the analysis. This perspective produces an estimator of symmetric KL divergence, a measure of disagreement between two distributions that accounts for both directions of comparison. The quantity being estimated concerns the algorithms' approximating distributions.

The paper illustrates AIDE on inference for regression, hidden Markov models, and Dirichlet process mixtures. In these experiments, it captures qualitative differences in how a broad range of inference methods behave. It also detects failures missed by standard diagnostic heuristics. These findings support its usefulness as a diagnostic for approximate inference on specific datasets.
summary.tldr: AIDE estimates disagreement between two approximate inference algorithms and can expose failures missed by standard diagnostics.

title: AIDE: An algorithm for measuring the accuracy of probabilistic inference algorithms

abstract: Coupled norms have emerged as a convex method to solve coupled tensor completion. A limitation with coupled norms is that they only induce low-rankness using the multilinear rank of coupled tensors. In this paper, we introduce a new set of coupled norms known as coupled nuclear norms by constraining the CP rank of coupled tensors. We propose new coupled completion models using the coupled nuclear norms as regularizers, which can be optimized using computationally efficient optimization methods. We derive excess risk bounds for proposed coupled completion models and show that proposed norms lead to better performance. Through simulation and real-data experiments, we demonstrate that proposed norms achieve better performance for coupled completion compared to existing coupled norms.

We propose new coupled completion models using the coupled nuclear norms as regularizers, which can be optimized using computationally efficient optimization methods. paragraphs: Coupled tensor completion fills in missing entries across related multidimensional arrays. Convex coupled norms provide a way to favor simpler, low-rank structure while solving this problem. The paper identifies a restriction of existing coupled norms: they encourage low rank through multilinear rank, which is one particular way of measuring a tensor's complexity.

The authors introduce coupled nuclear norms based on constraining CP rank, a different notion of tensor rank. They use these norms as regularizers in new completion models. The change matters because the regularizer determines what kind of shared simplicity the completion procedure favors, while the proposed models remain compatible with computationally efficient optimization methods.

The work provides excess-risk bounds for the new models and reports improved performance associated with the proposed norms. Simulations and experiments on real data also show better coupled completion than existing coupled norms. Together, the theoretical and experimental results support changing the rank structure promoted by the regularizer as a useful route to better completion.
summary.tldr: New coupled nuclear norms promote CP-rank structure to improve convex completion of related tensors.

title: Efficient Convex Completion of Coupled Tensors using Coupled Nuclear Norms

abstract: We consider the minimization of submodular functions subject to ordering constraints. We show that this potentially non-convex optimization problem can be cast as a convex optimization problem on a space of uni-dimensional measures, with ordering constraints corresponding to first-order stochastic dominance. We propose new discretization schemes that lead to simple and efficient algorithms based on zero-th, first, or higher order oracles; these algorithms also lead to improvements without isotonic constraints. Finally, our experiments show that non-convex loss functions can be much more robust to outliers for isotonic regression, while still being solvable in polynomial time.
