We propose new discretization schemes that lead to simple and efficient algorithms based on zero-th, first, or higher order oracles; these algorithms also lead to improvements without isotonic constraints. Finally, our experiments show that non-convex loss functions can be much more robust to outliers for isotonic regression, while still being solvable in polynomial time.

paragraphs: Isotonic regression fits values while requiring them to respect an ordering. This paper studies optimization with such ordering constraints when the objective is submodular and potentially non-convex. The challenge is to retain the useful flexibility of non-convex objectives while finding a formulation that supports efficient computation.

The authors show that the problem can be expressed as a convex optimization problem over one-dimensional measures. In that representation, the ordering constraints become first-order stochastic-dominance constraints. The important change is the space in which optimization happens: a problem that may be non-convex in its original form receives a convex formulation in the new space.

New discretization schemes turn this formulation into algorithms using function values, first-order information, or higher-order information. The algorithms also improve optimization without isotonic constraints. In experiments, non-convex loss functions can be much more resistant to outliers in isotonic regression, while the considered problems remain solvable in polynomial time. The result connects computational tractability with an empirically useful choice of loss.
summary.tldr: A convex reformulation enables efficient submodular optimization with ordering constraints and supports outlier-robust non-convex isotonic regression.

title: Efficient Algorithms for Non-convex Isotonic Regression through Submodular Optimization

abstract: We consider the problem of multi-objective maximization of monotone submodular functions subject to cardinality constraint, often formulated as $\max_{|A|=k}\min_{i\in\{1,\dots,m\}}f_i(A)$. While it is widely known that greedy methods work well for a single objective, the problem becomes much harder with multiple objectives. In fact, Krause et al.\ (2008) showed that when the number of objectives $m$ grows as the cardinality $k$ i.e., $m=\Omega(k)$, the problem is inapproximable (unless $P=NP$). On the other hand, when $m$ is constant Chekuri et al.\ (2010) showed a randomized $(1-1/e)-\epsilon$ approximation with runtime (number of queries to function oracle) $n^{m/\epsilon^3}$. %In fact, the result of Chekuri et al.\ (2010) is for the far more general case of matroid constant. We focus on finding a fast and practical algorithm that has (asymptotic) approximation guarantees even when $m$ is super constant. We first modify the algorithm of Chekuri et al.\ (2010) to achieve a $(1-1/e)$ approximation for $m=o(\frac{k}{\log^3 k})$. This demonstrates a steep transition from constant factor approximability to inapproximability around $m=\Omega(k)$. Then using Multiplicative-Weight-Updates (MWU), we find a much faster $\tilde{O}(n/\delta^3)$ time asymptotic $(1-1/e)^2-\delta$ approximation. While the above results are all randomized, we also give a simple deterministic $(1-1/e)-\epsilon$ approximation with runtime $kn^{m/\epsilon^4}$. Finally, we run synthetic experiments using Kronecker graphs and find that our MWU inspired heuristic outperforms existing heuristics.

The number of objectives, m, is crucial: the abstract identifies inapproximability when m grows on the order of k, unless P equals NP.

A deterministic alternative achieves a (1 − 1/e) − ε approximation, with runtime kn raised to m/ε⁴. Together, the results expose tradeoffs among speed, approximation quality, and the number of objectives. Synthetic experiments on Kronecker graphs also show that a heuristic inspired by the multiplicative-weight approach outperforms existing heuristics in those tests.
summary.tldr: New algorithms extend multi-objective submodular approximation guarantees beyond constant objective counts and offer a faster multiplicative-weight approach.

title: Multi-objective Maximization of Monotone Submodular Functions with Cardinality Constraint

abstract: Inference amortization methods share information across multiple posterior-inference problems, allowing each to be carried out more efficiently. Generally, they require the inversion of the dependency structure in the generative model, as the modeller must learn a mapping from observations to distributions approximating the posterior. Previous approaches have involved inverting the dependency structure in a heuristic way that fails to capture these dependencies correctly, thereby limiting the achievable accuracy of the resulting approximations. We introduce an algorithm for faithfully, and minimally, inverting the graphical model structure of any generative model. Such inverses have two crucial properties: (a) they do not encode any independence assertions that are absent from the model and; (b) they are local maxima for the number of true independencies encoded. We prove the correctness of our approach and empirically show that the resulting minimally faithful inverses lead to better inference amortization than existing heuristic approaches.

paragraphs: Amortized inference learns to reuse work across many posterior-inference problems. It maps observations to approximate distributions over the quantities that generated them. Designing that mapping requires reversing the dependency structure of a generative model, and the paper argues that heuristic reversals can introduce incorrect independence assumptions that limit inference accuracy.

The authors introduce an algorithm for constructing a minimally faithful inverse of any generative model’s graphical structure. Faithfulness means that the inverse does not assert independencies absent from the original model. Minimality is expressed through a local maximum in the number of valid independencies encoded, retaining structural simplification without introducing false separations between variables.

The paper proves the algorithm’s correctness and reports better amortized inference than existing heuristic inversion approaches. The distinction matters because an approximation’s architecture can restrict what dependencies it is capable of representing, regardless of how it is trained. Constructing the inverse systematically addresses that structural source of error while preserving as many true independencies as the stated local optimality property permits.
summary.tldr: A provably faithful inversion algorithm preserves the dependency structure needed for more accurate amortized inference.

title: Faithful Inversion of Generative Models for Effective Amortized Inference

abstract: Duplicate removal is a critical step to accomplish a reasonable amount of predictions in prevalent proposal-based object detection frameworks. Albeit simple and effective, most previous algorithms utilized a greedy process without making sufficient use of properties of input data. In this work, we design a new two-stage framework to effectively select the appropriate proposal candidate for each object. The first stage suppresses most of easy negative object proposals, while the second stage selects true positives in the reduced proposal set. These two stages share the same network structure, an encoder and a decoder formed as recurrent neural networks (RNN) with global attention and context gate. The encoder scans proposal candidates in a sequential manner to capture the global context information, which is then fed to the decoder to extract optimal proposals. In our extensive experiments, the proposed method outperforms other alternatives by a large margin.

paragraphs: Proposal-based object detectors can produce many candidate predictions for the same object. Duplicate removal reduces these to a useful set of detections. This paper argues that common greedy methods make insufficient use of information in the proposals and develops a learned framework for selecting an appropriate candidate for each object.

The framework uses two stages. The first suppresses most easily rejected negative proposals, leaving a smaller candidate set. The second selects true positives from that reduced set. Both stages use the same network structure: a recurrent encoder and decoder equipped with global attention and a context gate.

The encoder scans proposals sequentially to collect global context, which the decoder then uses to select proposals. This allows selection to draw on information across the candidate collection. The authors report large improvements over alternative methods in extensive experiments. The findings support combining early filtering with context-aware selection to improve duplicate removal within proposal-based detection.
summary.tldr: A two-stage recurrent framework uses global proposal context to filter negatives and select detections more effectively.

title: Sequential Context Encoding for Duplicate Removal

abstract: We propose stochastic optimization algorithms that can find local minima faster than existing algorithms for nonconvex optimization problems, by exploiting the third-order smoothness to escape non-degenerate saddle points more efficiently. More specifically, the proposed algorithm only needs $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-10/3})$ stochastic gradient evaluations to converge to an approximate local minimum $\mathbf{x}$, which satisfies $\|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|_2\leq\epsilon$ and $\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}))\geq -\sqrt{\epsilon}$ in unconstrained stochastic optimization, where $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides logarithm polynomial terms and constants. This improves upon the $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-7/2})$ gradient complexity achieved by the state-of-the-art stochastic local minima finding algorithms by a factor of $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1/6})$. Experiments on two nonconvex optimization problems demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm and corroborate our theory.

paragraphs: In nonconvex optimization, a small gradient does not by itself establish that a point is near a local minimum. Saddle points can also have small gradients. This paper develops stochastic optimization algorithms that exploit third-order smoothness to escape non-degenerate saddle points more efficiently and reach an approximate local minimum.

The target has two requirements: its gradient norm is at most epsilon, and the smallest eigenvalue of its Hessian is at least minus the square root of epsilon. In plain language, the point has little first-order incentive to move and no excessively negative curvature. For unconstrained stochastic optimization, the proposed algorithm reaches this target using roughly epsilon to the power minus ten-thirds stochastic gradient evaluations, with logarithmic factors suppressed.

The stated previous bound scales as epsilon to the power minus seven-halves, so the improvement becomes more consequential as the requested tolerance shrinks. Experiments on two nonconvex problems support the method’s effectiveness and its theoretical analysis. The contribution shows how the additional third-order smoothness structure can improve the cost of finding these approximate solutions.
summary.tldr: Exploiting third-order smoothness improves the stochastic gradient complexity of escaping saddle points and finding approximate local minima.

title: Third-order Smoothness Helps: Faster Stochastic Optimization Algorithms for Finding Local Minima

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been increasingly deployed to edge devices. Hence, many efforts have been made towards efficient CNN inference on resource-constrained platforms. This paper attempts to explore an orthogonal direction: how to conduct more energy-efficient training of CNNs, so as to enable on-device training? We strive to reduce the energy cost during training, by dropping unnecessary computations, from three complementary levels: stochastic mini-batch dropping on the data level; selective layer update on the model level; and sign prediction for low-cost, low-precision back-propagation, on the algorithm level. Extensive simulations and ablation studies, with real energy measurements from an FPGA board, confirm the superiority of our proposed strategies and demonstrate remarkable energy savings for training. For example, when training ResNet-74 on CIFAR-10, we achieve aggressive energy savings of >90% and >60%, while incurring a top-1 accuracy loss of only about 2% and 1.2%, respectively. When training ResNet-110 on CIFAR-100, an over 84% training energy saving is achieved without degrading inference accuracy.

paragraphs: E2-Train addresses the energy required to train convolutional networks, motivated by the possibility of training directly on devices with limited resources. Its central idea is to reduce the computations performed during learning. The paper combines changes at three levels so that savings can come from data processing, model updates, and the arithmetic used in back-propagation.

At the data level, it stochastically drops mini-batches. At the model level, it selectively updates layers. At the algorithm level, it uses sign prediction to support lower-cost, lower-precision back-propagation. These strategies target different parts of training, and the authors examine their contributions through simulations and ablation studies, supported by actual energy measurements from an FPGA board.

The reported tradeoffs depend on the training setting. For ResNet-74 on CIFAR-10, energy reductions above 90% and 60% accompany top-1 accuracy losses of about 2% and 1.2%, respectively. For ResNet-110 on CIFAR-100, savings exceed 84% without reduced inference accuracy. These examples demonstrate substantial measured savings, including both accuracy-preserving and accuracy-trading configurations.
summary.tldr: E2-Train reduces CNN training energy through batch dropping, selective layer updates, and cheaper back-propagation, with substantial savings in reported experiments.

title: E2-Train: Training State-of-the-art CNNs with Over 80% Energy Savings

abstract: In the classical contextual bandits problem, in each round $t$, a learner observes some context $c$, chooses some action $a$ to perform, and receives some reward $r_{a,t}(c)$. We consider the variant of this problem where in addition to receiving the reward $r_{a,t}(c)$, the learner also learns the values of $r_{a,t}(c')$ for all other contexts $c'$; i.e., the rewards that would have been achieved by performing that action under different contexts. This variant arises in several strategic settings, such as learning how to bid in non-truthful repeated auctions (in this setting the context is the decision maker's private valuation for each auction). We call this problem the contextual bandits problem with cross-learning. The best algorithms for the classical contextual bandits problem achieve $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{CKT})$ regret against all stationary policies, where $C$ is the number of contexts, $K$ the number of actions, and $T$ the number of rounds. We demonstrate algorithms for the contextual bandits problem with cross-learning that remove the dependence on $C$ and achieve regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ (when contexts are stochastic with known distribution), $\tilde{O}(K^{1/3}T^{2/3})$ (when contexts are stochastic with unknown distribution), and $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ (when contexts are adversarial but rewards are stochastic). We simulate our algorithms on real auction data from an ad exchange running first-price auctions (showing that they outperform traditional contextual bandit algorithms).

paragraphs: A contextual bandit chooses an action after observing a context, then learns the reward for that choice. This paper studies a richer feedback setting: after taking an action, the learner also discovers what that same action would have earned in every other context. The authors call this cross-learning because one decision supplies information across contexts.

This feedback can arise in repeated auctions, where a bidder's private valuation acts as the context. The theoretical benefit is that regret bounds can lose their dependence on the number of contexts. Regret measures the learner's accumulated shortfall against the stationary policies used for comparison.

The precise improvement depends on how contexts and rewards behave. With stochastic contexts of known distribution, regret scales as the square root of actions times rounds, ignoring logarithmic factors. The same rate holds for adversarial contexts with stochastic rewards. Unknown stochastic context distributions receive a different bound, scaling as actions to the one-third power times rounds to the two-thirds power. Simulations on real first-price auction data outperform traditional contextual bandit algorithms.
summary.tldr: Learning an action's rewards across contexts enables contextual bandit algorithms whose stated regret bounds avoid dependence on the number of contexts.

title: Contextual Bandits with Cross-Learning

abstract: Signal degradation is ubiquitous, and computational restoration of degraded signal has been investigated for many years. Recently, it is reported that the capability of signal restoration is fundamentally limited by the so-called perception-distortion tradeoff, i.e. the distortion and the perceptual difference between the restored signal and the ideal "original" signal cannot be made both minimal simultaneously. Distortion corresponds to signal fidelity and perceptual difference corresponds to perceptual naturalness, both of which are important metrics in practice. Besides, there is another dimension worthy of consideration--the semantic quality of the restored signal, i.e. the utility of the signal for recognition purpose. In this paper, we extend the previous perception-distortion tradeoff to the case of classification-distortion-perception (CDP) tradeoff, where we introduced the classification error rate of the restored signal in addition to distortion and perceptual difference. In particular, we consider the classification error rate achieved on the restored signal using a predefined classifier as a representative metric for semantic quality. We rigorously prove the existence of the CDP tradeoff, i.e. the distortion, perceptual difference, and classification error rate cannot be made all minimal simultaneously. We also provide both simulation and experimental results to showcase the CDP tradeoff. Our findings can be useful especially for computer vision research where some low-level vision tasks (signal restoration) serve for high-level vision tasks (visual understanding). Our code and models have been published.

paragraphs: Restoring a degraded signal can be judged in several ways. Distortion measures fidelity to the original, while perceptual difference measures how natural the restored signal appears. The paper adds a third concern: whether the restored result is useful for recognition. This matters when a restoration system supplies inputs to a later understanding task.

The authors represent this semantic usefulness through the error rate of a predefined classifier operating on restored signals. They extend the perception-distortion framework to include that error and rigorously establish a three-way tradeoff. Distortion, perceptual difference, and classification error cannot all be minimized simultaneously.

Simulations and experiments demonstrate the tradeoff alongside the theoretical result. Its practical meaning is that choosing a restoration objective involves deciding how to balance fidelity, naturalness, and recognition performance. The semantic measure here is specifically the chosen classifier's error, so the result makes recognition utility concrete within that setting. It gives computer vision researchers a framework for considering how improvements to low-level restoration relate to the needs of a higher-level classification task.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a three-way tradeoff between restored-signal fidelity, perceptual naturalness, and error from a predefined classifier.

title: On The Classification-Distortion-Perception Tradeoff

abstract: Real-world event sequences consist of complex mixtures of different types of events occurring in time. An event may depend on past events of the same type, as well as, the other types. Point processes define a general class of models for event sequences. ``Regressive point processes'' refer to point processes that directly model the dependency between an event and any past event, an example of which is a Hawkes process. In this work, we propose and develop a new nonparametric regressive point process model based on Gaussian processes. We show that our model can represent better many commonly observed real-world event sequences and capture the dependencies between events that are difficult to model using existing nonparametric Hawkes process variants. We demonstrate the improved predictive performance of our model against state-of-the-art baselines on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Event sequences often mix several event types, with each occurrence potentially depending on earlier events of its own type or other types. Point processes model such sequences over time. This paper focuses on regressive point processes, which represent dependencies directly between an event and past events, rather than considering only isolated occurrence times.

The authors develop a nonparametric model based on Gaussian processes, with conditional Gaussian processes identified in the title. The aim is to represent dependencies that existing nonparametric Hawkes-process variants find difficult to capture. The central modeling question is therefore how flexibly the history of different event types can influence predictions about subsequent events.

The paper reports that the model better represents many commonly observed event sequences and demonstrates improved predictive performance against state-of-the-art baselines on multiple synthetic and real datasets. These findings support the proposed treatment of event dependencies in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a new model within the regressive point-process family, extending the available ways to describe how a mixed event history shapes future occurrences.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process-based regressive point process models complex event dependencies and improves prediction on the reported synthetic and real datasets.

title: Nonparametric Regressive Point Processes Based on Conditional Gaussian Processes

abstract: We introduce a variational approach to learning and inference of temporally hierarchical structure and representation for sequential data. We propose the Variational Temporal Abstraction (VTA), a hierarchical recurrent state space model that can infer the latent temporal structure and thus perform the stochastic state transition hierarchically. We also propose to apply this model to implement the jumpy imagination ability in imagination-augmented agent-learning in order to improve the efficiency of the imagination. In experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed method can model 2D and 3D visual sequence datasets with interpretable temporal structure discovery and that its application to jumpy imagination enables more efficient agent-learning in a 3D navigation task.

We also propose to apply this model to implement the jumpy imagination ability in imagination-augmented agent-learning in order to improve the efficiency of the imagination. In experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed method can model 2D and 3D visual sequence datasets with interpretable temporal structure discovery and that its application to jumpy imagination enables more efficient agent-learning in a 3D navigation task.

paragraphs: Sequential data contain structure across time, and a useful model may need to represent that structure at multiple levels. This paper introduces Variational Temporal Abstraction, a variational approach for learning and inferring temporal hierarchies. Its goal is to discover latent temporal organization and use it to guide how the model's internal states change.

VTA is a hierarchical recurrent state-space model. It infers hidden temporal structure and performs stochastic state transitions hierarchically. The authors also propose using this model for jumpy imagination in agents that learn with imagined experience. The motivation is to make imagination more efficient by allowing it to operate through temporal abstractions.

Experiments on 2D and 3D visual sequences show that the model discovers interpretable temporal structure while modeling the data. In a 3D navigation task, applying VTA to jumpy imagination enables more efficient agent learning. These findings connect two uses of the same learned hierarchy: explaining temporal organization in observations and supporting a more efficient imagination process for an agent.
summary.tldr: Variational Temporal Abstraction learns temporal hierarchies in visual sequences and supports more efficient imagination-based learning in a 3D navigation task.

title: Variational Temporal Abstraction

abstract: We introduce the Neural State Machine, seeking to bridge the gap between the neural and symbolic views of AI and integrate their complementary strengths for the task of visual reasoning. Given an image, we first predict a probabilistic graph that represents its underlying semantics and serves as a structured world model. Then, we perform sequential reasoning over the graph, iteratively traversing its nodes to answer a given question or draw a new inference. In contrast to most neural architectures that are designed to closely interact with the raw sensory data, our model operates instead in an abstract latent space, by transforming both the visual and linguistic modalities into semantic concept-based representations, thereby achieving enhanced transparency and modularity. We evaluate our model on VQA-CP and GQA, two recent VQA datasets that involve compositionality, multi-step inference and diverse reasoning skills, achieving state-of-the-art results in both cases. We provide further experiments that illustrate the model's strong generalization capacity across multiple dimensions, including novel compositions of concepts, changes in the answer distribution, and unseen linguistic structures, demonstrating the qualities and efficacy of our approach.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning requires combining what is in an image with the relationships described by a question. The Neural State Machine aims to combine neural perception with a structured reasoning process, moving both visual and linguistic information into representations based on semantic concepts.

The model first predicts a probabilistic graph representing the image’s semantics. It then reasons sequentially over that graph, traversing nodes to answer a question or derive an inference. The graph functions as an intermediate world model, intended to make the reasoning more transparent and modular.

Evaluation on VQA-CP and GQA achieves state-of-the-art results in the reported comparisons. Additional experiments examine novel concept combinations, changes in answer distributions, and unseen linguistic structures, showing strong generalization across those tests. The abstract does not give scores or establish complete reasoning reliability; it supports the usefulness of this structured representation for the evaluated visual-question-answering tasks.
summary.tldr: The Neural State Machine answers image questions by reasoning over an inferred semantic graph.

title: Learning by Abstraction: The Neural State Machine

abstract: We study the problem of estimating a nonparametric probability distribution under a family of losses called Besov IPMs. This family is quite large, including, for example, L^p distances, total variation distance, and generalizations of both Wasserstein (earthmover's) and Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances. For a wide variety of settings, we provide both lower and upper bounds, identifying precisely how the choice of loss function and assumptions on the data distribution interact to determine the mini-max optimal convergence rate. We also show that, in many cases, linear distribution estimates, such as the empirical distribution or kernel density estimator, cannot converge at the optimal rate. These bounds generalize, unify, or improve on several recent and classical results. Moreover, IPMs can be used to formalize a statistical model of generative adversarial networks (GANs). Thus, we show how our results imply bounds on the statistical error of a GAN, showing, for example, that, in many cases, GANs can strictly outperform the best linear estimator.

paragraphs: Estimating a probability distribution requires choosing how to measure the difference between an estimate and the truth. This paper studies a broad family of such measures called Besov integral probability metrics. The family encompasses L^p and total variation distances, along with generalizations of Wasserstein and Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances.

The authors derive lower and upper bounds across a wide variety of settings. These bounds identify how assumptions about the underlying distribution interact with the chosen loss to determine the minimax convergence rate: the best achievable worst-case rate of improvement with more data. They also show that familiar linear estimates, including empirical distributions and kernel density estimates, fail to attain that rate in many cases.

The same framework supports a statistical formulation of generative adversarial networks. Applying the bounds yields guarantees on GAN statistical error and shows that GANs can, in many cases, strictly outperform the best linear estimator. This is a theoretical comparison under the studied distribution and loss settings. It explains how estimator choice and evaluation criterion can jointly change what statistical performance is achievable.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal distribution-estimation rates under broad losses and identifies settings where GANs can outperform every linear estimator.

title: Nonparametric Density Estimation & Convergence Rates for GANs under Besov IPM Losses

abstract: We introduce the gamma-model, a predictive model of environment dynamics with an infinite, probabilistic horizon. Replacing standard single-step models with gamma-models leads to generalizations of the procedures central to model-based control, including the model rollout and model-based value estimation. The gamma-model, trained with a generative reinterpretation of temporal difference learning, is a natural continuous analogue of the successor representation and a hybrid between model-free and model-based mechanisms. Like a value function, it contains information about the long-term future; like a standard predictive model, it is independent of task reward. We instantiate the gamma-model as both a generative adversarial network and normalizing flow, discuss how its training reflects an inescapable tradeoff between training-time and testing-time compounding errors, and empirically investigate its utility for prediction and control.

paragraphs: A standard model of environment dynamics predicts a single step into the future. The gamma-model instead represents the future over an infinite probabilistic horizon. This changes what a dynamics model contains: long-term information becomes part of the learned prediction, rather than something obtained only by repeatedly applying a one-step model.

The model is trained through a generative interpretation of temporal difference learning. The authors describe it as a continuous analogue of the successor representation and a combination of model-free and model-based mechanisms. Like a value function, it captures information about the distant future. Like a predictive dynamics model, it remains independent of the reward associated with a particular task.

Replacing one-step models with gamma-models leads to generalized procedures for model rollout and value estimation. The paper implements the idea using both generative adversarial networks and normalizing flows, and empirically studies prediction and control. It also identifies an unavoidable tradeoff involving compounding errors during training and testing, making the placement of prediction error a central consideration in learning long-horizon models.
summary.tldr: Gamma-models learn reward-independent, long-horizon predictions through generative temporal difference learning, connecting model-based and model-free mechanisms.

title: Gamma-Models: Generative Temporal Difference Learning for Infinite-Horizon Prediction

abstract: In this work, we tackle model efficiency by exploiting redundancy in the implicit structure of the building blocks of convolutional neural networks. We start our analysis by introducing a general definition of Composite Kernel structures that enable the execution of convolution operations in the form of efficient, scaled, sum-pooling components. As its special case, we propose Structured Convolutions and show that these allow decomposition of the convolution operation into a sum-pooling operation followed by a convolution with significantly lower complexity and fewer weights. We show how this decomposition can be applied to 2D and 3D kernels as well as the fully-connected layers. Furthermore, we present a Structural Regularization loss that promotes neural network layers to leverage on this desired structure in a way that, after training, they can be decomposed with negligible performance loss. By applying our method to a wide range of CNN architectures, we demonstrate 'structured' versions of the ResNets that are up to 2x smaller and a new Structured-MobileNetV2 that is more efficient while staying within an accuracy loss of 1% on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets. We also show similar structured versions of EfficientNet on ImageNet and HRNet architecture for semantic segmentation on the Cityscapes dataset. Our method performs equally well or superior in terms of the complexity reduction in comparison to the existing tensor decomposition and channel pruning methods.

paragraphs: This paper reduces neural network cost by exploiting structure within convolutional building blocks. It introduces Composite Kernel structures, which express convolutions through efficient scaled sum-pooling components. Structured Convolutions are a special case that decomposes an operation into sum-pooling followed by a smaller convolution with fewer weights and lower computational complexity.

The decomposition applies to two-dimensional and three-dimensional kernels as well as fully connected layers. A Structural Regularization loss encourages layers to adopt the required structure during training. This matters because the resulting layers can then be decomposed after training with the reported negligible performance loss, linking the training objective to the intended efficient implementation.

Experiments produce structured ResNets up to twice as small and a more efficient Structured-MobileNetV2 within a 1% accuracy loss on the stated image-classification datasets. The authors also demonstrate structured EfficientNet and HRNet variants. Across their comparisons, complexity reduction matches or exceeds existing tensor-decomposition and channel-pruning methods, supporting the approach across several architectures and vision applications.
summary.tldr: Structured Convolutions train layers to support efficient pooling-plus-convolution decompositions, reducing model size and complexity with small reported performance losses.

title: Structured Convolutions for Efficient Neural Network Design

abstract: We propose a distributionally robust model for the influence maximization problem. Unlike the classical independent cascade model of Kempe et al (2003), this model's diffusion process is adversarially adapted to the choice of seed set. So instead of optimizing under the assumption that all influence relationships in the network are independent, we seek a seed set whose expected influence under the worst correlation, i.e., the ``worst-case, expected influence", is maximized. We show that this worst-case influence can be efficiently computed, and though the optimization is NP-hard, a (1 - 1/e) approximation guarantee holds. We also analyze the structure to the adversary's choice of diffusion process, and contrast with established models. Beyond the key computational advantages, we also study the degree to which the independence assumption may be considered costly, and provide insights from numerical experiments comparing the adversarial and independent cascade model.

So instead of optimizing under the assumption that all influence relationships in the network are independent, we seek a seed set whose expected influence under the worst correlation, i.e., the ``worst-case, expected influence", is maximized. paragraphs: Influence maximization chooses a set of starting nodes to spread influence through a network. A classical model assumes that influence relationships operate independently. This paper studies a more cautious objective: choose seeds that maximize expected spread under the least favorable correlation structure allowed by the model.

The diffusion process can adapt adversarially to the selected seeds. Thus, a seed set is judged by its worst-case expected influence, rather than by spread under one independence assumption. The authors show that this quantity can be computed efficiently for a given seed set. Finding the best set remains NP-hard, but the optimization admits a 1 − 1/e approximation guarantee.

The paper also analyzes the structure of the adversary's diffusion choices and contrasts them with established models. Numerical experiments compare adversarial diffusion with the independent cascade model to investigate the possible cost of assuming independence. The contribution combines a robustness objective with computational guarantees, allowing seed selection to explicitly account for unfavorable dependence between influence relationships.
summary.tldr: A robust influence model selects network seeds against worst-case correlations while retaining efficient influence evaluation and an approximation guarantee.

title: Correlation Robust Influence Maximization

abstract: We present ShapeFlow, a flow-based model for learning a deformation space for entire classes of 3D shapes with large intra-class variations. ShapeFlow allows learning a multi-template deformation space that is agnostic to shape topology, yet preserves fine geometric details. Different from a generative space where a latent vector is directly decoded into a shape, a deformation space decodes a vector into a continuous flow that can advect a source shape towards a target. Such a space naturally allows the disentanglement of geometric style (coming from the source) and structural pose (conforming to the target). We parametrize the deformation between geometries as a learned continuous flow field via a neural network and show that such deformations can be guaranteed to have desirable properties, such as bijectivity, freedom from self-intersections, or volume preservation. We illustrate the effectiveness of this learned deformation space for various downstream applications, including shape generation via deformation, geometric style transfer, unsupervised learning of a consistent parameterization for entire classes of shapes, and shape interpolation.

This makes the learned space a space of transformations, where the source supplies geometric details and the target guides the resulting structural pose.

A neural network parameterizes the continuous flow field that moves the geometry. The approach supports multiple templates, is agnostic to shape topology, and preserves fine geometric detail. The authors show that deformations can be guaranteed to have desirable properties such as one-to-one correspondence, freedom from self-intersections, or volume preservation. These are properties that the flow formulation can support, rather than an assertion that every deformation automatically has all of them.

The paper demonstrates shape generation through deformation, transfer of geometric style, interpolation, and unsupervised learning of consistent parameterizations across shape classes. These applications illustrate why a learned transformation space is useful: it can organize relationships between shapes while retaining meaningful information from the source geometry.
summary.tldr: ShapeFlow learns continuous deformations between 3D shapes, supporting detailed geometry, style transfer, and controllable geometric properties.

title: ShapeFlow: Learnable Deformation Flows Among 3D Shapes

abstract: Learning expressive probabilistic models correctly describing the data is a ubiquitous problem in machine learning. A popular approach for solving it is mapping the observations into a representation space with a simple joint distribution, which can typically be written as a product of its marginals — thus drawing a connection with the field of nonlinear independent component analysis. Deep density models have been widely used for this task, but their maximum likelihood based training requires estimating the log-determinant of the Jacobian and is computationally expensive, thus imposing a trade-off between computation and expressive power. In this work, we propose a new approach for exact training of such neural networks. Based on relative gradients, we exploit the matrix structure of neural network parameters to compute updates efficiently even in high-dimensional spaces; the computational cost of the training is quadratic in the input size, in contrast with the cubic scaling of naive approaches. This allows fast training with objective functions involving the log-determinant of the Jacobian, without imposing constraints on its structure, in stark contrast to autoregressive normalizing flows.

This paper proposes an exact training approach based on relative gradients. It exploits the matrix structure of neural network parameters to compute updates efficiently, including in high-dimensional spaces. The reported computational scaling is quadratic in input size, compared with the cubic scaling of naive approaches. This targets a central computational burden of the learning objective.

The authors contrast this with autoregressive normalizing flows, whose structure is restricted. The significance is a way to reduce the computational cost of exact training while retaining greater structural freedom in the transformation. The paper also connects the representation-learning objective to nonlinear independent component analysis through its use of simple, factorized representation distributions.
summary.tldr: Relative gradients enable exact Jacobian-based density-model training with quadratic input-size scaling and without constraining Jacobian structure.

title: Relative gradient optimization of the Jacobian term in unsupervised deep learning

abstract: We study reinforcement learning in non-episodic factored Markov decision processes (FMDPs). We propose two near-optimal and oracle-efficient algorithms for FMDPs. Assuming oracle access to an FMDP planner, they enjoy a Bayesian and a frequentist regret bound respectively, both of which reduce to the near-optimal bound $O(DS\sqrt{AT})$ for standard non-factored MDPs. We propose a tighter connectivity measure, factored span, for FMDPs and prove a lower bound that depends on the factored span rather than the diameter $D$. In order to decrease the gap between lower and upper bounds, we propose an adaptation of the REGAL.C algorithm whose regret bound depends on the factored span. Our oracle-efficient algorithms outperform previously proposed near-optimal algorithms on computer network administration simulations.

It proposes two near-optimal algorithms that use access to an FMDP planning oracle. That oracle assumption is central to the stated computational efficiency: the learning procedures rely on an available planner.

One algorithm receives a Bayesian regret guarantee and the other a frequentist guarantee. For ordinary, non-factored Markov decision processes, both bounds reduce to the near-optimal O(DS√(AT)) form. This connects the proposed structural measure to both limits on learning and an achievable guarantee. In computer network administration simulations, the oracle-efficient algorithms outperform previously proposed near-optimal methods. The contribution combines new algorithms, a refined measure of problem difficulty, and empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: Planner-oracle algorithms and a new factored-span measure sharpen regret analysis for non-episodic reinforcement learning in factored environments.

title: Reinforcement Learning in Factored MDPs: Oracle-Efficient Algorithms and Tighter Regret Bounds for the Non-Episodic Setting

abstract: Representation learning of graph-structured data is challenging because both graph structure and node features carry important information. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) provide an expressive way to fuse information from network structure and node features. However, GNNs are prone to adversarial attacks. Here we introduce Graph Information Bottleneck (GIB), an information-theoretic principle that optimally balances expressiveness and robustness of the learned representation of graph-structured data. Inheriting from the general Information Bottleneck (IB), GIB aims to learn the minimal sufficient representation for a given task by maximizing the mutual information between the representation and the target, and simultaneously constraining the mutual information between the representation and the input data. Different from the general IB, GIB regularizes the structural as well as the feature information. We design two sampling algorithms for structural regularization and instantiate the GIB principle with two new models: GIB-Cat and GIB-Bern, and demonstrate the benefits by evaluating the resilience to adversarial attacks. We show that our proposed models are more robust than state-of-the-art graph defense models. GIB-based models empirically achieve up to 31% improvement with adversarial perturbation of the graph structure as well as node features.

This paper introduces the Graph Information Bottleneck principle to balance useful representation power with robustness. Its aim is a representation that retains the information needed for a task while limiting retained information about the input.

The formulation maximizes mutual information between the representation and the target while constraining mutual information between the representation and the input data. Its graph-specific contribution is to regularize structural information as well as feature information. The authors design two sampling algorithms for structural regularization and build two models, GIB-Cat and GIB-Bern.

The proposed models outperform state-of-the-art graph defense models in the reported evaluation, with empirical improvements reaching up to 31%. That figure describes the reported experimental gains rather than a uniform guarantee. The results support applying the information bottleneck to both components of graph data when learning representations intended to withstand adversarial perturbations.
summary.tldr: Graph Information Bottleneck regularizes both graph structure and node features to learn task-relevant representations with improved empirical adversarial robustness.

title: Graph Information Bottleneck

abstract: Human explanations of high-level decisions are often expressed in terms of key concepts the decisions are based on. In this paper, we study such concept-based explainability for Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). First, we define the notion of \emph{completeness}, which quantifies how sufficient a particular set of concepts is in explaining a model's prediction behavior based on the assumption that complete concept scores are sufficient statistics of the model prediction. Next, we propose a concept discovery method that aims to infer a complete set of concepts that are additionally encouraged to be interpretable, which addresses the limitations of existing methods on concept explanations. To define an importance score for each discovered concept, we adapt game-theoretic notions to aggregate over sets and propose \emph{ConceptSHAP}. Via proposed metrics and user studies, on a synthetic dataset with apriori-known concept explanations, as well as on real-world image and language datasets, we validate the effectiveness of our method in finding concepts that are both complete in explaining the decisions and interpretable.

paragraphs: Explaining a neural network through human-understandable concepts raises two questions: are the concepts interpretable, and do they capture enough of the model's prediction behavior? This paper formalizes the second question through completeness. The definition assumes that scores for a complete set of concepts contain sufficient information about the model's prediction.

The authors develop a concept-discovery method that seeks a complete concept set while also encouraging interpretability. This brings coverage of the model's behavior into the discovery objective. They also introduce ConceptSHAP to assign importance to individual concepts, adapting game-theoretic ideas that account for concepts across sets rather than considering each one only in isolation.

Evaluation combines proposed metrics with user studies. It includes synthetic data with known concept explanations and real image and language datasets. The authors report evidence that the method finds concepts that are both interpretable and complete in explaining decisions. The contribution connects what people can understand about a concept with how sufficiently the overall concept set accounts for the network's behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper defines concept completeness, discovers interpretable concept sets, and introduces ConceptSHAP to explain their importance.

title: On Completeness-aware Concept-Based Explanations in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We present a novel compression algorithm for reducing the storage of LiDAR sensor data streams. Our model exploits spatio-temporal relationships across multiple LiDAR sweeps to reduce the bitrate of both geometry and intensity values. Towards this goal, we propose a novel conditional entropy model that models the probabilities of the octree symbols by considering both coarse level geometry and previous sweeps’ geometric and intensity information. We then use the learned probability to encode the full data stream into a compact one. Our experiments demonstrate that our method significantly reduces the joint geometry and intensity bitrate over prior state-of-the-art LiDAR compression methods, with a reduction of 7–17% and 6–19% on the UrbanCity and SemanticKITTI datasets respectively.

paragraphs: LiDAR produces streams containing both geometric measurements and intensity values. Storing these streams efficiently requires exploiting structure within the data. MuSCLE uses spatial relationships and relationships across multiple sensor sweeps to reduce the bitrate needed for the two kinds of information together.

The method introduces a conditional entropy model that predicts probabilities for octree symbols. Its predictions use coarse geometric structure along with geometric and intensity information from previous sweeps. The learned probabilities then guide encoding of the complete stream into a compact representation. Earlier sweeps therefore become useful context for compressing later data, while coarse geometry supplies context within the spatial representation.

Experiments show reductions in joint geometry-and-intensity bitrate relative to prior state-of-the-art LiDAR compression methods. The reported reductions are 7–17% on UrbanCity and 6–19% on SemanticKITTI. These results support the value of learning probability models that combine spatial structure with information across time. The stated improvement concerns storage for both geometry and intensity, evaluated together on the two datasets.
summary.tldr: MuSCLE compresses LiDAR geometry and intensity using learned probabilities conditioned on spatial structure and previous sweeps.

title: MuSCLE: Multi Sweep Compression of LiDAR using Deep Entropy Models

abstract: Data augmentation is a simple yet effective way to improve the robustness of deep neural networks (DNNs). Diversity and hardness are two complementary dimensions of data augmentation to achieve robustness. For example, AugMix explores random compositions of a diverse set of augmentations to enhance broader coverage, while adversarial training generates adversarially hard samples to spot the weakness. Motivated by this, we propose a data augmentation framework, termed AugMax, to unify the two aspects of diversity and hardness. AugMax first randomly samples multiple augmentation operators and then learns an adversarial mixture of the selected operators. Being a stronger form of data augmentation, AugMax leads to a significantly augmented input distribution which makes model training more challenging. To solve this problem, we further design a disentangled normalization module, termed DuBIN (Dual-Batch-and-Instance Normalization), that disentangles the instance-wise feature heterogeneity arising from AugMax. Experiments show that AugMax-DuBIN leads to significantly improved out-of-distribution robustness, outperforming prior arts by 3.03%, 3.49%, 1.82% and 0.71% on CIFAR10-C, CIFAR100-C, Tiny ImageNet-C and ImageNet-C. Codes and pretrained models are available: https://github.com/VITA-Group/AugMax.

paragraphs: Data augmentation can help a network handle unfamiliar inputs by exposing it to varied training examples. This paper distinguishes two useful properties of augmentation: diversity, which broadens the changes a model sees, and hardness, which challenges its weaknesses. AugMax combines these properties in a single augmentation framework.

AugMax first randomly selects several augmentation operators, then learns an adversarial mixture of those selected operations. Random selection supplies variety, while the learned mixture makes the combined transformation challenging for the model. Because this substantially expands the input distribution and complicates training, the authors also introduce DuBIN, a normalization module that separates variation in features arising across individual examples.

summary.tldr: AugMax combines randomly selected augmentations adversarially, while DuBIN helps train on the resulting variation, improving robustness in the reported experiments.

title: AugMax: Adversarial Composition of Random Augmentations for Robust Training

abstract: Existing risk-aware multi-armed bandit models typically focus on risk measures of individual options such as variance. As a result, they cannot be directly applied to important real-world online decision making problems with correlated options. In this paper, we propose a novel Continuous Mean-Covariance Bandit (CMCB) model to explicitly take into account option correlation. Specifically, in CMCB, there is a learner who sequentially chooses weight vectors on given options and observes random feedback according to the decisions. The agent's objective is to achieve the best trade-off between reward and risk, measured with option covariance. To capture different reward observation scenarios in practice, we consider three feedback settings, i.e., full-information, semi-bandit and full-bandit feedback. We propose novel algorithms with optimal regrets (within logarithmic factors), and provide matching lower bounds to validate their optimalities. The experimental results also demonstrate the superiority of our algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that considers option correlation in risk-aware bandits and explicitly quantifies how arbitrary covariance structures impact the learning performance.The novel analytical techniques we developed for exploiting the estimated covariance to build concentration and bounding the risk of selected actions based on sampling strategy properties can likely find applications in other bandit analysis and be of independent interests.

paragraphs: Risk-aware decision making must sometimes account for how options vary together. Evaluating each option's uncertainty separately misses those relationships. This paper introduces Continuous Mean-Covariance Bandits, a model in which a learner repeatedly chooses weights over available options and balances expected reward against risk measured through their covariance.

The authors consider three ways the learner might observe outcomes: full-information, semi-bandit, and full-bandit feedback. These settings represent different amounts of information available after a decision. They develop algorithms with regret guarantees that are optimal up to logarithmic factors, supported by matching lower bounds. Here, regret measures the accumulated cost of learning while making decisions.

The contribution therefore extends beyond adding a risk penalty: it incorporates relationships between options into both decision making and performance analysis. The authors further suggest that their covariance-based analytical techniques may be useful in other bandit problems.
summary.tldr: Continuous Mean-Covariance Bandits incorporate correlations between options and admit algorithms with regret optimal up to logarithmic factors.

title: Continuous Mean-Covariance Bandits

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the causal MAG of a system from observational data in the presence of latent variables and selection bias. Constraint-based methods are one of the main approaches for solving this problem, but the existing methods are either computationally impractical when dealing with large graphs or lacking completeness guarantees. We propose a novel computationally efficient recursive constraint-based method that is sound and complete. The key idea of our approach is that at each iteration a specific type of variable is identified and removed. This allows us to learn the structure efficiently and recursively, as this technique reduces both the number of required conditional independence (CI) tests and the size of the conditioning sets. The former substantially reduces the computational complexity, while the latter results in more reliable CI tests. We provide an upper bound on the number of required CI tests in the worst case. To the best of our knowledge, this is the tightest bound in the literature. We further provide a lower bound on the number of CI tests required by any constraint-based method. The upper bound of our proposed approach and the lower bound at most differ by a factor equal to the number of variables in the worst case. We provide experimental results to compare the proposed approach with the state of the art on both synthetic and real-world structures.

paragraphs: This paper studies causal structure learning from observational data when some variables are hidden and the observations may be affected by selection bias. Its target is a causal maximal ancestral graph, or MAG. Existing constraint-based methods face a tradeoff described by the authors: they can become impractical on large graphs or lack completeness guarantees.

The proposed method recursively identifies and removes a particular type of variable. This reduces both the number of conditional independence tests and the number of variables included in their conditioning sets. Fewer tests lower computational cost, while smaller conditioning sets make the tests more reliable. The authors establish soundness and completeness for the method.

They also bound its worst-case number of conditional independence tests and provide a lower bound for any constraint-based method. The two bounds differ by at most a factor equal to the number of variables. Experiments compare the approach with state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real-world structures. The contribution combines recursive computational savings with explicit correctness and test-complexity guarantees.
summary.tldr: A recursive causal discovery method reduces conditional independence testing while providing soundness, completeness, and worst-case complexity guarantees.

title: Recursive Causal Structure Learning in the Presence of Latent Variables and Selection Bias

abstract: Point clouds and sets are input data-types which pose unique problems to deep learning. Since sets can have variable cardinality and are unchanged by permutation, the input space for these problems naturally form infinite-dimensional non-Euclidean spaces. Despite these mathematical difficulties, PointNet (Qi et al. 2017) and Deep Sets (Zaheer et al. 2017) introduced foundational neural network architectures to address these problems. In this paper we present a unified framework to study the expressive power of such networks as well as their extensions beyond point clouds (partially addressing a conjecture on the extendibility of DeepSets along the way). To this end, we demonstrate the crucial role that the Hausdorff and Wasserstein metrics play and prove new cardinality-agnostic universality results to characterize exactly which functions can be approximated by these models. In particular, these results imply that PointNet generally cannot approximate averages of continuous functions over sets (e.g. center-of-mass or higher moments) implying that DeepSets is strictly more expressive than PointNet in the constant cardinality setting. Moreover, we obtain explicit lower-bounds on the approximation error and present a simple method to produce arbitrarily many examples of this failure-mode. Counterintuitively, we also prove that in the unbounded cardinality setting that any function which can be uniformly approximated by both PointNet and normalized-DeepSets must be constant. Finally, we also prove theorems on the Lipschitz properties of PointNet and normalized-DeepSets which shed insight into exploitable inductive bias in these networks.

paragraphs: Sets create an unusual learning problem because their elements have no fixed order and their size can vary. This paper develops a unified mathematical framework for understanding which functions PointNet, DeepSets, and related architectures can approximate. Hausdorff and Wasserstein metrics play a central role in describing the relevant notions of similarity between inputs.

summary.tldr: The paper characterizes set-network expressiveness, exposing precise differences between PointNet and DeepSets across fixed and unbounded set sizes.

title: On the Representation Power of Set Pooling Networks

abstract: A recurring theme in statistical learning, online learning, and beyond is that faster convergence rates are possible for problems with low noise, often quantified by the performance of the best hypothesis; such results are known as first-order or small-loss guarantees. While first-order guarantees are relatively well understood in statistical and online learning, adapting to low noise in contextual bandits (and more broadly, decision making) presents major algorithmic challenges. In a COLT 2017 open problem, Agarwal, Krishnamurthy, Langford, Luo, and Schapire asked whether first-order guarantees are even possible for contextual bandits and---if so---whether they can be attained by efficient algorithms. We give a resolution to this question by providing an optimal and efficient reduction from contextual bandits to online regression with the logarithmic (or, cross-entropy) loss. Our algorithm is simple and practical, readily accommodates rich function classes, and requires no distributional assumptions beyond realizability. In a large-scale empirical evaluation, we find that our approach typically outperforms comparable non-first-order methods.On the technical side, we show that the logarithmic loss and an information-theoretic quantity called the triangular discrimination play a fundamental role in obtaining first-order guarantees, and we combine this observation with new refinements to the regression oracle reduction framework of Foster and Rakhlin (2020). While first-order guarantees are relatively well understood in statistical and online learning, adapting to low noise in contextual bandits (and more broadly, decision making) presents major algorithmic challenges. In a COLT 2017 open problem, Agarwal, Krishnamurthy, Langford, Luo, and Schapire asked whether first-order guarantees are even possible for contextual bandits and---if so---whether they can be attained by efficient algorithms. We give a resolution to this question by providing an optimal and efficient reduction from contextual bandits to online regression with the logarithmic (or, cross-entropy) loss. Our algorithm is simple and practical, readily accommodates rich function classes, and requires no distributional assumptions beyond realizability. In a large-scale empirical evaluation, we find that our approach typically outperforms comparable non-first-order methods.On the technical side, we show that the logarithmic loss and an information-theoretic quantity called the triangular discrimination play a fundamental role in obtaining first-order guarantees, and we combine this observation with new refinements to the regression oracle reduction framework of Foster and Rakhlin (2020). The use of triangular discrimination yields novel results even for the classical statistical learning model, and we anticipate that it will find broader use.

paragraphs: First-order, or small-loss, guarantees let learning performance improve when the best available hypothesis incurs little loss. Obtaining this kind of adaptation is challenging in contextual bandits, where decisions determine the feedback available to the learner. This paper resolves an open question about whether efficient algorithms can achieve such guarantees.

The authors give an optimal, efficient reduction from contextual bandits to online regression using logarithmic, or cross-entropy, loss. It accommodates rich function classes and requires no distributional assumption beyond realizability. The reduction makes the prediction problem’s loss choice central to obtaining a decision-making guarantee that adapts to easier instances.

The analysis connects logarithmic loss with triangular discrimination, an information-theoretic measure, and refines the regression-oracle reduction framework. This connection also produces new results for classical statistical learning. In a large empirical evaluation, the proposed approach typically outperforms comparable methods without first-order guarantees. The theoretical and experimental findings therefore support small-loss adaptation, with the empirical advantage stated as typical rather than universal.
summary.tldr: An efficient reduction to logarithmic-loss regression gives contextual bandits optimal small-loss guarantees under realizability.

title: Efficient First-Order Contextual Bandits: Prediction, Allocation, and Triangular Discrimination

abstract: In this paper, we consider a different data format for images: vector graphics. In contrast to raster graphics which are widely used in image recognition, vector graphics can be scaled up or down into any resolution without aliasing or information loss, due to the analytic representation of the primitives in the document. Furthermore, vector graphics are able to give extra structural information on how low-level elements group together to form high level shapes or structures. These merits of graphic vectors have not been fully leveraged in existing methods. To explore this data format, we target on the fundamental recognition tasks: object localization and classification. We propose an efficient CNN-free pipeline that does not render the graphic into pixels (i.e. rasterization), and takes textual document of the vector graphics as input, called YOLaT (You Only Look at Text). YOLaT builds multi-graphs to model the structural and spatial information in vector graphics, and a dual-stream graph neural network is proposed to detect objects from the graph. Our experiments show that by directly operating on vector graphics, YOLaT outperforms raster-graphic based object detection baselines in terms of both average precision and efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/YOLaT-VectorGraphicsRecognition.

paragraphs: Vector graphics describe images through analytic primitives and their organization. This representation supports scaling without the aliasing or information loss associated with rasterization and supplies structural information about how elements form larger shapes. The paper explores how object recognition can use that information directly.

The proposed YOLaT pipeline reads the textual vector-graphics document without rendering it into pixels. It builds multiple graphs to represent spatial relationships and structural information, then uses a dual-stream graph neural network to locate and classify objects. The pipeline does not use a convolutional neural network, placing the vector document's relationships at the center of recognition.

Experiments show better average precision and efficiency than the evaluated object-detection baselines operating on raster graphics. The results support the value of preserving the original representation during recognition. In this setting, the vector document provides more than instructions for drawing an image: its organization supplies information that the graph-based detector can use for identifying objects and determining where they are.
summary.tldr: YOLaT detects objects directly from vector-graphics documents using graph networks, improving reported precision and efficiency over raster-based baselines.

title: Recognizing Vector Graphics without Rasterization

abstract: Recent advances in off-policy deep reinforcement learning (RL) have led to impressive success in complex tasks from visual observations. Experience replay improves sample-efficiency by reusing experiences from the past, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) process high-dimensional inputs effectively. However, such techniques demand high memory and computational bandwidth. In this paper, we present Stored Embeddings for Efficient Reinforcement Learning (SEER), a simple modification of existing off-policy RL methods, to address these computational and memory requirements. To reduce the computational overhead of gradient updates in CNNs, we freeze the lower layers of CNN encoders early in training due to early convergence of their parameters. Additionally, we reduce memory requirements by storing the low-dimensional latent vectors for experience replay instead of high-dimensional images, enabling an adaptive increase in the replay buffer capacity, a useful technique in constrained-memory settings. In our experiments, we show that SEER does not degrade the performance of RL agents while significantly saving computation and memory across a diverse set of DeepMind Control environments and Atari games.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning often stores past experiences and revisits them during training. This improves sample efficiency, but retaining images and repeatedly processing them with convolutional networks requires considerable memory and computation. Stored Embeddings for Efficient Reinforcement Learning, or SEER, modifies existing off-policy methods to reduce both costs.

The approach freezes the lower layers of the visual encoder early in training, motivated by the early convergence of their parameters. Once these layers are frozen, their gradient updates no longer need to be computed. SEER also stores compact latent vectors for experience replay instead of high-dimensional images. This reduces the memory required per stored experience and enables the replay buffer's capacity to increase adaptively under a memory budget.

Across the tested DeepMind Control environments and Atari games, SEER saves substantial computation and memory without degrading agent performance. The result matters because it addresses the cost of reusing experience, alongside the amount of experience needed. Its two changes connect the stabilization of visual features during learning with a more economical way to store and train on past observations.
summary.tldr: SEER freezes early visual-encoder layers and replays compact embeddings to save computation and memory without degrading performance in the reported experiments.

title: Improving Computational Efficiency in Visual Reinforcement Learning via Stored Embeddings

abstract: Many of the challenges facing today's reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, such as robustness, generalization, transfer, and computational efficiency are closely related to compression. Prior work has convincingly argued why minimizing information is useful in the supervised learning setting, but standard RL algorithms lack an explicit mechanism for compression. The RL setting is unique because (1) its sequential nature allows an agent to use past information to avoid looking at future observations and (2) the agent can optimize its behavior to prefer states where decision making requires few bits. We take advantage of these properties to propose a method (RPC) for learning simple policies. This method brings together ideas from information bottlenecks, model-based RL, and bits-back coding into a simple and theoretically-justified algorithm. Our method jointly optimizes a latent-space model and policy to be self-consistent, such that the policy avoids states where the model is inaccurate. We demonstrate that our method achieves much tighter compression than prior methods, achieving up to 5$\times$ higher reward than a standard information bottleneck when constrained to use just 0.3 bits per observation. We also demonstrate that our method learns policies that are more robust and generalize better to new tasks.

paragraphs: Robust Predictable Control studies how compression can help reinforcement learning produce simple policies. Sequential decision making offers two useful opportunities: past information can reduce the need to inspect future observations, and an agent can choose behavior that leads to states requiring little information for decisions. The method explicitly takes advantage of both.

RPC combines information bottlenecks, model-based reinforcement learning, and bits-back coding in a theoretically justified algorithm. It jointly learns a latent-space model and a policy so that they are self-consistent. The policy avoids states where the model is inaccurate, connecting the agent's behavior to how predictably and compactly its experience can be represented.

Experiments show tighter compression than prior methods. Under a constraint of 0.3 bits per observation, RPC achieves up to five times the reward of a standard information bottleneck. The authors also demonstrate improved robustness and generalization to new tasks. These findings support treating information use as part of the control problem, with both prediction and action contributing to the resulting simplicity.
summary.tldr: RPC jointly learns predictive models and policies that use little information, with reported gains in reward, robustness, and transfer.

title: Robust Predictable Control

abstract: For many applications in image analysis, learning models that are invariant to translations and rotations is paramount. This is the case, for example, in medical imaging where the objects of interest can appear at arbitrary positions, with arbitrary orientations. As of today, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) are one of the most powerful tools for image analysis. They achieve, thanks to convolutions, an invariance with respect to translations. In this work, we present a new type of convolutional layer that takes advantage of Bessel functions, well known in physics, to build Bessel-CNNs (B-CNNs) that are invariant to all the continuous set of possible rotation angles by design.

This is the case, for example, in medical imaging where the objects of interest can appear at arbitrary positions, with arbitrary orientations. As of today, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) are one of the most powerful tools for image analysis. They achieve, thanks to convolutions, an invariance with respect to translations. In this work, we present a new type of convolutional layer that takes advantage of Bessel functions, well known in physics, to build Bessel-CNNs (B-CNNs) that are invariant to all the continuous set of possible rotation angles by design.

paragraphs: In many image-analysis problems, an object's orientation should not change how a model recognizes it. Medical images provide a motivating example because objects of interest can appear in different positions and at arbitrary angles. This paper focuses on building the desired response to rotation directly into a convolutional network's architecture.

The proposed component is a convolutional layer based on Bessel functions, mathematical functions also used in physics. Networks built with these layers are called Bessel-CNNs. Their defining property is rotational invariance by design: the construction covers the continuous range of rotation angles, rather than only a selected collection of orientations.

The significance lies in making rotation handling a property of the model's structure. When orientation is irrelevant to the analysis, the architecture expresses that requirement directly. The paper places this contribution alongside the role of conventional convolutions in handling translations, extending the architectural treatment of spatial transformations to rotation. Its stated contribution is the new layer construction and the resulting invariance across all possible rotation angles.
summary.tldr: Bessel-based convolutional layers build invariance to the continuous range of image rotations directly into a neural network.

title: Achieving Rotational Invariance with Bessel-Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Autoencoders exhibit impressive abilities to embed the data manifold into a low-dimensional latent space, making them a staple of representation learning methods. However, without explicit supervision, which is often unavailable, the representation is usually uninterpretable, making analysis and principled progress challenging. We propose a framework, called latent responses, which exploits the locally contractive behavior exhibited by variational autoencoders to explore the learned manifold. More specifically, we develop tools to probe the representation using interventions in the latent space to quantify the relationships between latent variables. We extend the notion of disentanglement to take the learned generative process into account and consequently avoid the limitations of existing metrics that may rely on spurious correlations. Our analyses underscore the importance of studying the causal structure of the representation to improve performance on downstream tasks such as generation, interpolation, and inference of the factors of variation.
