paragraphs: Autoencoders compress data into a low-dimensional latent representation, but the meaning of that representation can be difficult to interpret without supervision. This paper introduces latent responses, a framework for investigating the structure learned by an autoencoder through interventions on its latent variables.

The approach uses the locally contractive behavior of variational autoencoders to explore the learned data manifold. Its tools actively perturb latent representations and quantify relationships among their variables. This provides a way to examine how the representation responds to changes, giving the analysis a causal focus rather than relying only on associations observed among latent coordinates.

The authors also extend disentanglement to account for the learned generative process. This addresses limitations of existing metrics that may depend on spurious correlations. Their analyses emphasize the importance of causal structure for downstream generation, interpolation, and inference of underlying factors of variation. The contribution is a framework for probing learned representations and a broader way to judge whether their components are meaningfully separated.
summary.tldr: Latent responses use interventions to probe autoencoder representations and assess disentanglement through the learned generative process.

title: Exploring the Latent Space of Autoencoders with Interventional Assays

abstract: Graph Anomaly Detection (GAD) has recently become a hot research spot due to its practicability and theoretical value. Since GAD emphasizes the application and the rarity of anomalous samples, enriching the varieties of its datasets is fundamental. Thus, this paper present DGraph, a real-world dynamic graph in the finance domain. DGraph overcomes many limitations of current GAD datasets. It contains about 3M nodes, 4M dynamic edges, and 1M ground-truth nodes. We provide a comprehensive observation of DGraph, revealing that anomalous nodes and normal nodes generally have different structures, neighbor distribution, and temporal dynamics. Moreover, it suggests that 2M background nodes are also essential for detecting fraudsters. Furthermore, we conduct extensive experiments on DGraph. Observation and experiments demonstrate that DGraph is propulsive to advance GAD research and enable in-depth exploration of anomalous nodes.

paragraphs: Graph anomaly detection seeks unusual entities within a network of relationships. Because anomalous examples are rare and applications differ, the available datasets strongly shape what researchers can investigate. This paper introduces DGraph, a real-world financial graph that includes changing relationships over time, expanding the data available for studying this problem.

DGraph contains roughly three million nodes, four million dynamic edges, and one million nodes with ground-truth information. The authors examine how anomalous and normal nodes differ in their surrounding structure, distributions of neighbors, and temporal behavior. Their observations indicate that these groups generally have different patterns across all three aspects.

The analysis also suggests that the two million background nodes are essential for identifying fraudsters. This highlights the importance of the wider graph context alongside the nodes with ground-truth information. Extensive experiments accompany the dataset analysis. Together, they position DGraph as a resource for exploring how financial anomalies relate to both network structure and changes over time.
summary.tldr: DGraph provides a large dynamic financial graph whose analysis highlights structural, temporal, and background-node information for anomaly detection.

title: DGraph: A Large-Scale Financial Dataset for Graph Anomaly Detection

abstract: This paper proposes Branch & Learn, a framework for Predict+Optimize to tackle optimization problems containing parameters that are unknown at the time of solving. Given an optimization problem solvable by a recursive algorithm satisfying simple conditions, we show how a corresponding learning algorithm can be constructed directly and methodically from the recursive algorithm. Our framework applies also to iterative algorithms by viewing them as a degenerate form of recursion. Extensive experimentation shows better performance for our proposal over classical and state of the art approaches.
originalAbstract: This paper proposes Branch & Learn, a framework for Predict+Optimize to tackle optimization problems containing parameters that are unknown at the time of solving. Given an optimization problem solvable by a recursive algorithm satisfying simple conditions, we show how a corresponding learning algorithm can be constructed directly and methodically from the recursive algorithm. Our framework applies also to iterative algorithms by viewing them as a degenerate form of recursion. Extensive experimentation shows better performance for our proposal over classical and state of the art approaches.

paragraphs: Predict+Optimize addresses decisions made through optimization when some required parameters are unknown and must be learned. Branch & Learn provides a framework for constructing the learning component from the algorithm that solves the optimization problem. Its central idea is to use the solver’s existing computational structure as a guide for building the corresponding learning procedure.

The construction applies when a problem has a recursive solution algorithm satisfying the conditions required by the framework. Under those conditions, the authors show how to derive a learning algorithm directly and methodically. Iterative algorithms are also covered by interpreting iteration as a special form of recursion, expanding the scope beyond solvers normally described as recursive.

This connection matters because it supplies a systematic route from a suitable solver to a learning algorithm for decisions with unknown parameters. Extensive experiments report better performance than classical and state-of-the-art approaches. The result combines a conditional construction with empirical support: applicability follows from the solver requirements, while the reported performance advantage comes from the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: Branch & Learn systematically derives learning algorithms from suitable recursive or iterative optimization solvers.

title: Branch & Learn for Recursively and Iteratively Solvable Problems in Predict+Optimize

abstract: AlphaZero, an approach to reinforcement learning that couples neural networks and Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), has produced state-of-the-art strategies for traditional board games like chess, Go, shogi, and Hex. While researchers and game commentators have suggested that AlphaZero uses concepts that humans consider important, it is unclear how these concepts are captured in the network. We investigate AlphaZero's internal representations in the game of Hex using two evaluation techniques from natural language processing (NLP): model probing and behavioral tests. In doing so, we introduce several new evaluation tools to the RL community, and illustrate how evaluations other than task performance can be used to provide a more complete picture of a model's strengths and weaknesses. Our analyses in the game of Hex reveal interesting patterns and generate some testable hypotheses about how such models learn in general. For example, we find that the MCTS discovers concepts before the neural network learns to encode them. We also find that concepts related to short-term end-game planning are best encoded in the final layers of the model, whereas concepts related to long-term planning are encoded in the middle layers of the model.

paragraphs: Strong game performance does not by itself explain what a learning system represents internally. This paper examines AlphaZero in Hex to investigate whether and where its network captures strategically meaningful concepts. AlphaZero combines a neural network with Monte Carlo tree search, so the authors also examine how conceptual knowledge emerges across these two components.

They adapt model probing and behavioral tests from natural language processing. These tools add ways to evaluate learned representations and behavior beyond the final measure of playing strength. The aim is to build a fuller account of the system's strengths and weaknesses, including how concepts appear during learning and where they are represented within the network.

summary.tldr: Probes and behavioral tests reveal when and where AlphaZero learns Hex concepts beyond what its playing strength alone shows.

title: Evaluation beyond Task Performance: Analyzing Concepts in AlphaZero in Hex

abstract: We introduce UViM, a unified approach capable of modeling a wide range of computer vision tasks. In contrast to previous models, UViM has the same functional form for all tasks; it requires no task-specific modifications which require extensive human expertise. The approach involves two components: (I) a base model (feed-forward) which is trained to directly predict raw vision outputs, guided by a learned discrete code and (II) a language model (autoregressive) that is trained to generate the guiding code. These components complement each other: the language model is well-suited to modeling structured interdependent data, while the base model is efficient at dealing with high-dimensional outputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of UViM on three diverse and challenging vision tasks: panoptic segmentation, depth prediction and image colorization, where we achieve competitive and near state-of-the-art results. Our experimental results suggest that UViM is a promising candidate for a unified modeling approach in computer vision.

paragraphs: Different vision tasks often motivate different model designs, requiring substantial task-specific expertise. UViM proposes a shared functional form for a range of tasks without such modifications. Its central idea is to divide prediction between a learned discrete guiding code and a model that produces the full visual output.

The system has two complementary components. An autoregressive language model learns to generate the guiding code, making use of its ability to model structured dependencies. A feed-forward base model learns to predict raw vision outputs while being guided by that code. This assigns structured coordination to the code-generating component and high-dimensional output production to the base model.

The authors evaluate the approach on panoptic segmentation, depth prediction, and image colorization. UViM achieves competitive, near state-of-the-art results across these three different tasks. Those findings support the proposed division of labor as a promising route toward unified vision modeling. They demonstrate breadth across the evaluated tasks while retaining the same overall model form, rather than establishing that one architecture has already solved every vision problem.
summary.tldr: UViM combines autoregressively generated guiding codes with a feed-forward predictor to handle three diverse vision tasks using one model form.

title: UViM: A Unified Modeling Approach for Vision with Learned Guiding Codes

abstract: A simple model to study subspace clustering is the high-dimensional $k$-Gaussian mixture model where the cluster means are sparse vectors. Here we provide an exact asymptotic characterization of the statistically optimal reconstruction error in this model in the high-dimensional regime with extensive sparsity, i.e. when the fraction of non-zero components of the cluster means $\rho$, as well as the ratio $\alpha$ between the number of samples and the dimension are fixed, while the dimension diverges. We identify the information-theoretic threshold below which obtaining a positive correlation with the true cluster means is statistically impossible. Additionally, we investigate the performance of the approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm analyzed via its state evolution, which is conjectured to be optimal among polynomial algorithm for this task. We identify in particular the existence of a statistical-to-computational gap between the algorithm that requires a signal-to-noise ratio $\lambda_{\text{alg}} \ge k / \sqrt{\alpha}$ to perform better than random, and the information theoretic threshold at $\lambda_{\text{it}} \approx \sqrt{-k \rho \log{\rho}} / \sqrt{\alpha}$. Finally, we discuss the case of sub-extensive sparsity $\rho$ by comparing the performance of the AMP with other sparsity-enhancing algorithms, such as sparse-PCA and diagonal thresholding.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering through a high-dimensional Gaussian mixture model whose cluster means are sparse. Its main regime keeps the nonzero fraction of each mean and the sample-to-dimension ratio fixed while dimension grows without bound. Within that setting, the authors characterize the statistically optimal reconstruction error and identify when any positive correlation with the true means becomes impossible.

They separately analyze approximate message passing through its state evolution. The resulting algorithmic threshold can exceed the information-theoretic threshold, leaving a region where the data contains recoverable information but this algorithm cannot do better than random. Approximate message passing is conjectured to be optimal among polynomial-time algorithms for the task; the abstract does not establish that broader computational optimality.

The threshold expressions show how cluster count, sparsity, and sample density affect this separation. The paper also considers sub-extensive sparsity by comparing approximate message passing with sparse PCA and diagonal thresholding. Together, the results distinguish limits imposed by the available information from the performance of specific computational approaches.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes recovery thresholds for sparse Gaussian-mixture clustering and identifies a gap between statistical possibility and approximate message passing.

title: Subspace clustering in high-dimensions: Phase transitions & Statistical-to-Computational gap

abstract: We present Neural Correspondence Prior (NCP), a new paradigm for computing correspondences between 3D shapes. Our approach is fully unsupervised and can lead to high quality correspondences even in challenging cases such as sparse point clouds or non-isometric meshes, where current methods fail. Our first key observation is that, in line with neural priors observed in other domains, recent network architectures on 3D data, even without training, tend to produce pointwise features that induce plausible maps between rigid or non-rigid shapes. Secondly, we show that given a noisy map as input, training a feature extraction network with the input map as supervision, tends to remove artifacts from the input and can act as a powerful correspondence denoising mechanism, both between individual pairs and within a collection. With these observations in hand, we propose a two-stage unsupervised paradigm for shape matching, by (i) performing unsupervised training by adapting an existing approach to obtain an initial set of noisy matches, (ii) using these matches to train a network in a supervised manner. We demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the accuracy of the maps, especially when trained within a collection. We show that NCP is data-efficient, fast, and achieves state-of-the-art results on many tasks. Our code will be released after publication.
originalAbstract: We present Neural Correspondence Prior (NCP), a new paradigm for computing correspondences between 3D shapes. Our approach is fully unsupervised and can lead to high quality correspondences even in challenging cases such as sparse point clouds or non-isometric meshes, where current methods fail. Our first key observation is that, in line with neural priors observed in other domains, recent network architectures on 3D data, even without training, tend to produce pointwise features that induce plausible maps between rigid or non-rigid shapes. Secondly, we show that given a noisy map as input, training a feature extraction network with the input map as supervision, tends to remove artifacts from the input and can act as a powerful correspondence denoising mechanism, both between individual pairs and within a collection. With these observations in hand, we propose a two-stage unsupervised paradigm for shape matching, by (i) performing unsupervised training by adapting an existing approach to obtain an initial set of noisy matches, (ii) using these matches to train a network in a supervised manner. We demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the accuracy of the maps, especially when trained within a collection. We show that NCP is data-efficient, fast, and achieves state-of-the-art results on many tasks. Our code will be released after publication.

paragraphs: Matching 3D shapes means finding which points correspond across different objects or deformations. Neural Correspondence Prior, or NCP, builds on the observation that some 3D network architectures produce plausible matching features even before training. The authors also observe that training a feature extractor on noisy matches tends to remove artifacts from those matches.

The method turns these observations into a two-stage process. First, an adapted unsupervised approach produces an initial set of noisy correspondences. Second, those correspondences become supervision for training another network. Although the second stage uses a supervised training procedure, the overall approach remains unsupervised because the matching labels are generated by the method itself.

The authors report significant accuracy improvements, especially when training over a collection of shapes. NCP can also produce high-quality matches in challenging settings such as sparse point clouds and non-isometric meshes, where existing methods fail. Reported results describe the approach as fast, data-efficient, and state of the art on many tasks, supporting the use of neural feature learning as a correspondence-denoising mechanism.
summary.tldr: NCP improves unsupervised 3D shape matching by training networks on automatically generated noisy correspondences that the networks tend to denoise.

title: NCP: Neural Correspondence Prior for Effective Unsupervised Shape Matching

abstract: We investigate the optimal model size and number of tokens for training a transformer language model under a given compute budget. We find that current large language models are significantly undertrained, a consequence of the recent focus on scaling language models whilst keeping the amount of training data constant. By training over 400 language models ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, we find that for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled. We test this hypothesis by training a predicted compute-optimal model, Chinchilla, that uses the same compute budget as Gopher but with 70B parameters and 4$\times$ more data. Chinchilla uniformly and significantly outperformsGopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) on a large range of downstream evaluation tasks. This also means that Chinchilla uses substantially less compute for fine-tuning and inference, greatly facilitating downstream usage. As a highlight, Chinchilla reaches a state-of-the-art average accuracy of 67.5% on the MMLU benchmark, a 7% improvement over Gopher.

paragraphs: With a fixed training-compute budget, language-model developers must balance model size against the amount of text used for training. This paper investigates that balance through more than 400 models, ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters and trained on 5 to 500 billion tokens. The authors find that the large models they discuss are substantially undertrained.

Their empirical analysis indicates that compute-optimal scaling should increase model size and training tokens together: doubling the parameter count should also double the token count. They test this prediction with Chinchilla, a 70-billion-parameter model trained using the same compute budget as Gopher but four times as much data. Gopher has 280 billion parameters.

Chinchilla significantly outperforms Gopher and the other named large models across a broad range of downstream evaluations. It reaches 67.5% average accuracy on MMLU, reported as a 7% improvement over Gopher. Its smaller size also reduces fine-tuning and inference compute. The findings make data allocation a central part of efficient model scaling, with benefits extending beyond the initial training run.
summary.tldr: An empirical scaling study finds that increasing training data alongside model size yields better use of compute, as demonstrated by Chinchilla.

title: An empirical analysis of compute-optimal large language model training

abstract: Minimax optimization has served as the backbone of many machine learning problems. Although the convergence behavior of optimization algorithms has been extensively studied in minimax settings, their generalization guarantees, i.e., how the model trained on empirical data performs on the unseen testing data, have been relatively under-explored. A fundamental question remains elusive: What is a good metric to study generalization of minimax learners? In this paper, we aim to answer this question by first showing that primal risk, a universal metric to study generalization in minimization problems, fails in simple examples of minimax problems. Furthermore, another popular metric, the primal-dual risk, also fails to characterize the generalization behavior for minimax problems with nonconvexity, due to non-existence of saddle points. We thus propose a new metric to study generalization of minimax learners: the primal gap, to circumvent these issues. Next, we derive generalization bounds for the primal gap in nonconvex-concave settings. As byproducts of our analysis, we also solve two open questions: establishing generalization bounds for primal risk and primal-dual risk in this setting, and in the strong sense, i.e., without assuming that the maximization and expectation can be interchanged. Finally, we leverage this new metric to compare the generalization behavior of two popular algorithms - gradient descent-ascent (GDA) and gradient descent-max (GDMax) in minimax optimization.

paragraphs: Minimax learning involves interacting minimization and maximization problems, making generalization harder to assess than in ordinary minimization. This paper asks which metric properly captures how a solution learned from training data behaves on unseen data. The authors show that primal risk, a standard measure for minimization, fails in simple minimax examples.

They also identify a problem with primal-dual risk in nonconvex settings: saddle points may not exist, undermining its ability to characterize generalization. To address these issues, they introduce the primal gap and derive generalization bounds for nonconvex-concave problems. The metric is intended to make generalization analysis meaningful despite the identified failures of existing measures.

Their analysis additionally establishes bounds for primal and primal-dual risk in this setting without assuming that maximization can be interchanged with expectation. Finally, they use the new metric to compare gradient descent-ascent and gradient descent-max. The contribution is both a measurement framework and theoretical guarantees, clarifying how the choice of metric affects comparisons between minimax learners.
summary.tldr: The primal gap addresses failures of existing minimax generalization metrics and supports new bounds in nonconvex-concave settings.

title: What is a Good Metric to Study Generalization of Minimax Learners?

abstract: We propose a new fast algorithm to estimate any sparse generalized linear model with convex or non-convex separable penalties. Our algorithm is able to solve problems with millions of samples and features in seconds, by relying on coordinate descent, working sets and Anderson acceleration. It handles previously unaddressed models, and is extensively shown to improve state-of-art algorithms. We provide a flexible, scikit-learn compatible package, which easily handles customized datafits and penalties.
originalAbstract: We propose a new fast algorithm to estimate any sparse generalized linear model with convex or non-convex separable penalties. Our algorithm is able to solve problems with millions of samples and features in seconds, by relying on coordinate descent, working sets and Anderson acceleration. It handles previously unaddressed models, and is extensively shown to improve state-of-art algorithms. We provide a flexible, scikit-learn compatible package, which easily handles customized datafits and penalties.

paragraphs: This paper presents an algorithm and software package for fitting sparse generalized linear models. Sparsity means that a model can use only a subset of the available features, with a penalty encouraging unnecessary coefficients to disappear. The work extends beyond the familiar L1 penalty to support both convex and non-convex penalties, provided they are separable across coefficients.

The algorithm combines coordinate descent, working sets, and Anderson acceleration. These components organize optimization around individual coefficients, selected groups of variables, and accelerated progress between iterations. Their combination is intended to make a broad family of sparse modeling problems practical, rather than requiring a separate specialized solver for every choice of fitting objective and penalty.

The authors report solving problems involving millions of samples and features in seconds and show improvements over existing algorithms across extensive evaluations. They also report handling models previously unsupported by available approaches. The accompanying skglm package makes the method accessible through a scikit-learn-compatible interface and allows customized data-fitting terms and penalties, connecting the optimization contribution to flexible model development.
summary.tldr: skglm combines accelerated optimization with flexible software to fit large sparse models using convex or non-convex separable penalties.

title: Beyond L1: Faster and Better Sparse Models with skglm

abstract: In various engineering and applied science applications, repetitive numerical simulations of partial differential equations (PDEs) for varying input parameters are often required (e.g., aircraft shape optimization over many design parameters) and solvers are required to perform rapid execution. In this study, we suggest a path that potentially opens up a possibility for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), emerging deep-learning-based solvers, to be considered as one such solver. Although PINNs have pioneered a proper integration of deep-learning and scientific computing, they require repetitive time-consuming training of neural networks, which is not suitable for many-query scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a lightweight low-rank PINNs containing only hundreds of model parameters and an associated hypernetwork-based meta-learning algorithm, which allows efficient approximation of solutions of PDEs for varying ranges of PDE input parameters. Moreover, we show that the proposed method is effective in overcoming a challenging issue, known as "failure modes" of PINNs.

paragraphs: Engineering workflows often require solving a partial differential equation repeatedly as input parameters change. A solver that works well once may still be unsuitable when many such queries are needed. Physics-informed neural networks integrate physical equations with neural learning, but repeatedly training them can be too time-consuming for these applications.

The paper proposes lightweight, low-rank physics-informed networks containing only hundreds of model parameters, together with a hypernetwork-based meta-learning algorithm. This combination is designed to approximate PDE solutions efficiently across varying ranges of input parameters. It targets the repeated-solution workload directly, where the cost of obtaining a new solution matters alongside the ability to represent one.

The authors also report that their method effectively addresses challenging behavior described as PINN failure modes. The broader claim remains a potential pathway toward using PINNs as rapid solvers in many-query settings. The contribution is therefore a compact network design paired with a learning strategy for parameter variation, supported by the stated effectiveness on solution approximation and failure-mode challenges.
summary.tldr: Low-rank physics-informed networks and hypernetwork meta-learning offer a potential route to efficient repeated PDE solving across changing parameters.

title: Hypernetwork-based Meta-Learning for Low-Rank Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Diffusion-based image super-resolution (SR) methods are mainly limited by the low inference speed due to the requirements of hundreds or even thousands of sampling steps. Existing acceleration sampling techniques inevitably sacrifice performance to some extent, leading to over-blurry SR results. To address this issue, we propose a novel and efficient diffusion model for SR that significantly reduces the number of diffusion steps, thereby eliminating the need for post-acceleration during inference and its associated performance deterioration. Our method constructs a Markov chain that transfers between the high-resolution image and the low-resolution image by shifting the residual between them, substantially improving the transition efficiency. Additionally, an elaborate noise schedule is developed to flexibly control the shifting speed and the noise strength during the diffusion process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method obtains superior or at least comparable performance to current state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets, \textit{\textbf{even only with 20 sampling steps}}. Our code and model will be made publicly.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can produce high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs, but many require hundreds or thousands of sampling steps. Accelerating an existing sampling process can reduce output quality and introduce blur. ResShift addresses the source of this cost by designing a diffusion process for super-resolution that needs fewer steps from the outset.

The method constructs a Markov chain connecting high-resolution and low-resolution images by progressively shifting the residual, or difference, between them. This makes the transition directly reflect the super-resolution task. A specially designed noise schedule controls both how quickly the residual shifts and how much noise enters the process, providing flexibility in the transition.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show performance superior to or at least comparable with the state-of-the-art methods considered, using only 20 sampling steps. The result supports redesigning the diffusion process around the relationship between input and output images. Its efficiency comes from the proposed transition itself, avoiding the need to rely on a separate inference-time acceleration procedure.
summary.tldr: ResShift redesigns diffusion around the difference between low- and high-resolution images, achieving competitive super-resolution with 20 sampling steps.

title: ResShift: Efficient Diffusion Model for Image Super-resolution by Residual Shifting

abstract: Visual navigation has been widely studied under the assumption that there may be several clear routes to reach the goal. However, in more practical scenarios such as a house with several messy rooms, there may not. Interactive Navigation (InterNav) considers agents navigating to their goals more effectively with object interactions, posing new challenges of learning interaction dynamics and extra action space. Previous works learn single vision-to-action policy with the guidance of designed representations. However, the causality between actions and outcomes is prone to be confounded when the attributes of obstacles are diverse and hard to measure. Learning policy for long-term action planning in complex scenes also leads to extensive inefficient exploration. In this paper, we introduce a causal diagram of InterNav clarifying the confounding bias caused by obstacles. To address the problem, we propose a multi-policy model that enables the exploration of counterfactual interactions as well as reduces unnecessary exploration. We develop a large-scale dataset containing 600k task episodes in 12k multi-room scenes based on the ProcTHOR simulator and showcase the effectiveness of our method with the evaluations on our dataset.

paragraphs: Navigation through a cluttered home may require interacting with objects because a clear route to the destination may not exist. Interactive navigation therefore involves learning both where to move and how actions change the surroundings. Diverse obstacle properties complicate this learning, especially when those properties are difficult to measure.

The paper introduces a causal diagram to explain how obstacles can confound the relationship between actions and outcomes. This helps frame a difficulty with learning a single policy directly from vision to actions: an observed outcome may reflect obstacle attributes as well as the action taken. Long sequences of decisions also create opportunities for inefficient exploration.

CaMP uses multiple policies to support exploration of counterfactual interactions while reducing unnecessary exploration. The authors also build a ProcTHOR-based dataset with 600,000 task episodes across 12,000 multi-room scenes. Evaluations on that dataset demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution joins a causal account of interaction difficulties with a planning approach and a large evaluation setting for navigation that includes object interactions.
summary.tldr: CaMP uses causal reasoning and multiple policies to improve interactive navigation through cluttered multi-room scenes.

title: CaMP: Causal Multi-policy Planning for Interactive Navigation in Multi-room Scenes

abstract: We propose a general class of sample based explanations of machine learning models, which we term generalized representers. To measure the effect of a training sample on a model's test prediction, generalized representers use two components: a global sample importance that quantifies the importance of the training point to the model and is invariant to test samples, and a local sample importance that measures similarity between the training sample and the test point with a kernel. A key contribution of the paper is to show that generalized representers are the only class of sample based explanations satisfying a natural set of axiomatic properties. We discuss approaches to extract global importances given a kernel, and also natural choices of kernels given modern non-linear models. As we show, many popular existing sample based explanations could be cast as generalized representers with particular choices of kernels and approaches to extract global importances. Additionally, we conduct empirical comparisons of different generalized representers on two image classification datasets.

A key contribution of the paper is to show that generalized representers are the only class of sample based explanations satisfying a natural set of axiomatic properties. paragraphs: Sample-based explanations connect a model's prediction to particular training examples. This paper introduces generalized representers, a class of explanations that separates a training example's overall importance from its relevance to the specific test example. That separation provides a shared structure for reasoning about how training data contributes to individual predictions.

The global component assigns importance to a training point independently of which test point is being explained. The local component uses a kernel to measure similarity between the training and test points. The authors show that generalized representers are the only class satisfying their chosen set of natural axiomatic properties. This uniqueness is conditional on those properties.

The paper discusses how to extract global importance values for a given kernel and how to choose kernels for modern nonlinear models. It also shows that many popular explanation methods fit this framework through particular choices of these components. Empirical comparisons on two image classification datasets examine different generalized representers. The contribution supplies both an axiomatic characterization and a common language for comparing existing sample-based explanations.
summary.tldr: Generalized representers unify sample-based explanations through global training-point importance and local kernel similarity.

title: Sample based Explanations via Generalized Representers

abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting (CoT) and tool augmentation have been validated in recent work as effective practices for improving large language models (LLMs) to perform step-by-step reasoning on complex math-related tasks.However, most existing math reasoning datasets may not be able to fully evaluate and analyze the ability of LLMs in manipulating tools and performing reasoning, as they often only require very few invocations of tools or miss annotations for evaluating intermediate reasoning steps, thus supporting only outcome evaluation.To address the issue, we construct **CARP**, a new Chinese dataset consisting of 4,886 computation-intensive algebra problems with formulated annotations on intermediate steps, facilitating the evaluation of the intermediate reasoning process.In CARP, we test four LLMs with CoT prompting, and find that they are all prone to make mistakes at the early steps of the solution, leading to incorrect answers.Based on this finding, we propose a new approach that can facilitate the deliberation on reasoning steps with tool interfaces, namely **DELI**.In DELI, we first initialize a step-by-step solution based on retrieved exemplars, then iterate two deliberation procedures that check and refine the intermediate steps of the generated solution, from both tool manipulation and natural language reasoning perspectives, until solutions converge or the maximum iteration is achieved.Experimental results on CARP and six other datasets show that the proposed DELI mostly outperforms competitive baselines, and can further boost the performance of existing CoT methods.Our data and code are available at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/CARP.

paragraphs: Evaluating a final math answer alone can hide where a language model's reasoning or tool use went wrong. This paper introduces CARP, a Chinese dataset containing 4,886 computation-intensive algebra problems with annotations for intermediate steps. These annotations make it possible to examine the solution process as well as its outcome.

Tests of four language models using chain-of-thought prompting reveal a tendency to make errors early in solutions, leading to incorrect answers. The authors respond with DELI, an approach that revisits intermediate reasoning. It first generates a step-by-step solution using retrieved examples, then repeatedly checks and refines that solution.

DELI alternates two deliberation procedures, one addressing tool manipulation and the other natural-language reasoning. Iteration stops when solutions converge or a maximum iteration count is reached. Across CARP and six other datasets, DELI mostly outperforms competitive baselines and can improve existing chain-of-thought methods. The findings support evaluating and revising the intermediate process, especially when successful reasoning requires coordinating calculations with tool interfaces.
summary.tldr: CARP evaluates intermediate mathematical reasoning, while DELI improves solutions by repeatedly checking tool use and reasoning steps.

title: Evaluating and Improving Tool-Augmented Computation-Intensive Math Reasoning

abstract: Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance is a powerful tool for comparing and aligning probability distributions supported on different metric spaces. Recently, GW has become the main modeling technique for aligning heterogeneous data for a wide range of graph learning tasks. However, the GW distance is known to be highly sensitive to outliers, which can result in large inaccuracies if the outliers are given the same weight as other samples in the objective function. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a new and robust version of the GW distance called RGW. RGW features optimistically perturbed marginal constraints within a Kullback-Leibler divergence-based ambiguity set. To make the benefits of RGW more accessible in practice, we develop a computationally efficient and theoretically provable procedure using Bregman proximal alternating linearized minimization algorithm. Through extensive experimentation, we validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the effectiveness of RGW on real-world graph learning tasks, such as subgraph matching and partial shape correspondence.

To mitigate this issue, we introduce a new and robust version of the GW distance called RGW. RGW features optimistically perturbed marginal constraints within a Kullback-Leibler divergence-based ambiguity set. To make the benefits of RGW more accessible in practice, we develop a computationally efficient and theoretically provable procedure using Bregman proximal alternating linearized minimization algorithm. Through extensive experimentation, we validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the effectiveness of RGW on real-world graph learning tasks, such as subgraph matching and partial shape correspondence.

paragraphs: Gromov-Wasserstein distance compares distributions whose underlying spaces may differ, making it useful for aligning heterogeneous graph data. However, outliers can strongly distort the comparison when the objective gives them the same weight as ordinary samples. This paper introduces a robust variant, RGW, to reduce that sensitivity.

RGW permits favorable adjustments to the marginal constraints within an ambiguity set defined using Kullback-Leibler divergence. In plain terms, the formulation allows controlled flexibility in how distributional mass participates in the alignment. That flexibility is the mechanism used to address the inaccuracies caused by outliers in the original comparison objective.

The authors also develop a computationally efficient solution procedure based on Bregman proximal alternating linearized minimization and provide theoretical support for it. Experiments validate the theoretical results and demonstrate effectiveness on real-world graph tasks, including subgraph matching and partial shape correspondence. The contribution combines a more robust comparison objective with a practical optimization method, making the proposed treatment of outliers usable in graph alignment problems.
summary.tldr: RGW makes Gromov-Wasserstein graph alignment more resistant to outliers through controlled flexibility in its marginal constraints.

title: Outlier-Robust Gromov-Wasserstein for Graph Data

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms typically utilize learning and/or planning techniques to derive effective policies. The integration of both approaches has proven to be highly successful in addressing complex sequential decision-making challenges, as evidenced by algorithms such as AlphaZero and MuZero, which consolidate the planning process into a parametric search-policy. AIXI, the most potent theoretical universal agent, leverages planning through comprehensive search as its primary means to find an optimal policy. Here we define an alternative universal agent, which we call Self-AIXI, that on the contrary to AIXI, maximally exploits learning to obtain good policies. It does so by self-predicting its own stream of action data, which is generated, similarly to other TD(0) agents, by taking an action maximization step over the current on-policy (universal mixture-policy) Q-value estimates. We prove that Self-AIXI converges to AIXI, and inherits a series of properties like maximal Legg-Hutter intelligence and the self-optimizing property.

Here we define an alternative universal agent, which we call Self-AIXI, that on the contrary to AIXI, maximally exploits learning to obtain good policies. paragraphs: This paper studies how a theoretical universal reinforcement-learning agent can obtain good policies through learning. Its reference point is AIXI, which relies primarily on comprehensive planning search to identify an optimal policy. The authors define an alternative agent, Self-AIXI, that places self-prediction at the center of policy learning.

Self-AIXI predicts its own stream of actions. That stream is generated by selecting actions that maximize its current on-policy Q-value estimates, using a universal mixture policy. The authors relate this action-generation mechanism to TD(0) agents. The design connects the agent's present value estimates, its resulting actions, and the learning process that predicts those actions.

The main results are theoretical: Self-AIXI converges to AIXI and inherits properties including maximal Legg-Hutter intelligence and self-optimization. This establishes a formal connection between the proposed learning-centered agent and the planning-centered reference. The significance lies in demonstrating that self-prediction can underpin an alternative universal-agent construction with these stated properties, extending the theoretical picture of how learning and planning relate.
summary.tldr: Self-AIXI learns by predicting its own actions and is proved to converge to AIXI while inheriting key theoretical intelligence properties.

title: Self-Predictive Universal AI

abstract: Neural network based computer vision systems are typically built on a backbone, a pretrained or randomly initialized feature extractor. Several years ago, the default option was an ImageNet-trained convolutional neural network. However, the recent past has seen the emergence of countless backbones pretrained using various algorithms and datasets. While this abundance of choice has led to performance increases for a range of systems, it is difficult for practitioners to make informed decisions about which backbone to choose. Battle of the Backbones (BoB) makes this choice easier by benchmarking a diverse suite of pretrained models, including vision-language models, those trained via self-supervised learning, and the Stable Diffusion backbone, across a diverse set of computer vision tasks ranging from classification to object detection to OOD generalization and more. Furthermore, BoB sheds light on promising directions for the research community to advance computer vision by illuminating strengths and weakness of existing approaches through a comprehensive analysis conducted on more than 1500 training runs. While vision transformers (ViTs) and self-supervised learning (SSL) are increasingly popular, we find that convolutional neural networks pretrained in a supervised fashion on large training sets still perform best on most tasks among the models we consider. Moreover, in apples-to-apples comparisons on the same architectures and similarly sized pretraining datasets, we find that SSL backbones are highly competitive, indicating that future works should perform SSL pretraining with advanced architectures and larger pretraining datasets. We release the raw results of our experiments along with code that allows researchers to put their own backbones through the gauntlet here: https://github.com/hsouri/Battle-of-the-Backbones.

paragraphs: A vision backbone is the feature extractor on which a larger computer vision system is built. With many architectures, pretraining objectives, and training datasets available, choosing one has become difficult. Battle of the Backbones addresses this practical problem through a broad comparison of pretrained models across several kinds of vision tasks.

The benchmark includes vision-language models, self-supervised models, and the Stable Diffusion backbone. It examines tasks including classification, object detection, and generalization beyond the training distribution, using more than 1,500 training runs. Across the models considered, convolutional networks trained with supervision on large datasets perform best on most tasks.

The comparison also separates that overall finding from more controlled comparisons. When architecture and pretraining dataset size are comparable, self-supervised backbones are highly competitive. This suggests that architecture and data scale deserve attention alongside the learning objective. The authors consequently point toward self-supervised pretraining with stronger architectures and larger datasets, and release results and evaluation code so additional backbones can be assessed.
summary.tldr: A broad vision benchmark finds supervised convolutional backbones strongest on most tested tasks, with self-supervised models competitive in matched comparisons.

title: Battle of the Backbones: A Large-Scale Comparison of Pretrained Models across Computer Vision Tasks

abstract: Large language models have shown astonishing performance on a wide range of reasoning tasks. In this paper, we investigate whether they could reason about real-world events and help improve the prediction performance of event sequence models. We design LAMP, a framework that integrates a large language model in event prediction. Particularly, the language model performs abductive reasoning to assist an event sequence model: the event model proposes predictions on future events given the past; instructed by a few expert-annotated demonstrations, the language model learns to suggest possible causes for each proposal; a search module finds out the previous events that match the causes; a scoring function learns to examine whether the retrieved events could actually cause the proposal. Through extensive experiments on several challenging real-world datasets, we demonstrate that our framework---thanks to the reasoning capabilities of large language models---could significantly outperform the state-of-the-art event sequence models.

paragraphs: LAMP investigates whether a language model can help predict future events by reasoning about possible explanations for them. It combines this reasoning with an event sequence model that already proposes future events based on past observations. The language model contributes abductive reasoning: suggesting causes that could make a proposed event plausible.

A few expert-annotated demonstrations guide the language model in producing those possible causes. A search module then retrieves earlier events matching the suggestions. Finally, a learned scoring function examines whether those retrieved events could cause the proposed future event. The framework thus connects a proposed prediction to potentially relevant evidence in the observed history.

Experiments on several challenging real-world datasets show that LAMP can substantially outperform state-of-the-art event sequence models. The result supports using language-model reasoning as an additional component in event prediction. Its cause suggestions are intermediate hypotheses assessed through retrieval and scoring; the described evaluation establishes improved prediction performance rather than verified causal explanations for every event.
summary.tldr: LAMP improves event prediction by using language-model-generated possible causes to retrieve and score relevant historical events.

title: Language Models Can Improve Event Prediction by Few-Shot Abductive Reasoning

abstract: Achieving a balance between image quality (precision) and diversity (recall) is a significant challenge in the domain of generative models. Current state-of-the-art models primarily rely on optimizing heuristics, such as the Fr\'echet Inception Distance. While recent developments have introduced principled methods for evaluating precision and recall, they have yet to be successfully integrated into the training of generative models. Our main contribution is a novel training method for generative models, such as Generative Adversarial Networks and Normalizing Flows, which explicitly optimizes a user-defined trade-off between precision and recall. More precisely, we show that achieving a specified precision-recall trade-off corresponds to minimizing a unique $f$-divergence from a family we call the \mbox{\em PR-divergences}. Conversely, any $f$-divergence can be written as a linear combination of PR-divergences and corresponds to a weighted precision-recall trade-off. Through comprehensive evaluations, we show that our approach improves the performance of existing state-of-the-art models like BigGAN in terms of either precision or recall when tested on datasets such as ImageNet.

paragraphs: Generative image models face a trade-off between producing convincing individual images and covering a broad range of possibilities. The paper describes these goals as precision and recall. Although principled ways to evaluate them exist, training has largely relied on heuristic objectives. The authors propose training GANs and normalizing flows directly for a user-selected precision-recall balance.

The mathematical contribution connects each specified trade-off to minimizing a unique member of a family called PR-divergences. A divergence measures a difference between probability distributions, so this connection turns the desired balance into a training objective. Conversely, the authors show that any f-divergence can be expressed as a linear combination of PR-divergences, corresponding to a weighted precision-recall trade-off.

Evaluations show improvements in either precision or recall for existing models, including BigGAN on datasets such as ImageNet. The finding supports explicit control over which aspect of generation is emphasized. It does not imply that every choice improves both goals simultaneously; the method is designed to optimize the balance selected by the user.
summary.tldr: PR-divergences turn a user-chosen balance between image quality and diversity into an explicit generative-model training objective.

title: Precision-Recall Divergence Optimization for Generative Modeling with GANs and Normalizing Flows

abstract: Causal effect estimation from data typically requires assumptions about the cause-effect relations either explicitly in the form of a causal graph structure within the Pearlian framework, or implicitly in terms of (conditional) independence statements between counterfactual variables within the potential outcomes framework. When the treatment variable and the outcome variable are confounded, front-door adjustment is an important special case where, given the graph, causal effect of the treatment on the target can be estimated using post-treatment variables. However, the exact formula for front-door adjustment depends on the structure of the graph, which is difficult to learn in practice. In this work, we provide testable conditional independence statements to compute the causal effect using front-door-like adjustment without knowing the graph under limited structural side information. We show that our method is applicable in scenarios where knowing the Markov equivalence class is not sufficient for causal effect estimation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a class of random graphs as well as real causal fairness benchmarks.

paragraphs: Estimating a causal effect usually requires assumptions about how variables influence one another. When treatment and outcome are confounded, front-door adjustment can sometimes recover the effect using variables measured after treatment. The difficulty is that its exact formula depends on the causal graph, whose structure can be hard to learn from data.

This paper develops a way to perform front-door-like adjustment using testable conditional independence statements and limited structural side information. The method does not require knowing the full graph. It connects observable independence relationships with the additional structural knowledge needed to compute the causal effect in the settings covered by the theory.

The authors show that the approach applies in some scenarios where knowing the Markov equivalence class is insufficient for effect estimation. They also demonstrate it on a class of random graphs and real causal fairness benchmarks. The result identifies circumstances in which limited structural information, paired with testable relationships, can support causal estimation beyond what equivalence-class knowledge alone provides.
summary.tldr: Testable independence relationships and limited structural information enable front-door-like causal adjustment without a fully known graph.

title: Front-door Adjustment Beyond Markov Equivalence with Limited Graph Knowledge

abstract: We introduce MLFMF, a collection of data sets for benchmarking recommendation systems used to support formalization of mathematics with proof assistants. These systems help humans identify which previous entries (theorems, constructions, datatypes, and postulates) are relevant in proving a new theorem or carrying out a new construction. Each data set is derived from a library of formalized mathematics written in proof assistants Agda or Lean. The collection includes the largest Lean 4 library Mathlib, and some of the largest Agda libraries: the standard library, the library of univalent mathematics Agda-unimath, and the TypeTopology library. Each data set represents the corresponding library in two ways: as a heterogeneous network, and as a list of s-expressions representing the syntax trees of all the entries in the library. The network contains the (modular) structure of the library and the references between entries, while the s-expressions give complete and easily parsed information about every entry.We report baseline results using standard graph and word embeddings, tree ensembles, and instance-based learning algorithms. The MLFMF data sets provide solid benchmarking support for further investigation of the numerous machine learning approaches to formalized mathematics. The methodology used to extract the networks and the s-expressions readily applies to other libraries, and is applicable to other proof assistants. With more than $250\,000$ entries in total, this is currently the largest collection of formalized mathematical knowledge in machine learnable format.

paragraphs: When formalizing mathematics with a proof assistant, finding relevant existing knowledge is an important task. MLFMF provides datasets for benchmarking recommendation systems that help identify useful theorems, constructions, datatypes, and postulates. The collection draws on Lean’s Mathlib and several large Agda libraries, giving learning systems access to substantial bodies of formalized mathematics.

Each library is represented in two complementary forms. A heterogeneous network records its modular organization and references between entries. A collection of s-expressions represents the syntax trees of individual entries, preserving their complete contents in an easily parsed format. Together, these forms expose both how mathematical entries relate to one another and how each entry is structured internally.

The authors report baseline results using graph and word embeddings, tree ensembles, and instance-based learning. With more than 250,000 entries, they describe MLFMF as the largest collection of formalized mathematical knowledge in machine-learnable form at the time of the work. The extraction methodology can extend to other libraries and proof assistants, making the contribution a reusable benchmarking approach as well as a specific dataset collection.
summary.tldr: MLFMF turns large formal mathematics libraries into graph and syntax datasets for benchmarking recommendations of relevant mathematical knowledge.

title: MLFMF: Data Sets for Machine Learning for Mathematical Formalization

abstract: Common explanations for shortcut learning assume that the shortcut improves prediction only under the training distribution. Thus, models trained in the typical way by minimizing log-loss using gradient descent, which we call default-ERM, should utilize the shortcut. However, even when the stable feature determines the label in the training distribution and the shortcut does not provide any additional information, like in perception tasks, default-ERM exhibits shortcut learning. Why are such solutions preferred when the loss can be driven to zero when using the stable feature alone? By studying a linear perception task, we show that default-ERM’s preference for maximizing the margin, even without overparameterization, leads to models that depend more on the shortcut than the stable feature. This insight suggests that default-ERM’s implicit inductive bias towards max-margin may be unsuitable for perception tasks. Instead, we consider inductive biases toward uniform margins. We show that uniform margins guarantee sole dependence on the perfect stable feature in the linear perception task and suggest alternative loss functions, termed margin control (MARG-CTRL), that encourage uniform-margin solutions. MARG-CTRL techniques mitigate shortcut learning on a variety of vision and language tasks, showing that changing inductive biases can remove the need for complicated shortcut-mitigating methods in perception tasks.

paragraphs: Shortcut learning can occur even when a stable feature already determines the label and a shortcut adds no information in the training distribution. This paper investigates why standard training still favors the shortcut in that situation. Its focus is gradient descent applied to log-loss, a combination the authors call default-ERM.

Through a linear perception task, the authors show that this training procedure's preference for maximum-margin solutions can make predictions depend more on the shortcut than on the stable feature. This happens even without overparameterization. The result identifies the optimization procedure's implicit preference as a source of shortcut reliance, beyond explanations based solely on differences between training and deployment data.

The authors instead study uniform margins. In their linear task, uniform margins guarantee dependence only on the perfect stable feature. They propose margin-control losses that encourage such solutions and report reduced shortcut learning across vision and language tasks. The guarantee belongs to the analyzed linear setting; the broader task results provide empirical support for changing the training bias.
summary.tldr: Standard gradient-based log-loss training can favor redundant shortcuts, while losses encouraging uniform margins reduce shortcut reliance.

title: Don’t blame Dataset Shift! Shortcut Learning due to Gradients and Cross Entropy

abstract: We propose a novel neural algorithm for the fundamental problem of computing the entropic optimal transport (EOT) plan between probability distributions which are accessible by samples. Our algorithm is based on the saddle point reformulation of the dynamic version of EOT which is known as the Schrödinger Bridge problem. In contrast to the prior methods for large-scale EOT, our algorithm is end-to-end and consists of a single learning step, has fast inference procedure, and allows handling small values of the entropy regularization coefficient which is of particular importance in some applied problems. Empirically, we show the performance of the method on several large-scale EOT tasks. The code for the ENOT solver can be found at https://github.com/ngushchin/EntropicNeuralOptimalTransport

paragraphs: This paper develops a neural algorithm for computing an entropic optimal transport plan between two probability distributions available through samples. The task is to learn how the distributions should be connected under an entropy-regularized transport objective. Working from samples makes the formulation relevant when the distributions are represented by observed data.

The algorithm uses the dynamic version of this problem, known as the Schrödinger Bridge problem. Its mathematical starting point is a saddle point reformulation of that dynamic objective. This provides the basis for an end-to-end learning procedure with a single learning stage, connecting the transport problem to a diffusion-process formulation.

The authors emphasize fast inference and the ability to handle small entropy regularization coefficients, which matter in some applications. They demonstrate the method on several large-scale entropic transport tasks. The stated contribution combines the mathematical reformulation with a simpler overall training procedure and support for a practically relevant regularization regime; the abstract reports empirical demonstrations without claiming a particular numerical improvement.
summary.tldr: A diffusion-based neural solver computes entropic transport with one learning stage, fast inference, and support for small regularization coefficients.

title: Entropic Neural Optimal Transport via Diffusion Processes

abstract: While several recent matrix completion methods are developed to deal with non-uniform observation probabilities across matrix entries, very few allow the missingness to depend on the mostly unobserved matrix measurements, which is generally ill-posed. We aim to tackle a subclass of these ill-posed settings, characterized by a flexible separable observation probability assumption that can depend on the matrix measurements. We propose a regularized pairwise pseudo-likelihood approach for matrix completion and prove that the proposed estimator can asymptotically recover the low-rank parameter matrix up to an identifiable equivalence class of a constant shift and scaling, at a near-optimal asymptotic convergence rate of the standard well-posed (non-informative missing) setting, while effectively mitigating the impact of informative missingness. The efficacy of our method is validated via numerical experiments, positioning it as a robust tool for matrix completion to mitigate data bias.

paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates missing entries using patterns in the entries that remain visible. The problem becomes harder when an entry's chance of being observed depends on its own value. In that situation, the observed entries can systematically misrepresent the full matrix, and recovering the underlying structure is generally ill-posed.

The paper addresses a particular subclass of this problem under a flexible separability assumption on observation probabilities. That assumption still permits missingness to depend on matrix measurements. The authors develop a regularized pairwise pseudo-likelihood estimator, using pairwise relationships to estimate a low-rank parameter matrix while reducing the effects of informative missingness.

The recovery guarantee is asymptotic and has an important qualification: it identifies the matrix only up to a constant shift and scaling. Within that equivalence class, the convergence rate is near the optimal asymptotic rate for the standard setting without informative missingness. Numerical experiments support the method's effectiveness, showing how structured assumptions can make a difficult missing-data problem more tractable.
summary.tldr: A pairwise estimator addresses value-dependent missingness under a separability assumption, recovering low-rank structure asymptotically up to shift and scale.

title: A Pairwise Pseudo-likelihood Approach for Matrix Completion with Informative Missingness

abstract: Many computational tasks can be naturally expressed as a composition of a DNN followed by a program written in a traditional programming language or an API call to an LLM. We call such composites "neural programs" and focus on the problem of learning the DNN parameters when the training data consist of end-to-end input-output labels for the composite. When the program is written in a differentiable logic programming language, techniques from neurosymbolic learning are applicable, but in general, the learning for neural programs requires estimating the gradients of black-box components. We present an algorithm for learning neural programs, called ISED, that only relies on input-output samples of black-box components. For evaluation, we introduce new benchmarks that involve calls to modern LLMs such as GPT-4 and also consider benchmarks from the neurosymbolic learning literature. Our evaluation shows that for the latter benchmarks, ISED has comparable performance to state-of-the-art neurosymbolic frameworks. For the former, we use adaptations of prior work on gradient approximations of black-box components as a baseline, and show that ISED achieves comparable accuracy but in a more data- and sample-efficient manner.

paragraphs: A neural program combines a deep neural network with a downstream program or a call to a language model. The learning problem becomes difficult when examples label only the final output of this whole composition. Training must work out how changes to the neural network affect results after the downstream component has acted.

Differentiable logic programs offer one route through this problem, but ordinary programs and external model calls may not expose usable gradients. The paper introduces ISED, an algorithm that learns neural programs using only input-output samples from these black-box components. This makes the learning approach applicable without requiring access to their internal computations.

The evaluation includes established neurosymbolic benchmarks and new tasks involving modern language-model calls, including GPT-4. ISED achieves performance comparable to leading neurosymbolic frameworks on the former. On the language-model benchmarks, it matches the accuracy of adapted gradient-approximation baselines while using data and samples more efficiently. The reported benefit is thus efficiency without sacrificing comparable accuracy in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: ISED trains neural networks inside programs with black-box components using input-output samples, achieving comparable accuracy with greater efficiency on language-model benchmarks.

title: Data-Efficient Learning with Neural Programs

abstract: Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that incorporate E(3) symmetry have achieved significant success in various scientific applications. As one of the most successful models, EGNN leverages a simple scalarization technique to perform equivariant message passing over only Cartesian vectors (i.e., 1st-degree steerable vectors), enjoying greater efficiency and efficacy compared to equivariant GNNs using higher-degree steerable vectors. This success suggests that higher-degree representations might be unnecessary. In this paper, we disprove this hypothesis by exploring the expressivity of equivariant GNNs on symmetric structures, including $k$-fold rotations and regular polyhedra. We theoretically demonstrate that equivariant GNNs will always degenerate to a zero function if the degree of the output representations is fixed to 1 or other specific values. Based on this theoretical insight, we propose HEGNN, a high-degree version of EGNN to increase the expressivity by incorporating high-degree steerable vectors while maintaining EGNN's efficiency through the scalarization trick. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that HEGNN not only aligns with our theoretical analyses on toy datasets consisting of symmetric structures, but also shows substantial improvements on more complicated datasets such as $N$-body and MD17. Our theoretical findings and empirical results potentially open up new possibilities for the research of equivariant GNNs.

paragraphs: Equivariant graph neural networks are designed so that their outputs transform consistently with spatial transformations of their inputs. EGNN performs this computation using ordinary Cartesian vectors and a scalarization technique. Its efficiency and strong performance raise a natural question: do more elaborate, higher-degree representations provide anything essential?

The paper examines that question on symmetric structures, including repeated rotational arrangements and regular polyhedra. The authors prove that, for the symmetry settings they analyze, fixing output representations to degree one or certain other degrees forces the output to collapse to zero. This identifies an expressivity restriction tied to the interaction between structural symmetry and representation degree.

Their proposed HEGNN introduces higher-degree steerable vectors while retaining EGNN's scalarization approach to preserve efficiency. Experiments on symmetric toy structures agree with the theoretical analysis, and results on N-body and MD17 datasets show substantial improvements. Together, these findings establish that higher-degree representations can matter, with both a theoretical reason and empirical support in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies symmetry-driven expressivity failures in low-degree equivariant GNNs and introduces HEGNN to address them with higher-degree representations.

title: Are High-Degree Representations Really Unnecessary in Equivariant Graph Neural Networks?

abstract: Generative AI and large language models hold great promise in enhancing programming education by generating individualized feedback and hints for learners. Recent works have primarily focused on improving the quality of generated feedback to achieve human tutors' quality. While quality is an important performance criterion, it is not the only criterion to optimize for real-world educational deployments. In this paper, we benchmark language models for programming feedback generation across several performance criteria, including quality, cost, time, and data privacy. The key idea is to leverage recent advances in the new paradigm of in-browser inference that allow running these models directly in the browser, thereby providing direct benefits across cost and data privacy. To boost the feedback quality of small models compatible with in-browser inference engines, we develop a fine-tuning pipeline based on GPT-4 generated synthetic data. We showcase the efficacy of fine-tuned Llama3-8B and Phi3-3.8B 4-bit quantized models using WebLLM's in-browser inference engine on three different Python programming datasets. We will release the full implementation along with a web app and datasets to facilitate further research on in-browser language models.

While quality is an important performance criterion, it is not the only criterion to optimize for real-world educational deployments. In this paper, we benchmark language models for programming feedback generation across several performance criteria, including quality, cost, time, and data privacy. The key idea is to leverage recent advances in the new paradigm of in-browser inference that allow running these models directly in the browser, thereby providing direct benefits across cost and data privacy. To boost the feedback quality of small models compatible with in-browser inference engines, we develop a fine-tuning pipeline based on GPT-4 generated synthetic data. We showcase the efficacy of fine-tuned Llama3-8B and Phi3-3.8B 4-bit quantized models using WebLLM's in-browser inference engine on three different Python programming datasets. We will release the full implementation along with a web app and datasets to facilitate further research on in-browser language models.

This paper benchmarks language models across those criteria instead of judging them solely by how closely their feedback resembles that of a human tutor. It treats deployment requirements as part of the educational task.

The approach uses in-browser inference, allowing models to run directly within the browser. This offers direct cost and privacy benefits, while creating a need for smaller models that still generate good feedback. To improve their quality, the authors build a fine-tuning pipeline using synthetic training data generated by GPT-4.

The study demonstrates fine-tuned Llama3-8B and Phi3-3.8B models, both using 4-bit quantization, through WebLLM’s browser inference engine on three Python programming datasets. The results support the usefulness of adapting compact models for this setting. The contribution connects feedback quality with practical delivery constraints, showing how model training and local execution can be evaluated together when designing programming education tools.
summary.tldr: Hints-In-Browser evaluates locally running programming-feedback models across quality, cost, latency, and privacy, using synthetic-data fine-tuning to improve small models.

title: Hints-In-Browser: Benchmarking Language Models for Programming Feedback Generation

abstract: Predicting potential outcomes of interventions from observational data is crucial for decision-making in medicine, but the task is challenging due to the fundamental problem of causal inference. Existing methods are largely limited to point estimates of potential outcomes with no uncertain quantification; thus, the full information about the distributions of potential outcomes is typically ignored. In this paper, we propose a novel causal diffusion model called DiffPO, which is carefully designed for reliable inferences in medicine by learning the distribution of potential outcomes. In our DiffPO, we leverage a tailored conditional denoising diffusion model to learn complex distributions, where we address the selection bias through a novel orthogonal diffusion loss. Another strength of our DiffPO method is that it is highly flexible (e.g., it can also be used to estimate different causal quantities such as CATE). Across a wide range of experiments, we show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Its objective is to learn distributions of potential outcomes, giving a richer description of what an intervention could produce than a point estimate alone.

The method uses a conditional denoising diffusion model tailored to this causal task. This component learns complex outcome distributions, while a specially designed orthogonal diffusion loss addresses selection bias.
