summary.tldr: DiffPO combines conditional diffusion with a selection-bias-aware loss to learn distributions of potential intervention outcomes.

title: DiffPO: A causal diffusion model for learning distributions of potential outcomes

abstract: We present Causal Amortized Active Structure Learning (CAASL), an active intervention design policy that can select interventions that are adaptive, real-time and that does not require access to the likelihood. This policy, an amortized network based on the transformer, is trained with reinforcement learning on a simulator of the design environment, and a reward function that measures how close the true causal graph is to a causal graph posterior inferred from the gathered data. On synthetic data and a single-cell gene expression simulator, we demonstrate empirically that the data acquired through our policy results in a better estimate of the underlying causal graph than alternative strategies. Our design policy successfully achieves amortized intervention design on the distribution of the training environment while also generalizing well to distribution shifts in test-time design environments. Further, our policy also demonstrates excellent zero-shot generalization to design environments with dimensionality higher than that during training, and to intervention types that it has not been trained on.

This paper introduces CAASL, a policy that selects interventions adaptively and in real time without requiring access to a likelihood. Its aim is to learn the intervention-selection strategy in advance so that it can be reused during new causal investigations.

CAASL uses a transformer network trained through reinforcement learning in a simulator of the experimental environment. Its reward measures how closely the causal-graph posterior inferred from collected data matches the true graph. This connects intervention choice directly to the quality of causal inference, rather than treating data collection as a separate preliminary step.

On synthetic data and a single-cell gene expression simulator, data collected by CAASL produces better graph estimates than the alternative strategies tested. The policy also generalizes empirically to shifted test environments. Reported zero-shot results include environments with more variables than those used in training and unfamiliar intervention types, suggesting that the learned strategy can transfer beyond its original training configuration.
summary.tldr: CAASL learns a reusable intervention-selection policy that improves causal graph estimation and transfers to several unfamiliar experimental settings.

title: Amortized Active Causal Induction with Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Tabular data – structured, heterogeneous, spreadsheet-style data with rows and columns – is widely used in practice across many domains. However, while recent foundation models have reduced the need for developing task-specific datasets and predictors in domains such as language modeling and computer vision, this transfer learning paradigm has not had similar impact in the tabular domain. In this work, we seek to narrow this gap and present TABULA-8B, a language model for tabular prediction. We define a process for extracting a large, high-quality training dataset from the TabLib corpus, proposing methods for tabular data filtering and quality control. Using the resulting dataset, which comprises over 2.1B rows from 4.2M unique tables, we fine-tune a Llama 3-8B large language model (LLM) for tabular data prediction (classification and binned regression) using a novel packing and attention scheme for tabular prediction. Through evaluation across a test suite of 329 datasets, we find that TABULA-8B has zero-shot accuracy on unseen tables that is over 15 percentage points (pp) higher than random guessing, a feat that is not possible with existing state-of-the-art tabular prediction models (e.g. XGBoost, TabPFN). In the few-shot setting (1-32 shots), without any fine-tuning on the target datasets, TABULA-8B is 5-15 pp more accurate than XGBoost and TabPFN models that are explicitly trained on equal, or even up to 16× more data. We release our model, code, and data along with the publication of this paper.

summary.tldr: TABULA-8B learns across millions of tables to deliver strong zero-shot and few-shot predictions on unseen tabular datasets.

title: Large Scale Transfer Learning for Tabular Data via Language Modeling

abstract: Federated learning, a pioneering paradigm, enables collaborative model training without exposing users’ data to central servers. Most existing federated learning systems necessitate uniform model structures across all clients, restricting their practicality. Several methods have emerged to aggregate diverse client models; however, they either lack the ability of personalization, raise privacy and security concerns, need prior knowledge, or ignore the capability and functionality of personalized models. In this paper, we present an innovative approach, named pFedClub, which addresses these challenges. pFedClub introduces personalized federated learning through the substitution of controllable neural network blocks/layers. Initially, pFedClub dissects heterogeneous client models into blocks and organizes them into functional groups on the server. Utilizing the designed CMSR (Controllable Model Searching and Reproduction) algorithm, pFedClub generates a range of personalized candidate models for each client. A model matching technique is then applied to select the optimal personalized model, serving as a teacher model to guide each client’s training process. We conducted extensive experiments across three datasets, examining both IID and non-IID settings. The results demonstrate that pFedClub outperforms baseline approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Moreover, our model insight analysis reveals that pFedClub generates personalized models of reasonable size in a controllable manner, significantly reducing computational costs.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients collaborate without sending their private data to a central server, but many systems require every client to use the same model architecture. pFedClub addresses the more flexible setting where client models differ and each client needs a personalized result. Its approach operates on interchangeable network blocks or layers.

The server first divides heterogeneous models into blocks and groups them by function. A Controllable Model Searching and Reproduction algorithm constructs multiple candidate models for each client. A matching step then selects the best personalized candidate to serve as a teacher that guides that client's training.

Their model analysis also finds that the approach controls personalized model size and significantly reduces computational costs. The findings connect architectural flexibility with practical personalization through the selection and reuse of functional model components.
summary.tldr: pFedClub recombines functional blocks from heterogeneous client models to create controllable personalized teachers for federated learning.

title: pFedClub: Controllable Heterogeneous Model Aggregation for Personalized Federated Learning

abstract: The power of digital platforms is at the center of major ongoing policy and regulatory efforts. To advance existing debates, we designed and executed an experiment to measure the performative power of online search providers. Instantiated in our setting, performative power quantifies the ability of a search engine to steer web traffic by rearranging results. To operationalize this definition we developed a browser extension that performs unassuming randomized experiments in the background. These randomized experiments emulate updates to the search algorithm and identify the causal effect of different content arrangements on clicks. Analyzing tens of thousands of clicks, we discuss what our robust quantitative findings say about the power of online search engines, using the Google Shopping antitrust investigation as a case study. More broadly, we envision our work to serve as a blueprint for how the recent definition of performative power can help integrate quantitative insights from online experiments with future investigations into the economic power of digital platforms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much a search engine can influence where people go online by changing the arrangement of its results. The authors call this ability performative power. Framing the question this way makes platform power measurable through changes in user behavior, connecting an economic concern to an experimental quantity.

The researchers built a browser extension that runs unobtrusive randomized experiments in the background. It changes content arrangements in ways that emulate search-algorithm updates and measures the resulting clicks. Randomization allows the study to identify the causal effect of those arrangements, linking changes in presentation to changes in traffic.

The analysis covers tens of thousands of clicks and uses the Google Shopping antitrust investigation as a case study for interpreting the findings. The abstract describes the quantitative results as robust without giving a numerical effect size. The broader contribution is an experimental blueprint for bringing behavioral evidence into investigations of digital platforms' economic power.
summary.tldr: Randomized changes to search results measure how search engines can causally redirect web traffic.

title: An engine not a camera: Measuring performative power of online search

abstract: Ensuring that a DNN satisfies a desired property is critical when deploying DNNs in safety-critical applications. There are efficient methods that can verify whether a DNN satisfies a property, as seen in the annual DNN verification competition (VNN-COMP). However, the problem of provably editing a DNN to satisfy a property remains challenging. We present PREPARED, the first efficient technique for provable editing of DNNs. Given a DNN $\mathcal{N}$ with parameters $\theta$, input polytope $P$, and output polytope $Q$, PREPARED finds new parameters $\theta'$ such that $\forall \mathrm{x} \in P . \mathcal{N}(\mathrm{x}; \theta') \in Q$ while minimizing the changes $\lVert{\theta' - \theta}\rVert$. Given a DNN and a property it violates from the VNN-COMP benchmarks, PREPARED is able to provably edit the DNN to satisfy this property within 45 seconds. PREPARED is efficient because it relaxes the NP-hard provable editing problem to solving a linear program. The key contribution is the novel notion of Parametric Linear Relaxation, which enables PREPARED to construct tight output bounds of the DNN that are parameterized by the new parameters $\theta'$. We demonstrate that PREPARED is more efficient and effective compared to prior DNN editing approaches i) using the VNN-COMP benchmarks, ii) by editing CIFAR10 and TinyImageNet image-recognition DNNs, and BERT sentiment-classification DNNs for local robustness, and iii) by training a DNN to model a geodynamics process and satisfy physics constraints.

paragraphs: Checking that a neural network violates a requirement does not itself provide a way to repair it. This construction produces tight bounds on network outputs that depend on the proposed new parameters. Those bounds connect the parameter-editing process to a guarantee over the full specified input region.

For violated properties drawn from VNN-COMP benchmarks, the paper reports provable repairs within 45 seconds. It also evaluates local-robustness edits for CIFAR10 and TinyImageNet image classifiers and BERT sentiment models, plus physics constraints for a geodynamics model. Across these evaluations, PREPARED is more efficient and effective than prior editing approaches. Its guarantees concern the specified properties and regions, giving a precise meaning to successful repair.
summary.tldr: PREPARED uses parametric linear bounds to efficiently edit networks with guarantees that specified input regions map into required output regions.

title: Provable Editing of Deep Neural Networks using Parametric Linear Relaxation

abstract: Time series forecasting is crucial for applications across multiple domains and various scenarios. Although Transformers have dramatically advanced the landscape of forecasting, their effectiveness remains debated. Recent findings have indicated that simpler linear models might outperform complex Transformer-based approaches, highlighting the potential for more streamlined architectures. In this paper, we shift the focus from evaluating the overall Transformer architecture to specifically examining the effectiveness of self-attention for time series forecasting. To this end, we introduce a new architecture, Cross-Attention-only Time Series transformer (CATS), that rethinks the traditional transformer framework by eliminating self-attention and leveraging cross-attention mechanisms instead. By establishing future horizon-dependent parameters as queries and enhanced parameter sharing, our model not only improves long-term forecasting accuracy but also reduces the number of parameters and memory usage. Extensive experiment across various datasets demonstrates that our model achieves superior performance with the lowest mean squared error and uses fewer parameters compared to existing models.The implementation of our model is available at: https://github.com/dongbeank/CATS.

Its starting point is that simpler linear models have sometimes outperformed Transformer approaches, raising the possibility that forecasting can benefit from a more selective use of attention.

The authors introduce CATS, a Transformer architecture that removes self-attention and relies on cross-attention. Parameters associated with future forecast horizons serve as queries, making the attention mechanism explicitly depend on which future point is being predicted. Enhanced parameter sharing further reduces the amount of model machinery needed for forecasting.

Across the evaluated datasets, CATS achieves the lowest mean squared error among the compared models while using fewer parameters. The abstract also reports improved long-term forecasting accuracy and lower memory use. These results support a concrete architectural alternative: horizon-dependent cross-attention can deliver strong forecasts with reduced computational resources. They provide empirical evidence about the tested design, rather than establishing that self-attention is ineffective in every forecasting setting.
summary.tldr: CATS replaces self-attention with horizon-dependent cross-attention, improving forecasting results while reducing parameters and memory use in the reported experiments.

title: Are Self-Attentions Effective for Time Series Forecasting?

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) employing message passing for graph classification are inherently limited by the expressive power of the Weisfeiler-Leman (WL) test for graph isomorphism. Node individualization schemes, which assign unique identifiers to nodes (e.g., by adding random noise to features), are a common approach for achieving universal expressiveness. However, the ability of GNNs endowed with individualization schemes to generalize beyond the training data is still an open question. To address this question, this paper presents a theoretical analysis of the sample complexity of such GNNs from a statistical learning perspective, employing Vapnik–Chervonenkis (VC) dimension and covering number bounds. We demonstrate that node individualization schemes that are permutation-equivariant result in lower sample complexity, and design novel individualization schemes that exploit these results. As an application of this analysis, we also develop a novel architecture that can perform substructure identification (i.e., subgraph isomorphism) while having a lower VC dimension compared to competing methods. Finally, our theoretical findings are validated experimentally on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Message-passing graph neural networks have limits on which graph structures they can distinguish. Assigning unique identifiers to nodes can increase their expressive power, but expressiveness alone does not explain whether they will generalize beyond training examples. This paper investigates the amount of data required to learn with such node-individualization schemes.

The theoretical analysis uses VC dimension and covering-number bounds to study sample complexity. It shows that schemes respecting permutation equivariance yield lower sample complexity. In practical terms, the way identifiers respond to a reordering of nodes matters for learning guarantees, not just for the ability to distinguish structures. The authors design new individualization schemes based on this result.

They also develop an architecture for identifying substructures, formulated as subgraph isomorphism, with lower VC dimension than competing methods. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data validate the theoretical findings. The contribution connects the design of node identifiers to generalization: increasing structural discrimination can be paired with a principled analysis of how much training data the resulting model requires.
summary.tldr: Permutation-equivariant node individualization improves sample-complexity guarantees for expressive graph neural networks and informs new architectures.

title: On the Expressivity and Sample Complexity of Node-Individualized Graph Neural Networks

abstract: With the increasing inference cost of machine learning models, there is a growing interest in models with fast and efficient inference. Recently, an approach for learning logic gate networks directly via a differentiable relaxation was proposed. Logic gate networks are faster than conventional neural network approaches because their inference only requires logic gate operators such as NAND, OR, and XOR, which are the underlying building blocks of current hardware and can be efficiently executed. We build on this idea, extending it by deep logic gate tree convolutions, logical OR pooling, and residual initializations. This allows scaling logic gate networks up by over one order of magnitude and utilizing the paradigm of convolution. On CIFAR-10, we achieve an accuracy of 86.29% using only 61 million logic gates, which improves over the SOTA while being 29x smaller.

paragraphs: Machine-learning inference can become expensive as models grow. Logic gate networks offer an alternative in which prediction uses operations such as NAND, OR, and XOR. These operations are basic building blocks of computing hardware and can be executed efficiently. A differentiable relaxation makes it possible to learn such networks during training.

This paper extends that approach with deep logic gate tree convolutions, logical OR pooling, and residual initializations. Together, these additions introduce the convolutional paradigm into logic gate networks and allow the authors to scale them by more than an order of magnitude. The aim is to increase their modeling capacity while preserving inference based on simple logical operations.

On CIFAR-10, the proposed network reaches 86.29% accuracy with 61 million logic gates. The authors report that this improves on the prior state of the art while being 29 times smaller. The result demonstrates that the proposed architectural changes can make logic-based learning more competitive on an image-classification benchmark while retaining a compact representation in terms of gates.
summary.tldr: Convolutional extensions scale logic gate networks and achieve improved CIFAR-10 accuracy with a substantially smaller gate-based model.

title: Convolutional Differentiable Logic Gate Networks

abstract: We study the problem of learning under arbitrary distribution shift, where the learner is trained on a labeled set from one distribution but evaluated on a different, potentially adversarially generated test distribution. We focus on two frameworks: *PQ learning* [GKKM'20], allowing abstention on adversarially generated parts of the test distribution, and *TDS learning* [KSV'23], permitting abstention on the entire test distribution if distribution shift is detected. All prior known algorithms either rely on learning primitives that are computationally hard even for simple function classes, or end up abstaining entirely even in the presence of a tiny amount of distribution shift. We address both these challenges for natural function classes, including intersections of halfspaces and decision trees, and standard training distributions, including Gaussians. For PQ learning, we give efficient learning algorithms, while for TDS learning, our algorithms can tolerate moderate amounts of distribution shift. At the core of our approach is an improved analysis of spectral outlier-removal techniques from learning with nasty noise. Our analysis can (1) handle arbitrarily large fraction of outliers, which is crucial for handling arbitrary distribution shifts, and (2) obtain stronger bounds on polynomial moments of the distribution after outlier removal, yielding new insights into polynomial regression under distribution shifts. Lastly, our techniques lead to novel results for tolerant *testable learning* [RV'23], and learning with nasty noise.

At the core of our approach is an improved analysis of spectral outlier-removal techniques from learning with nasty noise. Our analysis can (1) handle arbitrarily large fraction of outliers, which is crucial for handling arbitrary distribution shifts, and (2) obtain stronger bounds on polynomial moments of the distribution after outlier removal, yielding new insights into polynomial regression under distribution shifts. Lastly, our techniques lead to novel results for tolerant *testable learning* [RV'23], and learning with nasty noise.

paragraphs: A learner may train on one distribution and encounter a very different, potentially adversarial test distribution. This paper studies two ways to allow abstention in that setting. PQ learning permits abstaining on adversarial portions of test data, while TDS learning permits rejecting the entire test distribution when a shift is detected.

Earlier algorithms either relied on computationally difficult learning procedures or could reject everything after even a small shift. The authors address these issues for specified natural function classes, including intersections of halfspaces and decision trees, and standard training distributions such as Gaussians. They provide efficient PQ algorithms and TDS algorithms that tolerate moderate distribution shifts.

The technical core is an improved analysis of spectral outlier removal. It handles arbitrarily large outlier fractions and gives stronger control over polynomial moments after removal, supporting polynomial regression under shift. The techniques also yield results for tolerant testable learning and learning with nasty noise. These guarantees retain their framework-specific abstention options and the stated function-class and training-distribution setting.
summary.tldr: Improved outlier-removal analysis yields efficient and more shift-tolerant learning algorithms in frameworks that permit abstention.

title: Tolerant Algorithms for Learning with Arbitrary Covariate Shift

abstract: Multimodal learning has developed very fast in recent years. However, during the multimodal training process, the model tends to rely on only one modality based on which it could learn faster, thus leading to inadequate use of other modalities. Existing methods to balance the training process always have some limitations on the loss functions, optimizers and the number of modalities and only consider modulating the magnitude of the gradients while ignoring the directions of the gradients. To solve these problems, in this paper, we present a novel method to balance multimodal learning with **C**lassifier-**G**uided **G**radient **M**odulation (CGGM), considering both the magnitude and directions of the gradients. We conduct extensive experiments on four multimodal datasets: UPMC-Food 101, CMU-MOSI, IEMOCAP and BraTS 2021, covering classification, regression and segmentation tasks. The results show that CGGM outperforms all the baselines and other state-of-the-art methods consistently, demonstrating its effectiveness and versatility. Our code is available at https://github.com/zrguo/CGGM.

paragraphs: A model trained on multiple modalities can learn unevenly: it may favor the input type that yields faster progress and underuse the others. This weakens the purpose of combining modalities, because useful information can remain poorly exploited. The paper addresses that imbalance through changes to the gradients that guide learning.

Classifier-Guided Gradient Modulation, or CGGM, considers both the magnitude and direction of those gradients. Magnitude concerns how strongly an update contributes, while direction concerns where it moves the model’s parameters. The authors identify direction as an overlooked component in existing balancing approaches, alongside restrictions those methods place on losses, optimizers, or modality counts.

The method is evaluated on UPMC-Food 101, CMU-MOSI, IEMOCAP, and BraTS 2021. These experiments span classification, regression, and segmentation, testing the proposal across different prediction tasks. CGGM consistently outperforms the compared baselines and state-of-the-art methods in these evaluations. The reported breadth supports its effectiveness and versatility for balancing multimodal training across the studied settings.
summary.tldr: CGGM balances multimodal learning by adjusting both gradient strength and direction, improving results across four evaluated datasets.

title: Classifier-guided Gradient Modulation for Enhanced Multimodal Learning

abstract: Text prompts enable intuitive content creation but may fall short in achieving high precision for intricate tasks; knob or slider controls offer precise adjustments at the cost of increased complexity. To address the gap between knobs and prompts, a new MCP (Model Context Protocol) server and a unique set of prompt design criteria are presented to enable exploring parametric OSC (OpenSoundControl) control by natural language prompts. Demonstrated by 15 practical QA examples with best practices and the generalized prompt templates, this study finds Claude integrated with the MCP2OSC server effective in generating OSC messages by natural language, interpreting, searching, and visualizing OSC messages, validating and debugging OSC messages, and managing OSC address patterns. MCP2OSC enhances human-machine collaboration by harnessing a LLM (Large Language Model) to handle intricate OSC development tasks. It empowers human creativity with an intuitive language interface featuring flexible precision controls: a prompt-based OSC tool. This study provides a novel perspective on the creative MCP application at the network protocol level by utilizing LLM's strength in directly processing and generating human-readable OSC messages. The results suggest its potential for a LLM-based universal control mechanism for multimedia devices.

Its contribution places the language model at the protocol level, where it can directly work with human-readable control messages. This provides an interface for creative technical work and suggests the possibility of a broader language-based multimedia control mechanism, while that universal role remains a potential application.
summary.tldr: MCP2OSC connects Claude to OpenSoundControl so natural-language prompts can generate, inspect, debug, and manage multimedia control messages.

title: MCP2OSC: Parametric Control by Natural Language

abstract: This work proposes the Lattice Boltzmann Model (LBM) to learn real-world pixel dynamicity for visual tracking. LBM decomposes visual representations into dynamic pixel lattices and solves pixel motion states through collision-streaming processes. Specifically, the high-dimensional distribution of the target pixels is acquired through a multilayer predict-update network to estimate the pixel positions and visibility. The predict stage formulates lattice collisions among the spatial neighborhood of target pixels and develops lattice streaming within the temporal visual context. The update stage rectifies the pixel distributions with online visual representations. Compared with existing methods, LBM demonstrates practical applicability in an online and real-time manner, which can efficiently adapt to real-world visual tracking tasks. Comprehensive evaluations of real-world point tracking benchmarks such as TAP-Vid and RoboTAP validate LBM's efficiency. A general evaluation of large-scale open-world object tracking benchmarks such as TAO, BFT, and OVT-B further demonstrates LBM's real-world practicality.

paragraphs: Visual tracking requires estimating where target pixels move and whether they remain visible. The Lattice Boltzmann Model represents this changing visual information through dynamic pixel lattices. It uses collision and streaming processes to model motion states, organizing tracking around interactions in space and movement through time.

A multilayer predict–update network estimates a high-dimensional distribution over target pixels. In the prediction stage, lattice collisions describe interactions among nearby target pixels, while lattice streaming uses temporal visual context. The update stage corrects those distributions with visual representations obtained online. This repeatedly connects motion predictions with incoming observations when estimating positions and visibility.

The authors emphasize online, real-time operation as a practical feature of the approach. Evaluations on TAP-Vid and RoboTAP support its efficiency for point tracking, while experiments on TAO, BFT, and OVT-B examine broader open-world object tracking. Together, these evaluations support the proposed motion representation’s practicality across the tested point- and object-tracking settings, connecting the lattice formulation to tasks involving real-world visual changes.
summary.tldr: The Lattice Boltzmann Model uses spatial collision, temporal streaming, and online correction to track pixel positions and visibility in real time.

title: Lattice Boltzmann Model for Learning Real-World Pixel Dynamicity

abstract: In this work, we study the scalability of offline reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. In principle, a truly scalable offline RL algorithm should be able to solve any given problem, regardless of its complexity, given sufficient data, compute, and model capacity. We investigate if and how current offline RL algorithms match up to this promise on diverse, challenging, previously unsolved tasks, using datasets up to 1000× larger than typical offline RL datasets. We observe that despite scaling up data, many existing offline RL algorithms exhibit poor scaling behavior, saturating well below the maximum performance. We hypothesize that the horizon is the main cause behind the poor scaling of offline RL. We empirically verify this hypothesis through several analysis experiments, showing that long horizons indeed present a fundamental barrier to scaling up offline RL. We then show that various horizon reduction techniques substantially enhance scalability on challenging tasks. Based on our insights, we also introduce a minimal yet scalable method named SHARSA that effectively reduces the horizon. SHARSA achieves the best asymptotic performance and scaling behavior among our evaluation methods, showing that explicitly reducing the horizon unlocks the scalability of offline RL.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether offline reinforcement learning keeps improving when supplied with much more data. Offline methods learn from previously collected experience, and the study evaluates them on diverse, difficult tasks using datasets up to 1,000 times larger than typical collections. Many tested algorithms plateau well below maximum performance despite this increase.

The authors identify the decision horizon as a potential explanation: learning becomes difficult when actions must be evaluated through their consequences across many future steps. Analysis experiments support their hypothesis that long horizons obstruct scaling. Several techniques that reduce the effective horizon substantially improve scalability on the challenging tasks.

Based on these findings, the paper introduces SHARSA, a minimal method designed to reduce the horizon. It achieves the strongest asymptotic performance and scaling behavior among the evaluated methods. The contribution is an empirical diagnosis paired with a practical response: increasing dataset size becomes more effective when the learning problem also reduces the burden of reasoning across long action sequences.
summary.tldr: Experiments identify long decision horizons as a barrier to offline RL scaling and show that horizon reduction improves it.

title: Horizon Reduction Makes RL Scalable

abstract: Designing regulatory DNA sequences that achieve precise cell-type-specific gene expression is crucial for advancements in synthetic biology, gene therapy and precision medicine. Although transformer-based language models (LMs) can effectively capture patterns in regulatory DNA, their generative approaches often struggle to produce novel sequences with reliable cell-specific activity. Here, we introduce Ctrl-DNA, a novel constrained reinforcement learning (RL) framework tailored for designing regulatory DNA sequences with controllable cell-type specificity. By formulating regulatory sequence design as a biologically informed constrained optimization problem, we apply RL to autoregressive genomic LMs, enabling the models to iteratively refine sequences that maximize regulatory activity in targeted cell types while constraining off-target effects. Our evaluation on human promoters and enhancers demonstrates that Ctrl-DNA consistently outperforms existing generative and RL-based approaches, generating high-fitness regulatory sequences and achieving state-of-the-art cell-type specificity. Moreover, Ctrl-DNA-generated sequences capture key cell-type-specific transcription factor binding sites (TFBS), short DNA motifs recognized by regulatory proteins that control gene expression, demonstrating the biological plausibility of the generated sequences.

paragraphs: Designing regulatory DNA requires control over where a sequence acts as well as how strongly it acts. A sequence intended for one cell type should support activity there while limiting unwanted activity elsewhere. Ctrl-DNA addresses this specificity problem, which remains difficult for genomic language models that can otherwise learn regulatory sequence patterns.

The framework formulates generation as constrained optimization informed by biology. Reinforcement learning adapts an autoregressive genomic language model to improve regulatory activity in selected cell types while constraining off-target effects. The constraints make unwanted activity part of the design objective, and the learning process iteratively refines the generated sequences.

Evaluations on human promoters and enhancers report higher-fitness sequences and stronger cell-type specificity than existing generative and reinforcement learning approaches. The generated sequences also contain key binding motifs associated with the target cell types. These short sequences are recognized by proteins involved in regulating gene expression, providing evidence of biological plausibility. The findings support constrained learning as a way to direct generation toward selective regulatory behavior.
summary.tldr: Ctrl-DNA uses constrained reinforcement learning to generate regulatory DNA with stronger target-cell activity and controlled off-target effects.

title: Ctrl-DNA: Controllable Cell-Type-Specific Regulatory DNA Design via Constrained RL

abstract: We analyze the global convergence of the single-timescale actor-critic (AC) algorithm for the infinite-horizon discounted Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with finite state spaces. To this end, we introduce an elegant analytical framework for handling complex, coupled recursions inherent in the algorithm. Leveraging this framework, we establish that the algorithm converges to an $\epsilon$-close \textbf{globally optimal} policy with a sample complexity of $ O(\epsilon^{-3}) $. This significantly improves upon the existing complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ to achieve $\epsilon$-close \textbf{stationary policy}, which is equivalent to the complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ to achieve $\epsilon$-close \textbf{globally optimal} policy using gradient domination lemma. Furthermore, we demonstrate that to achieve this improvement, the step sizes for both the actor and critic must decay as $ O(k^{-\frac{2}{3}}) $ with iteration $k$, diverging from the conventional $O(k^{-\frac{1}{2}}) $ rates commonly used in (non)convex optimization.

paragraphs: Actor-critic reinforcement learning couples two learning processes: an actor changes the policy while a critic evaluates behavior. When both operate on a single timescale, their interacting updates complicate convergence analysis. This paper studies that setting for infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision processes with finite state spaces.

The authors introduce an analytical framework for the coupled recursions and prove convergence to a policy within epsilon of global optimality using O(epsilon to the negative third power) samples. The global target matters. The earlier O(epsilon to the negative second power) bound addressed a stationary policy; translating it to global optimality through gradient domination gives O(epsilon to the negative fourth power).

The new result therefore improves the sample dependence when comparing the same global-optimality objective. The authors also show that obtaining this improvement requires both actor and critic step sizes to decay as O(k to the negative two-thirds power), where k is the iteration. That schedule differs from the conventional inverse-square-root decay, linking the stronger convergence guarantee to a specific choice of update rates.
summary.tldr: A new analysis improves the global-optimality sample bound for single-timescale actor-critic with appropriately decaying step sizes.

title: On the Convergence of Single-Timescale Actor-Critic

abstract: While recent diffusion-based generative image codecs have shown impressive performance, their iterative sampling process introduces unpleasant latency. In this work, we revisit the design of a diffusion-based codec and argue that multi-step sampling is not necessary for generative compression. Based on this insight, we propose OneDC, a One-step Diffusion-based generative image Codec—that integrates a latent compression module with a one-step diffusion generator. Recognizing the critical role of semantic guidance in one-step diffusion, we propose using the hyperprior as a semantic signal, overcoming the limitations of text prompts in representing complex visual content. To further enhance the semantic capability of the hyperprior, we introduce a semantic distillation mechanism that transfers knowledge from a pretrained generative tokenizer to the hyperprior codec. Additionally, we adopt a hybrid pixel- and latent-domain optimization to jointly enhance both reconstruction fidelity and perceptual realism. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OneDC achieves SOTA perceptual quality even with one-step generation, offering over 39% bitrate reduction and 20× faster decoding compared to prior multi-step diffusion-based codecs. Project: https://onedc-codec.github.io/

paragraphs: Diffusion-based image compression can produce visually convincing reconstructions, but repeated generation steps add decoding latency. OneDC revisits whether those multiple steps are needed for generative compression. It combines a latent compression module with a diffusion generator that reconstructs the image in one step, making semantic guidance especially important to the design.

Instead of relying on text prompts to convey complex visual content, OneDC uses the hyperprior as a semantic signal. A semantic distillation mechanism transfers knowledge from a pretrained generative tokenizer into the hyperprior codec. Training also combines objectives in the pixel and latent domains to improve both faithfulness to the input and perceptual realism.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art perceptual quality with one-step generation, alongside more than 39% bitrate reduction and 20-fold faster decoding compared with prior multi-step diffusion codecs. These findings support the authors’ argument that effective semantic guidance can make a single generation step sufficient for strong compression results in the evaluated setting, substantially reducing the cost of reconstruction.
summary.tldr: OneDC uses semantically distilled guidance for one-step image reconstruction, reporting lower bitrates and 20-fold faster decoding than prior multi-step codecs.

title: One-Step Diffusion-Based Image Compression with Semantic Distillation

abstract: Formal reasoning and automated theorem proving constitute a challenging subfield of machine learning, in which machines are tasked with proving mathematical theorems using formal languages like Lean. A formal verification system can check whether a formal proof is correct or not almost instantaneously, but generating a completely correct formal proof with large language models (LLMs) remains a formidable task. The usual approach in the literature is to prompt the LLM many times (up to several thousands) until one of the generated proofs passes the verification system. In this work, we present APOLLO (**A**utomated **P**r**O**of repair via**L**LM and **L**ean c**O**llaboration), a modular, model‑agnostic agentic framework that combines the strengths of the Lean compiler with an LLM’s reasoning abilities to achieve better proof‐generation results at a low token and sampling budgets. _Apollo_ directs a fully automated process in which the LLM generates proofs for theorems, a set of agents analyze the proofs, fix the syntax errors, identify the mistakes in the proofs using Lean, isolate failing sub‑lemmas, utilize automated solvers, and invoke an LLM on each remaining goal with a low top‑K budget. The repaired sub‑proofs are recombined and reverified, iterating up to a user‑controlled maximum number of attempts. On the miniF2F benchmark, we establish a new state‑of‑the‑art accuracy of 84.9% among sub 8B‑parameter models (as of August 2025) while keeping the sampling budget below one hundred. Moreover, _Apollo_ raises the state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for Goedel‑Prover‑SFT to 65.6% while cutting sample complexity from 25,600 to a few hundred. General‑purpose models (o3‑mini, o4‑mini) jump from 3–7% to over 40% accuracy. Our results demonstrate that targeted, compiler‑guided repair of LLM outputs yields dramatic gains in both efficiency and correctness, suggesting a general paradigm for scalable automated theorem proving. The codebase is available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/APOLLO

paragraphs: APOLLO addresses the gap between checking a mathematical proof and generating one correctly. Lean can quickly verify a formal proof, but language models often produce proofs containing mistakes. Repeatedly requesting complete replacements can consume large sampling budgets. APOLLO instead organizes a collaboration that repairs specific failures using feedback from Lean.

The framework starts with a generated proof, then uses agents to inspect it, repair syntax, and identify unsuccessful reasoning steps. It isolates failing sublemmas, applies automated solvers, and asks a language model to handle remaining goals with a small candidate budget. Repaired pieces are assembled and checked again, with repetition bounded by a user-controlled attempt limit.

On miniF2F, APOLLO reports 84.9% accuracy among models below eight billion parameters with fewer than one hundred samples, a category-leading result as of August 2025. It also improves Goedel-Prover-SFT and general-purpose models while reducing sampling requirements. These findings support targeted, compiler-guided repair as an effective way to improve both proof success and generation efficiency.
summary.tldr: APOLLO uses Lean feedback and targeted proof repair to improve automated theorem proving with smaller sampling budgets.

title: APOLLO: Automated LLM and Lean Collaboration for Advanced Formal Reasoning

abstract: Strategic classification (SC) explores how individuals or entities modify their features strategically to achieve favorable classification outcomes. However, existing SC methods, which are largely based on linear models or shallow neural networks, face significant limitations in terms of scalability and capacity when applied to real-world datasets with significantly increasing scale, especially in financial services and the internet sector. In this paper, we investigate how to leverage large language models to design a more scalable and efficient SC framework, especially in the case of growing individuals engaged with decision-making processes. Specifically, we introduce GLIM, a gradient-free SC method grounded in in-context learning. During the feed-forward process of self-attention, GLIM implicitly simulates the typical bi-level optimization process of SC, including both the feature manipulation and decision rule optimization. Without fine-tuning the LLMs, our proposed GLIM enjoys the advantage of cost-effective adaptation in dynamic strategic environments. Theoretically, we prove GLIM can support pre-trained LLMs to adapt to a broad range of strategic manipulations. We validate our approach through experiments with a collection of pre-trained LLMs on real-world and synthetic datasets in financial and internet domains, demonstrating that our GLIM exhibits both robustness and efficiency, and offering an effective solution for large-scale SC tasks.

paragraphs: Strategic classification studies decisions in settings where people or organizations change their features to obtain favorable outcomes. A classifier must therefore account for responses to its decision rule. The paper investigates how pretrained language models can support this process as datasets and the number of participating individuals grow.

The proposed method, GLIM, uses in-context learning without fine-tuning the language model. During a forward pass, its self-attention process implicitly simulates the two linked parts of strategic classification: feature manipulation and optimization of the decision rule. This gradient-free approach is intended to make adaptation to changing strategic environments more economical.

The authors provide a theoretical result showing that GLIM can help pretrained language models adapt to a broad range of strategic manipulations. Experiments with several pretrained models on real and synthetic financial and internet datasets demonstrate robustness and efficiency. The contribution is a way to use existing model capabilities for strategic decision-making without repeatedly updating model weights, supported by both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: GLIM uses pretrained language models and in-context learning to handle strategic classification without gradient-based fine-tuning.

title: Breaking the Gradient Barrier: Unveiling Large Language Models for Strategic Classification

abstract: Human annotations play a crucial role in evaluating the performance of GenAI models. Two common challenges in practice, however, are missing annotations (the response variable of interest) and cluster dependence among human-AI interactions (e.g., questions asked by the same user may be highly correlated). Reliable inference must address both issues to achieve unbiased estimation and appropriately quantify uncertainty when estimating average scores from human annotations. In this paper, we analyze the doubly robust estimator, a widely used method in missing data analysis and causal inference, applied to this setting and establish novel theoretical properties under cluster dependence. We further illustrate our findings through simulations and a real-world conversation quality dataset. Our theoretical and empirical results underscore the importance of incorporating cluster dependence in missing response problems to perform valid statistical inference.

Two common challenges in practice, however, are missing annotations (the response variable of interest) and cluster dependence among human-AI interactions (e.g., questions asked by the same user may be highly correlated). Reliable inference must address both issues to achieve unbiased estimation and appropriately quantify uncertainty when estimating average scores from human annotations. In this paper, we analyze the doubly robust estimator, a widely used method in missing data analysis and causal inference, applied to this setting and establish novel theoretical properties under cluster dependence. We further illustrate our findings through simulations and a real-world conversation quality dataset. Our theoretical and empirical results underscore the importance of incorporating cluster dependence in missing response problems to perform valid statistical inference.

paragraphs: Human ratings are important for evaluating generative models, but the available ratings can have two complications at once. Some interactions receive no annotation, and interactions within a group can be correlated. For example, questions from the same user may resemble one another, so their ratings cannot simply be treated as independent observations.

This paper studies estimation of average annotation scores when both missing responses and cluster dependence are present. It analyzes the doubly robust estimator, an established method in missing-data analysis and causal inference, and develops theoretical properties for this dependent setting. The goal is to address bias in the estimated average while also quantifying its uncertainty appropriately.

The authors illustrate their theoretical findings with simulations and a real-world dataset of conversation quality. Their combined results emphasize that handling missing annotations alone is insufficient for valid inference when clustered dependence also matters. The contribution provides a statistical foundation for evaluating average human scores while taking the grouping of interactions seriously in the analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper develops theory for estimating average human evaluation scores when annotations are missing and interactions are correlated within clusters.

title: Handling Missing Responses under Cluster Dependence with Applications to Language Model Evaluation

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) typically assumes repetitive resets to provide an agent with diverse and unbiased experiences. These resets require significant human intervention and result in poor training efficiency in real-world settings. Autonomous RL (ARL) addresses this challenge by jointly training forward and reset policies. While recent ARL algorithms have shown promise in reducing human intervention, they assume narrow support over the distributions of initial or goal states and rely on task-specific knowledge to identify irreversible states. In this paper, we propose a robust and scalable ARL algorithm, called RSA, that enables an agent to handle diverse initial and goal states and to avoid irreversible states without task-specific knowledge. RSA generates a curriculum by identifying informative states based on the learning progress of an agent. We hypothesize that informative states are neither overly difficult nor trivially easy for the agent being trained. To detect and avoid irreversible states without task-specific knowledge, RSA encodes the behaviors exhibited in those states rather than the states themselves. Experimental results demonstrate that RSA outperforms existing ARL algorithms with fewer manual resets in both reversible and irreversible environments.

summary.tldr: RSA combines progress-based curricula and behavior-based detection of irreversible situations to improve autonomous reinforcement learning with fewer manual resets.

title: Robust and Scalable Autonomous Reinforcement Learning in Irreversible Environments

abstract: In reinforcement learning, distributional off-policy evaluation (OPE) focuses on estimating the return distribution of a target policy using offline data collected under a different policy. This work focuses on extending the widely used fitted Q-evaluation---developed for expectation-based reinforcement learning---to the distributional OPE setting. We refer to this extension as fitted distributional evaluation (FDE). While only a few related approaches exist, there remains no unified framework for designing FDE methods. To fill this gap, we present a set of guiding principles for constructing theoretically grounded FDE methods. Building on these principles, we develop several new FDE methods with convergence analysis and provide theoretical justification for existing methods, even in non-tabular environments. Extensive experiments, including simulations on linear quadratic regulators and Atari games, demonstrate the superior performance of the FDE methods.

paragraphs: Evaluating a decision policy from previously collected data becomes more informative when the goal is to estimate its entire distribution of returns. Distributional off-policy evaluation does this using data gathered under a different policy. The paper studies how to extend fitted Q-evaluation, an established method for estimating expected returns, to this broader task.

The authors call the extension fitted distributional evaluation, or FDE. Their main contribution is a set of principles for designing methods with theoretical support. These principles provide a common foundation for an area that previously had only a few related approaches without a unified design framework. They use this foundation both to develop new methods and to explain why existing ones are justified.

The theoretical results include convergence analyses and extend beyond settings represented by explicit tables. Experiments involving linear quadratic regulators and Atari games report superior performance for the FDE methods. Together, these contributions connect practical estimation of return distributions with a more systematic account of how such estimators should be constructed and analyzed.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes design principles and convergence analyses for estimating a policy’s return distribution from data collected under another policy.

title: A Principled Path to Fitted Distributional Evaluation

abstract: Long-form video understanding presents significant challenges due to extensive temporal-spatial complexity and the difficulty of question answering under such extended contexts. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable advancements in video analysis capabilities and long context handling, they continue to exhibit limitations when processing information-dense hour-long videos. To overcome such limitations, we propose the $\textbf{D}eep \ \textbf{V}ideo \ \textbf{D}iscovery \ (\textbf{DVD})$ agent to leverage an $\textit{agentic search}$ strategy over segmented video clips. Different from previous video agents manually designing a rigid workflow, our approach emphasizes the autonomous nature of agents. By providing a set of search-centric tools on multi-granular video database, our DVD agent leverages the advanced reasoning capability of LLM to plan on its current observation state, strategically selects tools to orchestrate adaptive workflow for different queries in light of the gathered information. We perform comprehensive evaluation on multiple long video understanding benchmarks that demonstrates our advantage. Our DVD agent achieves state-of-the-art performance on the challenging LVBench dataset, reaching an accuracy of $\textbf{74.2\%}$, which substantially surpasses all prior works, and further improves to $\textbf{76.0\%}$ with transcripts.

Deep Video Discovery addresses the problem by treating video understanding as an adaptive search over segmented clips.

The DVD agent receives search-oriented tools operating on a video database organized at multiple levels of detail. It uses its current observations to plan what to inspect and select the next tool. As evidence accumulates, the workflow can change to fit the question. This makes the search process responsive to what the agent has already learned.

Evaluations across multiple long-video benchmarks show advantages for the approach. On LVBench, the agent reaches 74.2% accuracy, reported as state of the art, and reaches 76.0% when transcripts are available. These results support the value of combining language-model reasoning with selective access to video evidence. The transcript result also shows that additional textual information improves performance in that evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: DVD adaptively searches segmented videos with tools, achieving strong long-video question-answering results that improve further with transcripts.

title: Deep Video Discovery: Agentic Search with Tool Use for Long-form Video Understanding

abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for generative sequential recommendation, which typically generate next items to recommend guided by user interaction histories with a multi-step denoising process. However, the multi-step process relies on discrete approximations, introducing discretization error that creates a trade-off between computational efficiency and recommendation effectiveness. To address this trade-off, we propose TA-Rec, a two-stage framework that achieves one-step generation by smoothing the denoising function during pretraining while alleviating trajectory deviation by aligning with user preferences during fine-tuning. Specifically, to improve the efficiency without sacrificing the recommendation performance, TA-Rec pretrains the denoising model with Temporal Consistency Regularization (TCR), enforcing the consistency between the denoising results across adjacent steps. Thus, we can smooth the denoising function to map the noise as oracle items in one step with bounded error. To further enhance effectiveness, TA-Rec introduces Adaptive Preference Alignment (APA) that aligns the denoising process with user preference adaptively based on preference pair similarity and timesteps. Extensive experiments prove that TA-Rec’s two-stage objective effectively mitigates the discretization errors-induced trade-off, enhancing both efficiency and effectiveness of diffusion-based recommenders. Our code is available at https://github.com/maowenyu-11/TA-Rec.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based sequential recommenders generate suggested next items from a user’s interaction history through repeated denoising. The paper attributes an efficiency–effectiveness trade-off to errors introduced by discretizing that process. TA-Rec addresses the issue with two training stages intended to enable one-step generation while maintaining useful recommendations.

During pretraining, Temporal Consistency Regularization encourages neighboring denoising steps to produce consistent results. This smooths the denoising function, allowing noise to be mapped to target items in one step with bounded error. During fine-tuning, Adaptive Preference Alignment adjusts the process toward user preferences, with adaptation based on preference-pair similarity and timesteps.

The findings support the combined objective as a way to mitigate the discretization-induced trade-off, rather than requiring the recommendation process to retain all of its original denoising steps.
summary.tldr: TA-Rec combines denoising consistency and adaptive preference alignment to achieve effective one-step diffusion-based recommendation.

title: On Efficiency-Effectiveness Trade-off of Diffusion-based Recommenders

abstract: Real-world image super-resolution (RealSR) aims to enhance the visual quality of in-the-wild images, such as those captured by mobile phones. While existing methods leveraging large generative models demonstrate impressive results, the high computational cost and latency make them impractical for edge deployment. In this paper, we introduce PocketSR, an ultra-lightweight, single-step model that brings generative modeling capabilities to RealSR while maintaining high fidelity. To achieve this, we design LiteED, a highly efficient alternative to the original computationally intensive VAE in SD, reducing parameters by 97.5\% while preserving high-quality encoding and decoding. Additionally, we propose online annealing pruning for the U-Net, which progressively shifts generative priors from heavy modules to lightweight counterparts, ensuring effective knowledge transfer and further optimizing efficiency. To mitigate the loss of prior knowledge during pruning, we incorporate a multi-layer feature distillation loss. Through an in-depth analysis of each design component, we provide valuable insights for future research. PocketSR, with a model size of 146M parameters, processes 4K images in just 0.8 seconds, achieving a remarkable speedup over previous methods. Notably, it delivers performance on par with state-of-the-art single-step and even multi-step RealSR models, making it a highly practical solution for edge-device applications.

PocketSR is a single-step model designed to retain generative image-enhancement capabilities while substantially reducing the computational burden and preserving fidelity.

Its evaluated performance is comparable to state-of-the-art single-step and even multi-step super-resolution models. The contribution combines a smaller image representation component with gradual pruning and knowledge transfer, showing how several coordinated efficiency changes can preserve strong enhancement quality in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: PocketSR combines efficient encoding, gradual pruning, and feature distillation to deliver single-step image super-resolution with substantially reduced computation.

title: PocketSR: The Super-Resolution Expert in Your Pocket Mobiles

abstract: Vision-language models have been explored for radiology report generation with promising results. Yet, uncertainty elaborated in findings and the reasoning process for reaching clinical impressions are seldom explicitly modeled, reducing the clinical accuracy and trustworthiness of the generated reports. We present CURV, a novel framework that alleviates the limitations through integrated awareness of uncertainty and explicit reasoning capabilities. Our approach consists of three key components: (1) an uncertainty modeling mechanism that teaches the model to recognize and express appropriate levels of diagnostic confidence, (2) a structured reasoning framework that generates intermediate explanatory steps connecting visual findings to clinical impressions, and (3) a reasoning coherence reward that ensures logical consistency among findings, reasoning, and impressions. We implement CURV through a three-stage training pipeline that combines uncertainty-aware fine-tuning, reasoning initialization, and reinforcement learning. In particular, we adopt a comprehensive reward function addresses multiple aspects of report quality, incorporating medical term matching, uncertainty expression evaluation, and semantic coherence evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that CURV generates clinically relevant reports with appropriate uncertainty expressions and transparent reasoning traces, significantly outperforming previous methods. CURV represents a substantial advancement toward interpretable and trustworthy AI-generated radiology reports, with broader implications for the deployment of vision-language models in high-stakes clinical environments where uncertainty awareness and reasoning transparency are essential.

Existing vision-language approaches often leave diagnostic uncertainty and the connection between findings and conclusions implicit. CURV trains a model to express uncertainty and provide intermediate explanations as explicit parts of report generation.

The framework combines three components. An uncertainty mechanism teaches appropriate confidence language, a structured reasoning component connects visual findings to clinical impressions, and a coherence reward encourages agreement among findings, explanations, and conclusions. Training proceeds through uncertainty-aware fine-tuning, reasoning initialization, and reinforcement learning. Its reward function evaluates medical terminology, uncertainty expressions, and semantic consistency together.

The reported experiments show clinically relevant reports with appropriate uncertainty language and visible reasoning traces, with significant improvements over previous methods. The contribution is therefore broader than generating fluent medical text: it targets how evidence, confidence, and conclusions fit together within a report. These findings support progress toward more interpretable radiology reporting, with relevance to clinical settings where readers need to understand the basis and confidence of generated impressions.
summary.tldr: CURV improves X-ray report generation by jointly training diagnostic uncertainty, explanatory reasoning, and consistency between findings and impressions.

title: CURV: Coherent Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning in Vision-Language Models for X-Ray Report Generation

abstract: With the increasing adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems for knowledge-intensive tasks, ensuring the adequacy of retrieved documents has become critically important for generation quality. Traditional reranking approaches face three significant challenges: substantial computational overhead that scales with document length, dependency on plain text that limits application in sensitive scenarios, and insufficient assessment of document value beyond simple relevance metrics. We propose EAReranker, an efficient embedding-based adequacy assessment framework that evaluates document utility for RAG systems without requiring access to original text content. The framework quantifies document adequacy through a comprehensive scoring methodology considering verifiability, coverage, completeness and structural aspects, providing interpretable adequacy classifications for downstream applications. EAReranker employs a Decoder-Only Transformer architecture that introduces embedding dimension expansion method and bin-aware weighted loss, designed specifically to predict adequacy directly from embedding vectors. Our comprehensive evaluation across four public benchmarks demonstrates that EAReranker achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art plaintext rerankers while maintaining constant memory usage ($\sim$550MB) regardless of input length and processing 2-3x faster than traditional approaches. The semantic bin adequacy prediction accuracy of 92.85\% LACC@10 and 86.12\% LACC@25 demonstrates its capability to effectively filter out inadequate documents that could potentially mislead or adversely impact RAG system performance, thereby ensuring only high-utility information serves as generation context. These results establish EAReranker as an efficient and practical solution for enhancing RAG system performance through improved context selection while addressing the computational and privacy challenges of existing methods.

title: EAReranker: Efficient Embedding Adequacy Assessment for Retrieval Augmented Generation

abstract: Machine learning has promised to change the landscape of laboratory chemistry, with impressive results in molecular property prediction and reaction retro-synthesis. However, chemical datasets are often inaccessible to the machine learning community as they tend to require cleaning, thorough understanding of the chemistry, or are simply not available. In this paper, we introduce a novel dataset for yield prediction, providing the first-ever transient flow dataset for machine learning benchmarking, covering over 1200 process conditions. While previous datasets focus on discrete parameters, our experimental set-up allow us to sample a large number of continuous process conditions, generating new challenges for machine learning models. We focus on solvent selection, a task that is particularly difficult to model theoretically and therefore ripe for machine learning applications. We showcase benchmarking for regression algorithms, transfer-learning approaches, feature engineering, and active learning, with important applications towards solvent replacement and sustainable manufacturing.

Its transient-flow experiments cover more than 1,200 process conditions.

This differs from datasets centered on discrete parameter choices and creates additional challenges for learning how yield varies across conditions. The time-series data provide a benchmark for studying those relationships, making the experimental setup itself an important part of the contribution.

The paper demonstrates benchmarking with regression algorithms, transfer learning, feature engineering, and active learning. These uses establish several ways to investigate prediction and learning from the dataset, rather than presenting only one modeling approach. The intended applications include solvent replacement and more sustainable manufacturing. The contribution is experimental data and a benchmarking foundation for those aims, without claiming that the dataset alone achieves a particular manufacturing outcome.
summary.tldr: The Catechol Benchmark provides transient-flow yield data across over 1,200 process conditions for studying solvent selection and data-efficient learning.

title: The Catechol Benchmark: Time-series Solvent Selection Data for Few-shot Machine Learning

abstract: Longitudinal multimodal data, including electronic health records (EHR) and sequential chest X-rays (CXRs), is critical for modeling disease progression, yet remains underutilized due to two key challenges: (1) redundancy in consecutive CXR sequences, where static anatomical regions dominate over clinically-meaningful dynamics, and (2) temporal misalignment between sparse, irregular imaging and continuous EHR data. We introduce $\texttt{DiPro}$, a novel framework that addresses these challenges through region-aware disentanglement and multi-timescale alignment. First, we disentangle static (anatomy) and dynamic (pathology progression) features in sequential CXRs, prioritizing disease-relevant changes. Second, we hierarchically align these static and dynamic CXR features with asynchronous EHR data via local (pairwise interval-level) and global (full-sequence) synchronization to model coherent progression pathways. Extensive experiments on the MIMIC dataset demonstrate that $\texttt{DiPro}$ could effectively extract temporal clinical dynamics and achieve state-of-the-art performance on both disease progression identification and general ICU prediction tasks.

paragraphs: DiPro models disease progression using sequences of chest X-rays together with electronic health records. Combining these sources is difficult because successive images contain much unchanged anatomy, while clinically relevant changes may be less prominent. Imaging also arrives sparsely and irregularly, creating timing mismatches with the more continuous health-record data.

The framework first separates static anatomical features from dynamic features associated with pathology progression. This region-aware separation prioritizes changes relevant to disease over repeated visual content. It then aligns both types of imaging features with asynchronous health records at two timescales: local intervals and the full sequence.

The two alignment levels connect nearby observations while also modeling a coherent progression across the complete record. These findings support jointly addressing visual redundancy and temporal mismatch when learning from longitudinal multimodal data. The reported contribution concerns modeling and prediction on those tasks, rather than a demonstrated change in clinical care.
summary.tldr: DiPro separates anatomical stability from disease-related changes and aligns X-rays with health records across local and global timescales.

title: Multimodal Disease Progression Modeling via Spatiotemporal Disentanglement and Multiscale Alignment

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have significantly enhanced their capabilities in complex problem-solving by introducing a thinking draft that enables multi-path Chain-of-Thought explorations before producing final answers. Ensuring the faithfulness of these intermediate reasoning processes is crucial for reliable monitoring, interpretation, and effective control. In this paper, we propose a systematic counterfactual intervention framework to rigorously evaluate *thinking draft faithfulness*. Our approach focuses on two complementary dimensions: **(1) Intra-Draft Faithfulness**, which assesses whether individual reasoning steps causally influence subsequent steps and the final draft conclusion through counterfactual step insertions; and **(2) Draft-to-Answer Faithfulness**, which evaluates whether final answers are logically consistent with and dependent on the thinking draft, by perturbing the draft’s concluding logic. We conduct extensive experiments across six state-of-the-art LRMs. Our findings show that current LRMs demonstrate selective faithfulness to intermediate reasoning steps and frequently fail to faithfully align with the draft conclusions. These results underscore the need for more faithful and interpretable reasoning in advanced LRMs.

In this paper, we propose a systematic counterfactual intervention framework to rigorously evaluate *thinking draft faithfulness*. Our approach focuses on two complementary dimensions: **(1) Intra-Draft Faithfulness**, which assesses whether individual reasoning steps causally influence subsequent steps and the final draft conclusion through counterfactual step insertions; and **(2) Draft-to-Answer Faithfulness**, which evaluates whether final answers are logically consistent with and dependent on the thinking draft, by perturbing the draft’s concluding logic. We conduct extensive experiments across six state-of-the-art LRMs. Our findings show that current LRMs demonstrate selective faithfulness to intermediate reasoning steps and frequently fail to faithfully align with the draft conclusions. These results underscore the need for more faithful and interpretable reasoning in advanced LRMs.

paragraphs: Reasoning models often produce intermediate thinking drafts before their final answers, potentially exploring several reasoning paths. For those drafts to support monitoring and interpretation, their contents need to meaningfully influence the model's subsequent reasoning and response. This paper evaluates that relationship through deliberate counterfactual changes to the draft.

The framework separates two questions. Intra-draft faithfulness asks whether individual steps causally affect later steps and the draft's conclusion; the authors test this by inserting counterfactual reasoning steps. Draft-to-answer faithfulness asks whether the final answer depends on, and is logically consistent with, the draft. To test that relationship, they perturb the logic at the draft's conclusion.

Experiments across six leading reasoning models find selective responsiveness to intermediate steps and frequent failures to align final answers with draft conclusions. These findings distinguish the presence of an elaborate reasoning trace from evidence that its stated steps guide the outcome. They motivate more faithful reasoning processes if thinking drafts are to provide reliable tools for interpretation, monitoring, and control.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual interventions reveal selective faithfulness within reasoning drafts and frequent mismatches between draft conclusions and final answers.

title: Measuring the Faithfulness of Thinking Drafts in Large Reasoning Models

abstract: We introduce Linearly Constrained Diffusion Implicit Models (CDIM), a fast and accurate approach to solving noisy linear inverse problems using diffusion models. Traditional diffusion-based inverse methods rely on numerous projection steps to enforce measurement consistency in addition to unconditional denoising steps. CDIM achieves a 10–50× reduction in projection steps by dynamically adjusting the number and size of projection steps to align a residual measurement energy with its theoretical distribution under the forward diffusion process. This adaptive alignment preserves measurement consistency while substantially accelerating constrained inference. For noise-free linear inverse problems, CDIM exactly satisfies the measurement constraints with few projection steps, even when existing methods fail. We demonstrate CDIM’s effectiveness across a range of applications, including super-resolution, denoising, inpainting, deblurring, and 3D point cloud reprojection.

paragraphs: Linear inverse problems reconstruct an underlying signal from measurements, potentially corrupted by noise. Diffusion models can support reconstruction, but existing approaches often alternate denoising with many projection steps that enforce agreement with the measurements. CDIM makes this constraint-handling process adaptive to reduce the work required during inference.

The method adjusts both the number and size of projection steps. Its target is to align the residual measurement energy with the theoretical distribution induced by forward diffusion. That alignment provides a criterion for maintaining measurement consistency as denoising progresses. The authors report a tenfold to fiftyfold reduction in projection steps while substantially accelerating constrained inference.
