Evaluations cover super-resolution, denoising, inpainting, deblurring, and reprojection of 3D point clouds. These results demonstrate the approach across different reconstruction tasks, with its central contribution being a more economical way to coordinate diffusion-based denoising and the constraints imposed by observed measurements.
summary.tldr: CDIM adaptively enforces measurement consistency in diffusion reconstruction, reducing projection steps by 10–50×.

title: Linearly Constrained Diffusion Implicit Models

abstract: Modern LLMs are increasingly deep, and depth correlates with performance, albeit with diminishing returns. However, do these models use their depth efficiently? Do they compose more features to create higher-order computations that are impossible in shallow models, or do they merely spread the same kinds of computation out over more layers? To address these questions, we analyze the residual stream of the Llama 3.1, Qwen 3, and OLMo 2 family of models. We find: First, comparing the output of the sublayers to the residual stream reveals that layers in the second half contribute much less than those in the first half, with a clear phase transition between the two halves. Second, skipping layers in the second half has a much smaller effect on future computations and output predictions. Third, for multihop tasks, we are unable to find evidence that models are using increased depth to compose subresults in examples involving many hops. Fourth, we seek to directly address whether deeper models are using their additional layers to perform new kinds of computation. To do this, we train linear maps from the residual stream of a shallow model to a deeper one. We find that layers with the same relative depth map best to each other, suggesting that the larger model simply spreads the same computations out over its many layers. All this evidence suggests that deeper models are not using their depth to learn new kinds of computation, but only using the greater depth to perform more fine-grained adjustments to the residual. This may help explain why increasing scale leads to diminishing returns for stacked Transformer architectures.

paragraphs: Adding layers to a language model often improves performance, but this paper asks what those extra layers actually accomplish. The authors examine the residual stream, the representation carried through the layers, in Llama 3.1, Qwen 3, and OLMo 2 models. Several observations point toward the second interpretation. Layers in the latter half make much smaller contributions to the residual stream, with a distinct transition between the halves. Skipping later layers also has less effect on subsequent computation and predictions. On multihop tasks, the authors do not find evidence that additional depth combines intermediate results across many reasoning hops.

They also learn linear mappings between shallow and deep models' representations. Layers at matching relative positions align best, suggesting that deeper models distribute similar computations across more layers. Taken together, the evidence supports the authors' interpretation of increasingly fine-grained adjustments. It does not establish that depth can never enable new computations, but may help explain diminishing returns from scaling stacked Transformers.
summary.tldr: Analyses of three model families suggest extra depth often spreads similar computations across more layers instead of introducing new kinds of computation.

title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?

abstract: We introduce FAEclust, a novel functional autoencoder framework for cluster analysis of multi-dimensional functional data, data that are random realizations of vector-valued random functions. Our framework features a universal-approximator encoder that captures complex nonlinear interdependencies among component functions, and a universal-approximator decoder capable of accurately reconstructing both Euclidean and manifold-valued functional data. Stability and robustness are enhanced through innovative regularization strategies applied to functional weights and biases. Additionally, we incorporate a clustering loss into the network's training objective, promoting the learning of latent representations that are conducive to effective clustering. A key innovation is our shape-informed clustering objective, ensuring that the clustering results are resistant to phase variations in the functions. We establish the universal approximation property of our non-linear decoder and validate the effectiveness of our model through extensive experiments.

paragraphs: FAEclust groups multidimensional functional data: observations represented by several related functions rather than a single fixed vector. The framework uses a functional autoencoder to learn a compact representation and reconstruct the original functions. Its encoder is designed to capture complex nonlinear relationships between component functions, while its decoder supports both Euclidean-valued and manifold-valued data.

The training objective includes a clustering loss, so learning the representation directly supports forming useful groups. A shape-informed objective makes those groups resistant to phase variations in the functions. This matters when changes in the alignment of a functional pattern should not dominate the grouping. Regularization of functional weights and biases further supports stability and robustness.

The authors establish a universal approximation property for the nonlinear decoder and evaluate the model through extensive experiments. The theoretical result concerns the decoder's representational capacity, while the experiments support the overall framework's effectiveness. The contribution brings nonlinear reconstruction, cluster-oriented representation learning, and resistance to phase variation into one functional-data approach.
summary.tldr: FAEclust learns functional-data representations for clustering, emphasizing shape and reducing sensitivity to phase variations.

title: Shape-Informed Clustering of Multi-Dimensional Functional Data via Deep Functional Autoencoders

abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) bypasses complex reward engineering by learning from human feedback. However, due to the high cost of obtaining feedback, PbRL typically relies on a limited set of preference-labeled samples. This data scarcity introduces two key inefficiencies: (1) the reward model overfits to the limited feedback, leading to poor generalization to unseen samples, and (2) the agent exploits the learned reward model, exacerbating overestimation of action values in temporal difference (TD) learning. To address these issues, we propose STAR, an efficient PbRL method that integrates preference margin regularization and policy regularization. Preference margin regularization mitigates overfitting by introducing a bounded margin in reward optimization, preventing excessive bias toward specific feedback. Policy regularization bootstraps a conservative estimate $\widehat{Q}$ from well-supported state-action pairs in the replay memory, reducing overestimation during policy learning. Experimental results show that STAR improves feedback efficiency, achieving 34.8\% higher performance in online settings and 29.7\% in offline settings compared to state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies confirm that STAR facilitates more robust reward and value function learning. The videos of this project are released at https://sites.google.com/view/pbrl-star.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning learns rewards from human feedback, reducing the need to design them manually. Because feedback is expensive, training often relies on few labeled comparisons. The paper identifies two resulting problems: reward models overfit those comparisons, and agents exploit the learned rewards in ways that worsen action-value overestimation.

STAR addresses both problems with separate regularizers. Preference margin regularization places a bounded margin in reward optimization to limit excessive bias toward particular feedback. Policy regularization builds conservative value estimates using state-action pairs with good support in replay memory. This links caution in policy learning to evidence already represented in the agent’s stored experience.

The authors report improved feedback efficiency, with performance gains of 34.8 percent in online settings and 29.7 percent in offline settings over state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies support more robust learning of both rewards and value functions. The findings emphasize that scarce preference data affects two connected learning processes, so improving the reward model and controlling policy overestimation can be complementary.
summary.tldr: STAR improves preference-based reinforcement learning by jointly limiting reward-model overfitting and overly optimistic policy value estimates.

title: STAR: Efficient Preference-based Reinforcement Learning via Dual Regularization

abstract: Large Multi-modality Models (LMMs) have made significant progress in visual understanding and generation, but they still face challenges in General Visual Editing, particularly in following complex instructions, preserving appearance consistency, and supporting flexible input formats. To study this gap, we introduce RISEBench, the first benchmark for evaluating Reasoning-Informed viSual Editing (RISE). RISEBench focuses on four key reasoning categories: Temporal, Causal, Spatial, and Logical Reasoning. We curate high-quality test cases for each category and propose an robust evaluation framework that assesses Instruction Reasoning, Appearance Consistency, and Visual Plausibility with both human judges and the LMM-as-a-judge approach. We conducted experiments evaluating nine prominent visual editing models, comprising both open-source and proprietary models. The evaluation results demonstrate that current models face significant challenges in reasoning-based editing tasks. Even the most powerful model evaluated, GPT-image-1, achieves an accuracy of merely 28.8%. RISEBench effectively highlights the limitations of contemporary editing models, provides valuable insights, and indicates potential future directions for the field of reasoning-aware visual editing. Our code and data have been released at https://github.com/PhoenixZ810/RISEBench.

paragraphs: Visual editing requires models to connect an instruction to the changes an image needs. This paper studies edits that demand reasoning, alongside the need to maintain a consistent appearance. Its motivation is that progress in understanding and generating images has not resolved the challenges of following complex editing instructions.

The authors introduce RISEBench, a benchmark organized around four kinds of reasoning: temporal, causal, spatial, and logical. These categories examine reasoning about time, cause and effect, spatial relationships, and logic. By curating test cases for each category, the benchmark gives researchers a structured way to investigate reasoning in visual editing.

The evaluation considers three aspects of an edited image: whether it follows the instruction’s reasoning requirements, whether its appearance remains consistent, and whether the result is visually plausible. Both human judges and large multimodal models serve as evaluators. This combination examines instruction fulfillment alongside the visual qualities of the output.

The authors evaluate nine editing models, including open-source and proprietary systems, and report substantial difficulties with these tasks. GPT-image-1, the strongest model evaluated, reaches only 28.8% accuracy. That result points to a considerable gap on this benchmark between existing editing capabilities and successful reasoning-based edits. RISEBench provides a way to expose that gap and inform future research.
summary.tldr: RISEBench tests reasoning in visual editing and finds substantial challenges across nine models, with the strongest evaluated model achieving 28.8% accuracy.

title: Envisioning Beyond the Pixels: Benchmarking Reasoning-Informed Visual Editing

abstract: Thompson Sampling is one of the oldest heuristics for multi-armed bandit problems. It is a randomized algorithm based on Bayesian ideas, and has recently generated significant interest after several studies demonstrated it to have better empirical performance compared to the state of the art methods. However, many questions regarding its theoretical performance remained open. In this paper, we design and analyze Thompson Sampling algorithm for the stochastic contextual multi-armed bandit problem with linear payoff functions, when the contexts are provided by an adaptive adversary. This is among the most important and widely studied version of the contextual bandits problem. We prove a high probability regret bound of \tildeO(\fracd\sqrtε\sqrtT^1+ε) in time T for any ε∈(0,1), where d is the dimension of each context vector and εis a parameter used by the algorithm. Our results provide the first theoretical guarantees for the contextual version of Thompson Sampling, and are close to the lower bound of Ω(\sqrtdT) for this problem. This essentially solves the COLT open problem of Chapelle and Li [COLT 2012] regarding regret bounds for Thompson Sampling for contextual bandits problem with linear payoff functions. Our version of Thompson sampling uses Gaussian prior and Gaussian likelihood function. Our novel martingale-based analysis techniques also allow easy extensions to the use of other distributions, satisfying certain general conditions.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling chooses actions through randomized reasoning about uncertain rewards. This paper develops and analyzes a version for stochastic contextual bandits with linear payoffs, where the information describing available actions can be supplied by an adaptive adversary. The objective is to control regret, the accumulated reward lost relative to better choices.

The algorithm uses a Gaussian prior and Gaussian likelihood. For any algorithm parameter ε between zero and one, the authors prove a high-probability regret bound of order d T^((1+ε)/2) / sqrt(ε), with logarithmic factors suppressed. The result makes explicit how the guarantee depends on context dimension, elapsed time, and the chosen parameter.

The paper presents the first theoretical guarantees for contextual Thompson sampling and describes them as close to the problem's lower bound. Its analysis addresses a previously open question about linear contextual payoffs. The proof uses martingale techniques that also allow extensions to other distributions satisfying specified general conditions, broadening the potential reach of the analytical method beyond the Gaussian construction.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian Thompson sampling algorithm receives high-probability regret guarantees for linear contextual bandits with adaptively chosen contexts.

title: Thompson Sampling for Contextual Bandits with Linear Payoffs

abstract: We introduce DropConnect, a generalization of DropOut, for regularizing large fully-connected layers within neural networks. When training with Dropout, a randomly selected subset of activations are set to zero within each layer. DropConnect instead sets a randomly selected subset of weights within the network to zero. Each unit thus receives input from a random subset of units in the previous layer. We derive a bound on the generalization performance of both Dropout and DropConnect. We then evaluate DropConnect on a range of datasets, comparing to Dropout, and show state-of-the-art results on several image recoginition benchmarks can be obtained by aggregating multiple DropConnect-trained models.

When training with Dropout, a randomly selected subset of activations are set to zero within each layer. DropConnect instead sets a randomly selected subset of weights within the network to zero. Each unit thus receives input from a random subset of units in the previous layer. We derive a bound on the generalization performance of both Dropout and DropConnect. We then evaluate DropConnect on a range of datasets, comparing to Dropout, and show state-of-the-art results on several image recoginition benchmarks can be obtained by aggregating multiple DropConnect-trained models.

paragraphs: The paper introduces DropConnect, a regularization method for large fully connected neural network layers. It generalizes the idea behind Dropout by changing what is randomly removed during training. Dropout sets selected activations to zero; DropConnect instead sets selected network weights to zero.

With random weights removed, each unit receives input from a random subset of units in the preceding layer. The resulting training procedure varies which connections contribute to the computation. The paper also derives a bound on generalization performance for both Dropout and DropConnect, giving the proposed method a theoretical treatment alongside its relationship to the existing approach.

The authors evaluate DropConnect across a range of datasets and compare it with Dropout. They report that combining multiple models trained with DropConnect can achieve state-of-the-art results on several image recognition benchmarks. That finding specifically concerns aggregated models. The contribution includes both the connection-level regularization mechanism and evidence that ensembles using it can deliver strong image recognition performance.
summary.tldr: DropConnect randomly removes weights during training, with generalization analysis and strong image recognition results from aggregating trained models.

title: Regularization of Neural Networks using DropConnect

abstract: We present a novel Newton-type method for distributed optimization, which is particularly well suited for stochastic optimization and learning problems. For quadratic objectives, the method enjoys a linear rate of convergence which provably \emphimproves with the data size, requiring an essentially constant number of iterations under reasonable assumptions. We provide theoretical and empirical evidence of the advantages of our method compared to other approaches, such as one-shot parameter averaging and ADMM.
originalAbstract: We present a novel Newton-type method for distributed optimization, which is particularly well suited for stochastic optimization and learning problems. For quadratic objectives, the method enjoys a linear rate of convergence which provably \emphimproves with the data size, requiring an essentially constant number of iterations under reasonable assumptions. We provide theoretical and empirical evidence of the advantages of our method compared to other approaches, such as one-shot parameter averaging and ADMM.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization must coordinate computation across multiple locations, making communication an important part of the cost. This paper proposes an approximate Newton-type method designed for that setting. The authors identify stochastic optimization and learning problems as particularly suitable applications for the approach.

The central theoretical result concerns quadratic objectives. For this class, the method has a linear convergence rate, meaning that optimization error decreases geometrically across iterations. More unusually, the proven rate improves as the amount of data grows. Under the assumptions described by the authors as reasonable, the required number of iterations is essentially constant.

This links larger datasets to potentially easier coordination: more data can improve the iteration behavior rather than merely adding computational work. The paper provides both theoretical and empirical evidence of advantages over approaches including one-shot parameter averaging and ADMM. The strongest stated convergence conclusion is specifically for quadratic objectives and remains conditional on the assumptions used in that analysis.
summary.tldr: An approximate Newton method offers communication-efficient distributed optimization, with a quadratic-objective convergence rate that improves as data size grows.

title: Communication-Efficient Distributed Optimization using an Approximate Newton-type Method

abstract: We study the effectiveness of learning low degree polynomials using neural networks by the gradient descent method. While neural networks have been shown to have great expressive power, and gradient descent has been widely used in practice for learning neural networks, few theoretical guarantees are known for such methods. In particular, it is well known that gradient descent can get stuck at local minima, even for simple classes of target functions. In this paper, we present several positive theoretical results to support the effectiveness of neural networks. We focus on two-layer neural networks (i.e. one hidden layer) where the top layer node is a linear function, similar to \citebarron93. First we show that for a randomly initialized neural network with sufficiently many hidden units, the gradient descent method can learn any low degree polynomial. Secondly, we show that if we use complex-valued weights (the target function can still be real), then under suitable conditions, there are no “robust local minima”: the neural network can always escape a local minimum by performing a random perturbation. This property does not hold for real-valued weights. Thirdly, we discuss whether sparse polynomials can be learned with \emphsmall neural networks, where the size is dependent on the sparsity of the target function.

paragraphs: A neural network's ability to represent a function does not by itself establish that gradient descent can learn it. This paper studies that distinction for low-degree polynomials. It focuses on networks with one hidden layer and a linear output, seeking theoretical conditions under which optimization succeeds despite the possibility of local minima.

The first result shows that gradient descent can learn any low-degree polynomial from a randomly initialized network with sufficiently many hidden units. A second result concerns complex-valued weights, even when the desired output function is real. Under suitable conditions, these networks have no robust local minima: random perturbations allow escape from a local minimum. The authors state that this property does not hold for real-valued weights.

The paper also discusses whether sparse polynomials can be learned using small networks whose size depends on the target's sparsity. That discussion is distinct from the stated guarantees for sufficiently wide networks and suitable complex-weight settings. Together, the results give conditional theoretical support for neural-network learning, while showing why network size and the choice of weight domain matter.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional guarantees for learning low-degree polynomials and escaping local minima in certain complex-weight neural networks.

title: Learning Polynomials with Neural Networks

abstract: We investigate the statistical convergence rate of a Bayesian low-rank tensor estimator, and derive the minimax optimal rate for learning a low-rank tensor. Our problem setting is the regression problem where the regression coefficient forms a tensor structure. This problem setting occurs in many practical applications, such as collaborative filtering, multi-task learning, and spatio-temporal data analysis. The convergence rate of the Bayes tensor estimator is analyzed in terms of both in-sample and out-of-sample predictive accuracies. It is shown that a fast learning rate is achieved without any strong convexity of the observation. Moreover, we show that the method has adaptivity to the unknown rank of the true tensor, that is, the near optimal rate depending on the true rank is achieved even if it is not known a priori. Finally, we show the minimax optimal learning rate for the tensor estimation problem, and thus show that the derived bound of the Bayes estimator is tight and actually near minimax optimal.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression problems whose coefficients form a tensor, a multidimensional arrangement of parameters. The setting appears in collaborative filtering, multi-task learning, and analysis of data varying across space and time. The authors investigate how quickly a Bayesian estimator learns when that coefficient tensor has a low-rank structure.

The analysis covers predictive accuracy both on the observed inputs and on new inputs. It establishes a fast learning rate without requiring strong convexity of the observation. It also shows adaptation to an unknown true rank: the estimator can achieve a nearly optimal rate that depends on that rank even when the rank is not supplied beforehand.

To judge how strong this result is, the authors derive a minimax learning rate for the tensor-estimation problem. This provides a benchmark for the best achievable worst-case statistical performance. Comparing the Bayesian estimator's bound with that benchmark shows that the bound is tight and the estimator is near minimax optimal, rather than merely statistically consistent.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian low-rank tensor estimator achieves fast, rank-adaptive prediction rates that are near minimax optimal.

title: Convergence rate of Bayesian tensor estimator and its minimax optimality

abstract: We present a new, fully generative model of optical telescope image sets, along with a variational procedure for inference. Each pixel intensity is treated as a Poisson random variable, with a rate parameter dependent on latent properties of stars and galaxies. Key latent properties are themselves random, with scientific prior distributions constructed from large ancillary data sets. We check our approach on synthetic images. We also run it on images from a major sky survey, where it exceeds the performance of the current state-of-the-art method for locating celestial bodies and measuring their colors.

paragraphs: Celeste models optical telescope images by connecting observed pixel intensities to hidden properties of stars and galaxies. Its generative approach describes how those underlying celestial objects could produce the images. Inference then works in the opposite direction, using the images to estimate the properties of the objects that generated them.

Each pixel intensity follows a Poisson distribution whose rate depends on the latent properties of celestial sources. Important source properties are also treated as random quantities. Their prior distributions draw on scientific information constructed from large ancillary datasets. This creates a probabilistic connection between prior knowledge about celestial objects and the evidence contained in the telescope images.

The authors introduce a variational procedure for carrying out inference in this model. They check the approach on synthetic images and apply it to images from a major sky survey. In that survey evaluation, it exceeds the existing state-of-the-art method for locating celestial bodies and measuring their colors. These findings support the practical value of combining a generative image model with scientifically informed priors.
summary.tldr: Celeste combines a generative telescope-image model with variational inference to improve celestial object localization and color measurement.

title: Celeste: Variational inference for a generative model of astronomical images

abstract: We consider a broad class of first-order optimization algorithms which are \emphoblivious, in the sense that their step sizes are scheduled regardless of the function under consideration, except for limited side-information such as smoothness or strong convexity parameters. With the knowledge of these two parameters, we show that any such algorithm attains an iteration complexity lower bound of Ω(\sqrtL/ε) for L-smooth convex functions, and \tildeΩ(\sqrtL/μ\ln(1/ε)) for L-smooth μ-strongly convex functions. These lower bounds are stronger than those in the traditional oracle model, as they hold independently of the dimension. To attain these, we abandon the oracle model in favor of a structure-based approach which builds upon a framework recently proposed in Arjevani et al. (2015). We further show that without knowing the strong convexity parameter, it is impossible to attain an iteration complexity better than \tildeΩ\sqrt(L/μ)\ln(1/ε). This result is then used to formalize an observation regarding L-smooth convex functions, namely, that the iteration complexity of algorithms employing time-invariant step sizes must be at least Ω(L/ε).

It calls these algorithms oblivious. The question is how few iterations methods in this class can require to achieve a given accuracy.

The authors establish lower bounds for smooth convex and smooth strongly convex objectives when the relevant parameters are known. These bounds hold independently of dimension, strengthening the corresponding traditional oracle-model bounds in that respect. The analysis uses a structure-based framework, making the form of the algorithm central to the impossibility results.

The paper also examines what can be achieved without knowledge of the strong convexity parameter. It uses this analysis to formalize a restriction on methods with time-invariant step sizes: their iteration complexity for smooth convex functions must be at least proportional to L/ε. The findings clarify how algorithm structure, parameter knowledge, and step-size scheduling constrain attainable convergence speed.
summary.tldr: Dimension-independent lower bounds reveal how fixed scheduling rules and limited parameter knowledge constrain first-order optimization.

title: On the Iteration Complexity of Oblivious First-Order Optimization Algorithms

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) are powerful non-parametric function estimators. However, their applications are largely limited by the expensive computational cost of the inference procedures. Existing stochastic or distributed synchronous variational inferences, although have alleviated this issue by scaling up GPs to millions of samples, are still far from satisfactory for real-world large applications, where the data sizes are often orders of magnitudes larger, say, billions. To solve this problem, we propose ADVGP, the first Asynchronous Distributed Variational Gaussian Process inference for regression, on the recent large-scale machine learning platform, PARAMETER SERVER. ADVGP uses a novel, flexible variational framework based on a weight space augmentation, and implements the highly efficient, asynchronous proximal gradient optimization. While maintaining comparable or better predictive performance, ADVGP greatly improves upon the efficiency of the existing variational methods. With ADVGP, we effortlessly scale up GP regression to a real-world application with billions of samples and demonstrate an excellent, superior prediction accuracy to the popular linear models.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer flexible function estimation, but the computational cost of inference limits their use on very large datasets. This paper targets a scale beyond the millions of observations already handled by stochastic or synchronously distributed variational methods. Its goal is practical Gaussian process regression on datasets containing billions of samples.

The proposed ADVGP method combines a new variational framework with asynchronous distributed optimization on the PARAMETER SERVER platform. The framework uses a weight-space augmentation, while optimization proceeds through asynchronous proximal gradient updates. Together, these choices address both the mathematical formulation of approximate inference and the execution of that inference across distributed computing resources.

The authors report substantially improved efficiency over existing variational methods while preserving comparable or better predictive performance. They also demonstrate regression on a real application containing billions of samples, where prediction accuracy exceeds that of popular linear models. The result supports the feasibility of using Gaussian process regression at this scale, rather than treating computational expense as an unavoidable barrier.
summary.tldr: ADVGP combines variational inference with asynchronous distributed optimization to scale Gaussian process regression to billions of samples.

title: Asynchronous Distributed Variational Gaussian Process for Regression

abstract: The likelihood-ratio method is often used to estimate gradients of stochastic computations, for which baselines are required to reduce the estimation variance. Many types of baselines have been proposed, although their degree of optimality is not well understood. In this study, we establish a novel framework of gradient estimation that includes most of the common gradient estimators as special cases. The framework gives a natural derivation of the optimal estimator that can be interpreted as a special case of the likelihood-ratio method so that we can evaluate the optimal degree of practical techniques with it. It bridges the likelihood-ratio method and the reparameterization trick while still supporting discrete variables. It is derived from the exchange property of the differentiation and integration. To be more specific, it is derived by the reparameterization trick and local marginalization analogous to the local expectation gradient. We evaluate various baselines and the optimal estimator for variational learning and show that the performance of the modern estimators is close to the optimal estimator.

paragraphs: Gradients of stochastic computations are often estimated with the likelihood-ratio method. These estimates can have substantial variance, so practical methods use baselines to reduce their noise. This paper asks how close such techniques come to the best estimator available within a common mathematical framework.

The authors develop a framework that contains most common gradient estimators as special cases and naturally yields an optimal estimator. That estimator can itself be interpreted through the likelihood-ratio method, making it a reference for assessing practical alternatives. The derivation uses the interchange of differentiation and integration, together with reparameterization and local marginalization.

The framework also connects likelihood-ratio estimation with the reparameterization trick while retaining support for discrete variables. This connection lets methods often treated separately be analyzed within one formulation. In variational-learning evaluations, the authors compare several baselines with the optimal estimator and find that modern estimators perform close to it. The result provides evidence that the evaluated practical techniques already capture much of the improvement available under this framework.
summary.tldr: A unified gradient-estimation framework derives an optimal reference estimator and finds modern methods perform close to it in variational-learning evaluations.

title: Evaluating the Variance of Likelihood-Ratio Gradient Estimators

abstract: Deep learning on graph structures has shown exciting results in various applications. However, few attentions have been paid to the robustness of such models, in contrast to numerous research work for image or text adversarial attack and defense. In this paper, we focus on the adversarial attacks that fool deep learning models by modifying the combinatorial structure of data. We first propose a reinforcement learning based attack method that learns the generalizable attack policy, while only requiring prediction labels from the target classifier. We further propose attack methods based on genetic algorithms and gradient descent in the scenario where additional prediction confidence or gradients are available. We use both synthetic and real-world data to show that, a family of Graph Neural Network models are vulnerable to these attacks, in both graph-level and node-level classification tasks. We also show such attacks can be used to diagnose the learned classifiers.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether deep learning models on graphs remain reliable when an attacker changes the structure of their input. Its focus is the combinatorial arrangement of the data: structural modifications can cause a classifier to make a different prediction. The work examines this vulnerability for both classifying whole graphs and classifying individual nodes.

The authors develop attacks for different levels of access to the target model. A reinforcement learning approach learns a generalizable attack policy using only predicted labels. When richer information is available, they also propose methods based on genetic algorithms and gradient descent, using prediction confidence or gradients to guide the attack.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that a family of graph neural networks is vulnerable to these methods. The findings establish weaknesses in the evaluated models and tasks, without implying that every graph classifier fails. The authors also show that attacks can help diagnose learned classifiers, making structural perturbations useful for examining model behavior as well as exposing errors.
summary.tldr: Structural attacks can fool graph neural networks, including through a learned attack policy that needs only prediction labels.

title: Adversarial Attack on Graph Structured Data

abstract: Bayesian neural networks with latent variables are scalable and flexible probabilistic models: they account for uncertainty in the estimation of the network weights and, by making use of latent variables, can capture complex noise patterns in the data. Using these models we show how to perform and utilize a decomposition of uncertainty in aleatoric and epistemic components for decision making purposes. This allows us to successfully identify informative points for active learning of functions with heteroscedastic and bimodal noise. Using the decomposition we further define a novel risk-sensitive criterion for reinforcement learningto identify policies that balance expected cost, model-bias and noise aversion.

Using these models we show how to perform and utilize a decomposition of uncertainty in aleatoric and epistemic components for decision making purposes. This allows us to successfully identify informative points for active learning of functions with heteroscedastic and bimodal noise. paragraphs: Uncertain predictions can reflect uncertainty about the model or noise in the observations themselves. This paper separates those sources using Bayesian neural networks with latent variables. Uncertainty in the network weights represents incomplete knowledge of the model, while latent variables allow the model to capture complex patterns of noise in the data.

The authors show how to decompose predictive uncertainty into epistemic and aleatoric components and use that distinction when choosing what to learn next. In active learning, they successfully identify informative points for functions with heteroscedastic noise, whose level varies, and bimodal noise. The decomposition makes the source of uncertainty relevant to the selection decision.

The paper also uses the same distinction to define a risk-sensitive reinforcement learning criterion. This criterion balances expected cost, model bias, and aversion to noise when identifying policies. Its contribution is to turn uncertainty into separate decision-relevant quantities, allowing learning and control choices to account for why an outcome is uncertain.
summary.tldr: Separating model uncertainty from data noise supports informative data selection and reinforcement learning policies that balance distinct sources of risk.

title: Decomposition of Uncertainty in Bayesian Deep Learning for Efficient and Risk-sensitive Learning

abstract: Predicting structured outputs can be computationally onerous due to the combinatorially large output spaces. In this paper, we focus on reducing the prediction time of a trained black-box structured classifier without losing accuracy. To do so, we train a speedup classifier that learns to mimic a black-box classifier under the learning-to-search approach. As the structured classifier predicts more examples, the speedup classifier will operate as a learned heuristic to guide search to favorable regions of the output space. We present a mistake bound for the speedup classifier and identify inference situations where it can independently make correct judgments without input features. We evaluate our method on the task of entity and relation extraction and show that the speedup classifier outperforms even greedy search in terms of speed without loss of accuracy.

To do so, we train a speedup classifier that learns to mimic a black-box classifier under the learning-to-search approach. As the structured classifier predicts more examples, the speedup classifier will operate as a learned heuristic to guide search to favorable regions of the output space. We present a mistake bound for the speedup classifier and identify inference situations where it can independently make correct judgments without input features. We evaluate our method on the task of entity and relation extraction and show that the speedup classifier outperforms even greedy search in terms of speed without loss of accuracy.

paragraphs: Structured prediction can be slow because the number of possible combined outputs grows combinatorially. This paper seeks to accelerate a trained structured classifier while preserving its accuracy. The original classifier is treated as a black box, and an additional classifier learns to imitate its behavior through a learning-to-search approach.

As the original model processes more examples, the additional model becomes a learned search heuristic. It guides inference toward promising parts of the output space, reducing the work required to locate useful predictions. The authors also establish a mistake bound and identify particular inference situations in which this speedup classifier can make correct judgments without accessing input features.

The method is evaluated on entity and relation extraction. In those experiments, the learned speedup classifier is faster even than greedy search, with no loss of accuracy. The result shows that information acquired from a classifier’s prediction behavior can help organize subsequent search efficiently, making inference itself a target for learning.
summary.tldr: A classifier trained to imitate structured prediction learns search guidance that improves inference speed without accuracy loss in reported experiments.

title: Learning to Speed Up Structured Output Prediction

abstract: In order to integrate uncertainty estimates into deep time-series modelling, Kalman Filters (KFs) (Kalman et al., 1960) have been integrated with deep learning models, however, such approaches typically rely on approximate inference tech- niques such as variational inference which makes learning more complex and often less scalable due to approximation errors. We propose a new deep approach to Kalman filtering which can be learned directly in an end-to-end manner using backpropagation without additional approximations. Our approach uses a high-dimensional factorized latent state representation for which the Kalman updates simplify to scalar operations and thus avoids hard to backpropagate, computationally heavy and potentially unstable matrix inversions. Moreover, we use locally linear dynamic models to efficiently propagate the latent state to the next time step. The resulting network architecture, which we call Recurrent Kalman Network (RKN), can be used for any time-series data, similar to a LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) but uses an explicit representation of uncertainty. As shown by our experiments, the RKN obtains much more accurate uncertainty estimates than an LSTM or Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) (Cho et al., 2014) while also showing a slightly improved prediction performance and outperforms various recent generative models on an image imputation task.

paragraphs: Recurrent Kalman Networks combine deep time-series modeling with an explicit representation of uncertainty. The paper addresses the complexity of earlier combinations of Kalman filtering and deep learning, which typically rely on approximate inference. Its proposed architecture can instead be trained directly through backpropagation without adding those inference approximations.

This avoids computationally heavy matrix inversions that can be unstable and difficult to differentiate through. Locally linear dynamics then propagate the latent state to the next time step, combining learned representations with structured temporal updates.

In the reported experiments, the network provides much more accurate uncertainty estimates than LSTMs or GRUs, along with slightly better predictions. It also outperforms several recent generative models on image imputation. The contribution is therefore both computational and predictive: a tractable filtering architecture preserves explicit uncertainty while achieving the stated empirical improvements in uncertainty quality and task performance.
summary.tldr: Recurrent Kalman Networks simplify uncertainty-aware temporal inference to scalar updates and report better uncertainty estimates than LSTMs and GRUs.

title: Recurrent Kalman Networks: Factorized Inference in High-Dimensional Deep Feature Spaces

abstract: We present a unified framework based on primal-dual stochastic mirror descent for approximately solving infinite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) given a generative model. When applied to an average-reward MDP with $A_{tot}$ total actions and mixing time bound $t_{mix}$ our method computes an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with an expected $\widetilde{O}(t_{mix}^2 A_{tot} \epsilon^{-2})$ samples from the state-transition matrix, removing the ergodicity dependence of prior art. When applied to a $\gamma$-discounted MDP with $A_{tot}$ total actions our method computes an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with an expected $\widetilde{O}((1-\gamma)^{-4} A_{tot} \epsilon^{-2})$ samples, improving over the best-known primal-dual methods while matching the state-of-the-art up to a $(1-\gamma)^{-1}$ factor. Both methods are model-free, update state values and policies simultaneously, and run in time linear in the number of samples taken. We achieve these results through a more general stochastic mirror descent framework for solving bilinear saddle-point problems with simplex and box domains and we demonstrate the flexibility of this framework by providing further applications to constrained MDPs.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common optimization framework for approximately solving infinite-horizon Markov decision processes when a generative model supplies transition samples. It uses primal-dual stochastic mirror descent to update state values and policies together. The methods are model-free despite relying on access to this sampling model.

For average-reward problems, the expected sample bound scales with the square of a mixing-time bound, the total number of actions, and inverse squared target error, up to logarithmic factors. It removes the ergodicity dependence of earlier work. For discounted problems, the corresponding bound contains the fourth inverse power of one minus the discount factor, improving earlier primal-dual methods while remaining one such factor from the stated best-known rate.

Both algorithms run in time linear in their sample counts, connecting statistical requirements directly to computational work. Their common foundation is a more general method for bilinear saddle-point problems over simplex and box domains. Applications to constrained decision processes further demonstrate the flexibility of that optimization framework.
summary.tldr: A stochastic mirror-descent framework provides efficient sampling-based algorithms for average-reward, discounted, and constrained decision processes.

title: Efficiently Solving MDPs with Stochastic Mirror Descent

abstract: To analyze high-dimensional and complex data in the real world, deep generative models, such as variational autoencoder (VAE) embed data in a low-dimensional space (latent space) and learn a probabilistic model in the latent space. However, they struggle to accurately reproduce the probability distribution function (PDF) in the input space from that in the latent space. If the embedding were isometric, this issue can be solved, because the relation of PDFs can become tractable. To achieve isometric property, we propose Rate-Distortion Optimization guided autoencoder inspired by orthonormal transform coding. We show our method has the following properties: (i) the Jacobian matrix between the input space and a Euclidean latent space forms a constantly-scaled orthonormal system and enables isometric data embedding; (ii) the relation of PDFs in both spaces can become tractable one such as proportional relation. Furthermore, our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised anomaly detection with four public datasets.

paragraphs: Generative models often compress high-dimensional data into a smaller latent space and learn probabilities there. Recovering an accurate probability density in the original input space can still be difficult. This paper connects that difficulty to embedding geometry: an isometric embedding can make the relationship between the two densities tractable.

The authors propose an autoencoder guided by rate-distortion optimization and inspired by orthonormal transform coding. They show that the Jacobian relating input and Euclidean latent spaces forms an orthonormal system with constant scaling. This property enables the stated isometric embedding and links the geometry of the representation to the transformation of probability densities.

With this structure, the density relationship can take a tractable form, such as proportionality. The paper also reports better unsupervised anomaly detection than state-of-the-art methods on four public datasets. The contribution connects a geometric property of the learned embedding with more manageable density relationships and demonstrates the method's usefulness in the reported anomaly-detection evaluations.
summary.tldr: A rate-distortion-guided autoencoder enables isometric embeddings with tractable density relationships and improves reported anomaly detection.

title: Rate-distortion optimization guided autoencoder for isometric embedding in Euclidean latent space

abstract: While deep neural networks achieve great performance on fitting the training distribution, the learned networks are prone to overfitting and are susceptible to adversarial attacks. In this regard, a number of mixup based augmentation methods have been recently proposed. However, these approaches mainly focus on creating previously unseen virtual examples and can sometimes provide misleading supervisory signal to the network. To this end, we propose Puzzle Mix, a mixup method for explicitly utilizing the saliency information and the underlying statistics of the natural examples. This leads to an interesting optimization problem alternating between the multi-label objective for optimal mixing mask and saliency discounted optimal transport objective. Our experiments show Puzzle Mix achieves the state of the art generalization and the adversarial robustness results compared to other mixup methods on CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet datasets, and the source code is available at https://github.com/snu-mllab/PuzzleMix.
originalAbstract: While deep neural networks achieve great performance on fitting the training distribution, the learned networks are prone to overfitting and are susceptible to adversarial attacks. In this regard, a number of mixup based augmentation methods have been recently proposed. However, these approaches mainly focus on creating previously unseen virtual examples and can sometimes provide misleading supervisory signal to the network. To this end, we propose Puzzle Mix, a mixup method for explicitly utilizing the saliency information and the underlying statistics of the natural examples. This leads to an interesting optimization problem alternating between the multi-label objective for optimal mixing mask and saliency discounted optimal transport objective. Our experiments show Puzzle Mix achieves the state of the art generalization and the adversarial robustness results compared to other mixup methods on CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet datasets, and the source code is available at https://github.com/snu-mllab/PuzzleMix.

paragraphs: Mixup methods create virtual training examples by combining existing examples, helping address overfitting and vulnerability to adversarial attacks. However, a newly combined example can sometimes give the network a misleading training signal. Puzzle Mix addresses this issue by explicitly considering salient content and the underlying statistics of the source examples.

The method formulates mixing as an optimization problem with alternating stages. One stage optimizes a multi-label mixing mask, which controls how the examples are combined. The other uses a saliency-discounted optimal transport objective. Together, these stages make the construction of augmented examples depend on information in the original examples rather than treating novelty alone as the goal.

On CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet, the authors report state-of-the-art generalization and adversarial robustness relative to the other mixup methods considered. The results support using saliency and local statistics to guide augmentation. The stated advantage is an empirical comparison on those datasets and against that class of methods, rather than an unrestricted guarantee for every augmentation setting.
summary.tldr: Puzzle Mix uses saliency and local statistics to construct mixed training examples, improving reported generalization and robustness over other mixup methods.

title: Puzzle Mix: Exploiting Saliency and Local Statistics for Optimal Mixup

abstract: We consider the batch reinforcement learning problem where the agent needs to learn only from a fixed batch of data, without further interaction with the environment. In such a scenario, we want to prevent the optimized policy from deviating too much from the data collection policy since the estimation becomes highly unstable otherwise due to the off-policy nature of the problem. However, imposing this requirement too strongly will result in a policy that merely follows the data collection policy. Unlike prior work where this trade-off is controlled by hand-tuned hyperparameters, we propose a novel batch reinforcement learning approach, batch optimization of policy and hyperparameter (BOPAH), that uses a gradient-based optimization of the hyperparameter using held-out data. We show that BOPAH outperforms other batch reinforcement learning algorithms in tabular and continuous control tasks, by finding a good balance to the trade-off between adhering to the data collection policy and pursuing the possible policy improvement.

However, imposing this requirement too strongly will result in a policy that merely follows the data collection policy. Unlike prior work where this trade-off is controlled by hand-tuned hyperparameters, we propose a novel batch reinforcement learning approach, batch optimization of policy and hyperparameter (BOPAH), that uses a gradient-based optimization of the hyperparameter using held-out data. paragraphs: Batch reinforcement learning trains an agent using a fixed dataset, without allowing further interaction with the environment. This creates a difficult balance. A policy that moves too far from the behavior that collected the data can have highly unstable estimates. A policy constrained too closely to that behavior may simply reproduce it, leaving potential improvements unused.

The paper introduces batch optimization of policy and hyperparameter, or BOPAH. Instead of relying on a manually tuned hyperparameter to control this balance, the method adjusts that hyperparameter through gradient-based optimization using held-out data. Policy learning and the choice of how strongly to stay near the data collection policy are therefore part of the same approach.

The authors report that BOPAH outperforms other batch reinforcement learning algorithms on tabular and continuous control tasks. They attribute this performance to finding a useful balance between adherence and improvement. The result supports using held-out data to guide a consequential optimization choice when collecting additional experience is unavailable.
summary.tldr: BOPAH uses held-out data and hyperparameter gradients to balance policy improvement against staying close to the behavior represented in a fixed dataset.

title: Batch Reinforcement Learning with Hyperparameter Gradients

abstract: Random forests on the one hand, and neural networks on the other hand, have met great success in the machine learning community for their predictive performance. Combinations of both have been proposed in the literature, notably leading to the so-called deep forests (DF) (Zhou & Feng,2019). In this paper, our aim is not to benchmark DF performances but to investigate instead their underlying mechanisms. Additionally, DF architecture can be generally simplified into more simple and computationally efficient shallow forest networks. Despite some instability, the latter may outperform standard predictive tree-based methods. We exhibit a theoretical framework in which a shallow tree network is shown to enhance the performance of classical decision trees. In such a setting, we provide tight theoretical lower and upper bounds on its excess risk. These theoretical results show the interest of tree-network architectures for well-structured data provided that the first layer, acting as a data encoder, is rich enough.
originalAbstract: Random forests on the one hand, and neural networks on the other hand, have met great success in the machine learning community for their predictive performance. Combinations of both have been proposed in the literature, notably leading to the so-called deep forests (DF) (Zhou & Feng,2019). In this paper, our aim is not to benchmark DF performances but to investigate instead their underlying mechanisms. Additionally, DF architecture can be generally simplified into more simple and computationally efficient shallow forest networks. Despite some instability, the latter may outperform standard predictive tree-based methods. We exhibit a theoretical framework in which a shallow tree network is shown to enhance the performance of classical decision trees. In such a setting, we provide tight theoretical lower and upper bounds on its excess risk. These theoretical results show the interest of tree-network architectures for well-structured data provided that the first layer, acting as a data encoder, is rich enough.

paragraphs: Deep forests combine tree-based prediction with a layered architecture. This paper investigates what those layers contribute, rather than primarily comparing benchmark scores. Its central question is whether the useful mechanisms of a deep forest can be retained in a simpler structure that requires less computation.

The authors argue that deep forest architectures can generally be simplified into shallow forest networks. These simpler networks can outperform standard tree-based prediction methods, although the abstract also reports some instability. This makes the simplification interesting both computationally and conceptually: it provides a more manageable setting for studying how layers of trees interact.

The theoretical contribution identifies a setting where a shallow tree network improves on classical decision trees and establishes tight lower and upper bounds on excess risk. The benefit depends on well-structured data and a sufficiently rich first layer, which acts as an encoder. Thus, the results support layered tree representations under these conditions, rather than establishing that adding layers always improves prediction.
summary.tldr: Shallow forest networks can capture useful mechanisms of deep forests, with theoretical benefits when the data and first-layer representation have suitable structure.

title: Analyzing the tree-layer structure of Deep Forests

abstract: There recently has been a surge of interest in developing a new class of deep learning (DL) architectures that integrate an explicit time dimension as a fundamental building block of learning and representation mechanisms. In turn, many recent results show that topological descriptors of the observed data, encoding information on the shape of the dataset in a topological space at different scales, that is, persistent homology of the data, may contain important complementary information, improving both performance and robustness of DL. As convergence of these two emerging ideas, we propose to enhance DL architectures with the most salient time-conditioned topological information of the data and introduce the concept of zigzag persistence into time-aware graph convolutional networks (GCNs). Zigzag persistence provides a systematic and mathematically rigorous framework to track the most important topological features of the observed data that tend to manifest themselves over time. To integrate the extracted time-conditioned topological descriptors into DL, we develop a new topological summary, zigzag persistence image, and derive its theoretical stability guarantees. We validate the new GCNs with a time-aware zigzag topological layer (Z-GCNETs), in application to traffic forecasting and Ethereum blockchain price prediction. Our results indicate that Z-GCNET outperforms 13 state-of-the-art methods on 4 time series datasets.

paragraphs: Time-series models can benefit from information about how the shape of observed data changes over time. This paper combines that idea with graph convolutional networks. It uses topological descriptors to capture structural information that may complement the representations learned by a time-aware neural network.

The method introduces zigzag persistence into the network’s temporal processing. Zigzag persistence provides a mathematical framework for tracking important topological features as observations evolve. To make the resulting information usable by the model, the authors develop a summary called a zigzag persistence image. They also derive theoretical stability guarantees for this summary, giving a mathematical basis for its use as a representation.

The resulting Z-GCNET architecture includes a time-aware topological layer. Evaluation covers traffic forecasting and Ethereum blockchain price prediction across four time-series datasets. The reported results outperform 13 state-of-the-art comparison methods. These findings support the usefulness of time-conditioned topological information in the evaluated forecasting settings, while the stability analysis separately addresses a theoretical property of the proposed summary.
summary.tldr: Z-GCNET adds stable summaries of evolving topological structure to graph neural networks and improves forecasting across four evaluated datasets.

title: Z-GCNETs: Time Zigzags at Graph Convolutional Networks for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Deep neural networks give state-of-the-art accuracy for reconstructing images from few and noisy measurements, a problem arising for example in accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, recent works have raised concerns that deep-learning-based image reconstruction methods are sensitive to perturbations and are less robust than traditional methods: Neural networks (i) may be sensitive to small, yet adversarially-selected perturbations, (ii) may perform poorly under distribution shifts, and (iii) may fail to recover small but important features in an image. In order to understand the sensitivity to such perturbations, in this work, we measure the robustness of different approaches for image reconstruction including trained and un-trained neural networks as well as traditional sparsity-based methods. We find, contrary to prior works, that both trained and un-trained methods are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Moreover, both trained and un-trained methods tuned for a particular dataset suffer very similarly from distribution shifts. Finally, we demonstrate that an image reconstruction method that achieves higher reconstruction quality, also performs better in terms of accurately recovering fine details. Our results indicate that the state-of-the-art deep-learning-based image reconstruction methods provide improved performance than traditional methods without compromising robustness.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an image from a small number of noisy measurements is important in applications such as accelerated MRI. Deep networks offer strong reconstruction accuracy, but concerns about their reliability include sensitivity to adversarial perturbations, distribution shifts, and loss of small image features. This paper investigates these concerns through comparisons across reconstruction approaches.

The evaluation includes trained neural networks, untrained neural networks, and traditional sparsity-based methods. The authors find adversarial vulnerability in both trained and untrained approaches. They also find that trained and untrained methods tuned to a particular dataset suffer similarly under distribution shifts. These observations challenge the view that the examined robustness problems distinguish learned reconstruction methods from their alternatives.

The study additionally demonstrates that a method with higher reconstruction quality performs better at recovering fine details. Taken together, the reported results indicate that state-of-the-art deep reconstruction methods can improve performance over traditional approaches without sacrificing robustness in the comparisons studied. The finding is comparative: adversarial vulnerabilities remain present, even though they do not establish a relative robustness disadvantage for the deep methods.
summary.tldr: Comparative tests indicate that deep image reconstruction improves quality without a robustness penalty, while trained and untrained approaches remain vulnerable.

title: Measuring Robustness in Deep Learning Based Compressive Sensing

abstract: Decision analysis deals with modeling and enhancing decision processes. A principal challenge in improving behavior is in obtaining a transparent *description* of existing behavior in the first place. In this paper, we develop an expressive, unifying perspective on *inverse decision modeling*: a framework for learning parameterized representations of sequential decision behavior. First, we formalize the *forward* problem (as a normative standard), subsuming common classes of control behavior. Second, we use this to formalize the *inverse* problem (as a descriptive model), generalizing existing work on imitation/reward learning—while opening up a much broader class of research problems in behavior representation. Finally, we instantiate this approach with an example (*inverse bounded rational control*), illustrating how this structure enables learning (interpretable) representations of (bounded) rationality—while naturally capturing intuitive notions of suboptimal actions, biased beliefs, and imperfect knowledge of environments.

paragraphs: Improving a decision process first requires a useful description of how decisions are currently made. This paper develops inverse decision modeling as a framework for learning interpretable, parameterized representations of sequential behavior. Its focus extends beyond reproducing actions or finding a reward that could explain them.

The framework begins by formalizing the forward problem: a normative description of how a decision process operates. This formulation includes common classes of control behavior. The authors then use it to define the inverse problem, which learns a descriptive model from behavior. That structure generalizes existing imitation and reward-learning approaches while creating room for a broader range of behavioral explanations.

An example called inverse bounded rational control illustrates the approach. It learns representations of bounded rationality that can express suboptimal actions, biased beliefs, and incomplete environmental knowledge. These are distinct ingredients that may shape observed choices. The example shows how a structured decision model can make such ingredients interpretable within a common framework for describing sequential behavior.
summary.tldr: Inverse decision modeling provides a unified framework for interpretable behavioral representations, including bounded rationality, biased beliefs, and imperfect knowledge.

title: Inverse Decision Modeling: Learning Interpretable Representations of Behavior

abstract: We present a method for efficient differentiable simulation of articulated bodies. This enables integration of articulated body dynamics into deep learning frameworks, and gradient-based optimization of neural networks that operate on articulated bodies. We derive the gradients of the contact solver using spatial algebra and the adjoint method. Our approach is an order of magnitude faster than autodiff tools. By only saving the initial states throughout the simulation process, our method reduces memory requirements by two orders of magnitude. We demonstrate the utility of efficient differentiable dynamics for articulated bodies in a variety of applications. We show that reinforcement learning with articulated systems can be accelerated using gradients provided by our method. In applications to control and inverse problems, gradient-based optimization enabled by our work accelerates convergence by more than an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Articulated bodies consist of connected parts whose movements interact through joints and contacts. Differentiable simulation makes it possible to compute how changes in inputs affect their simulated behavior. This paper develops an efficient method for obtaining those gradients, allowing articulated-body dynamics to participate in neural-network training and gradient-based optimization.

The authors derive gradients for the contact solver using spatial algebra and the adjoint method. They also reduce the information retained during simulation by saving only initial states. The reported approach is an order of magnitude faster than automatic-differentiation tools and reduces memory requirements by two orders of magnitude.

The paper demonstrates the method in reinforcement learning, control, and inverse problems. Simulation gradients can accelerate reinforcement learning with articulated systems, while gradient-based optimization speeds convergence by more than an order of magnitude in the reported control and inverse applications. These results connect improvements in differentiation cost to improvements in the larger optimization process: making dynamics gradients cheaper can make them more useful for learning and solving physical-system tasks.
summary.tldr: A specialized differentiation method makes articulated-body simulation faster and more memory-efficient, accelerating the reported learning and optimization applications.

title: Efficient Differentiable Simulation of Articulated Bodies

abstract: Intensive care units (ICU) are increasingly looking towards machine learning for methods to provide online monitoring of critically ill patients. In machine learning, online monitoring is often formulated as a supervised learning problem. Recently, contrastive learning approaches have demonstrated promising improvements over competitive supervised benchmarks. These methods rely on well-understood data augmentation techniques developed for image data which do not apply to online monitoring. In this work, we overcome this limitation by supplementing time-series data augmentation techniques with a novel contrastive learning objective which we call neighborhood contrastive learning (NCL). Our objective explicitly groups together contiguous time segments from each patient while maintaining state-specific information. Our experiments demonstrate a marked improvement over existing work applying contrastive methods to medical time-series.

paragraphs: Online patient monitoring uses evolving measurements to support the monitoring of critically ill patients. Contrastive learning has shown promise for this setting, but many successful contrastive methods rely on image augmentation techniques that do not apply to medical time series. This paper develops a training objective suited to the temporal structure of patient data.

Neighborhood contrastive learning supplements time-series augmentations by explicitly grouping contiguous time segments from the same patient. At the same time, it maintains information specific to the patient’s state. Both aspects matter to the proposed objective: neighboring observations should inform the learned representation, while distinctions in state should remain available for monitoring.

The experiments show a marked improvement over earlier applications of contrastive learning to medical time series. The finding supports tailoring the contrastive objective to the relationships present in the data, alongside choosing suitable augmentations. The paper’s contribution is a representation-learning approach that uses temporal proximity without discarding the state-specific information the monitoring task needs.
summary.tldr: Neighborhood contrastive learning groups adjacent patient time segments while retaining state information, improving reported medical time-series representations.

title: Neighborhood Contrastive Learning Applied to Online Patient Monitoring

abstract: The remarkable performance achieved by Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in many applications is followed by the rising concern about data privacy and security. Since DNNs usually require large datasets to train, many practitioners scrape data from external sources such as the Internet. However, an external data owner may not be willing to let this happen, causing legal or ethical issues. In this paper, we study the generalization attacks against DNNs, where an attacker aims to slightly modify training data in order to spoil the training process such that a trained network lacks generalizability. These attacks can be performed by data owners and protect data from unexpected use. However, there is currently no efficient generalization attack against DNNs due to the complexity of a bilevel optimization involved. We propose the Neural Tangent Generalization Attack (NTGA) that, to the best of our knowledge, is the first work enabling clean-label, black-box generalization attack against DNNs. We conduct extensive experiments, and the empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of NTGA. Our code and perturbed datasets are available at: https://github.com/lionelmessi6410/ntga.

paragraphs: This paper studies modifications to training data intended to make a neural network generalize poorly after learning from that data. The motivation is that people collecting large datasets may scrape material whose owners do not want it used for training. A generalization attack gives such owners a possible way to interfere with that use.

The attacker aims to change the training examples only slightly while disrupting the eventual training outcome. Designing those changes is difficult because it involves a bilevel optimization problem: the attack must account for how a network will learn from the modified data. The authors introduce Neural Tangent Generalization Attack, or NTGA, to address this computational obstacle.

The authors describe NTGA, to their knowledge, as the first approach enabling clean-label, black-box generalization attacks against deep networks. This means the attack preserves labels and operates in a black-box setting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in the studied cases, supporting the possibility of impairing later generalization through small changes to the supplied training data.
summary.tldr: NTGA slightly modifies training data while preserving labels to impair the generalization of neural networks trained on it.

title: Neural Tangent Generalization Attacks

abstract: Retrieval-based language models (R-LM) model the probability of natural language text by combining a standard language model (LM) with examples retrieved from an external datastore at test time. While effective, a major bottleneck of using these models in practice is the computationally costly datastore search, which can be performed as frequently as every time step. In this paper, we present RetoMaton - retrieval automaton - which approximates the datastore search, based on (1) saving pointers between consecutive datastore entries, and (2) clustering of entries into "states". This effectively results in a weighted finite automaton built on top of the datastore, instead of representing the datastore as a flat list. The creation of the automaton is unsupervised, and a RetoMaton can be constructed from any text collection: either the original training corpus or from another domain. Traversing this automaton at inference time, in parallel to the LM inference, reduces its perplexity by up to 1.85, or alternatively saves up to 83% of the nearest neighbor searches over $k$NN-LM (Khandelwal et al., 2020) without hurting perplexity. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/neulab/retomaton .
