paragraphs: Retrieval-based language models combine a standard language model with examples fetched from an external datastore during prediction. Searching that datastore can be expensive, especially when retrieval happens at every step. RetoMaton addresses this bottleneck by giving the datastore structure that can be traversed, reducing dependence on repeated nearest-neighbor searches.

The method stores pointers between consecutive datastore entries and groups entries into states. Together, these turn the datastore into a weighted finite automaton, which is traversed alongside the language model during inference. Construction is unsupervised and can use any text collection, including the original training corpus or material from another domain. The automaton approximates the datastore search by exploiting this organization.

The reported results offer two benefits: perplexity can decrease by up to 1.85, or nearest-neighbor searches can be reduced by up to 83% relative to kNN-LM without worsening perplexity. These are alternative reported outcomes, rather than a claim that both maxima occur together. The work shows how a symbolic structure over retrieved examples can improve the quality or computational efficiency of retrieval-assisted language modeling.
summary.tldr: RetoMaton organizes a language-model datastore into an automaton, improving perplexity or reducing nearest-neighbor searches by up to 83%.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Language Modeling with Automaton-augmented Retrieval

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation is critical to many real-world applications where label information is unavailable in the target domain. In general, without further assumptions, the joint distribution of the features and the label is not identifiable in the target domain. To address this issue, we rely on a property of minimal changes of causal mechanisms across domains to minimize unnecessary influences of domain shift. To encode this property, we first formulate the data generating process using a latent variable model with two partitioned latent subspaces: invariant components whose distributions stay the same across domains, and sparse changing components that vary across domains. We further constrain the domain shift to have a restrictive influence on the changing components. Under mild conditions, we show that the latent variables are partially identifiable, from which it follows that the joint distribution of data and labels in the target domain is also identifiable. Given the theoretical insights, we propose a practical domain adaptation framework, called iMSDA. Extensive experimental results reveal that iMSDA outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation algorithms on benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our framework.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers learning to a target domain without target labels. The paper begins with a fundamental obstacle: without additional assumptions, the target relationship between features and labels cannot generally be identified. It addresses this ambiguity by assuming that causal mechanisms change minimally across domains.

The authors encode that idea in a latent-variable model with two parts. One contains components whose distributions remain unchanged across domains; the other contains a sparse set of changing components. They further restrict how domain shift influences the changing part. Under conditions described as mild, they prove partial identifiability of the latent variables, which in turn establishes identifiability of the target data-label distribution.

The practical framework, iMSDA, follows these theoretical insights. Experiments show that it outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods on benchmark datasets. The approach matters because it explicitly models limited change alongside invariant structure. Its identification result depends on the stated structural assumptions, while the experiments provide evidence for the resulting method in the evaluated adaptation settings.
summary.tldr: iMSDA models invariant and sparsely changing latent factors to support target-domain identification under assumptions and improve adaptation benchmarks.

title: Partial disentanglement for domain adaptation

abstract: A large number of neural network models of associative memory have been proposed in the literature. These include the classical Hopfield networks (HNs), sparse distributed memories (SDMs), and more recently the modern continuous Hopfield networks (MCHNs), which possess close links with self-attention in machine learning. In this paper, we propose a general framework for understanding the operation of such memory networks as a sequence of three operations: similarity, separation, and projection. We derive all these memory models as instances of our general framework with differing similarity and separation functions. We extend the mathematical framework of Krotov et al (2020) to express general associative memory models using neural network dynamics with local computation, and derive a general energy function that is a Lyapunov function of the dynamics. Finally, using our framework, we empirically investigate the capacity of using different similarity functions for these associative memory models, beyond the dot product similarity measure, and demonstrate empirically that Euclidean or Manhattan distance similarity metrics perform substantially better in practice on many tasks, enabling a more robust retrieval and higher memory capacity than existing models.

paragraphs: Associative memory models retrieve stored information from a related query. Many such models exist, including classical Hopfield networks, sparse distributed memories, and modern continuous Hopfield networks. This paper organizes them through a shared sequence of three operations: measuring similarity, separating candidate matches, and projecting to a retrieved memory.

Different choices of similarity and separation functions recover the different model families. The authors also extend a mathematical framework that expresses associative memory through neural dynamics with local computation. They derive a general energy function that serves as a Lyapunov function for those dynamics, giving the unified formulation a dynamical foundation as well as an operational one.

The framework then enables an empirical comparison of similarity measures beyond the commonly used dot product. Across many tasks, Euclidean- or Manhattan-distance-based similarities substantially improve retrieval robustness and memory capacity relative to existing models. These findings indicate that the similarity operation can materially affect practical memory performance. The contribution therefore both connects established architectures and identifies useful alternatives within their shared design space.
summary.tldr: A unified associative-memory framework connects Hopfield-style models and shows empirical benefits from Euclidean and Manhattan similarity measures.

title: Universal Hopfield Networks: A General Framework for Single-Shot Associative Memory Models

abstract: Training of graph neural networks (GNNs) for large-scale node classification is challenging. A key difficulty lies in obtaining accurate hidden node representations while avoiding the neighborhood explosion problem. Here, we propose a new technique, named feature momentum (FM), that uses a momentum step to incorporate historical embeddings when updating feature representations. We develop two specific algorithms, known as GraphFM-IB and GraphFM-OB, that consider in-batch and out-of-batch data, respectively. GraphFM-IB applies FM to in-batch sampled data, while GraphFM-OB applies FM to out-of-batch data that are 1-hop neighborhood of in-batch data. We provide a convergence analysis for GraphFM-IB and some theoretical insight for GraphFM-OB. Empirically, we observe that GraphFM-IB can effectively alleviate the neighborhood explosion problem of existing methods. In addition, GraphFM-OB achieves promising performance on multiple large-scale graph datasets.

GraphFM-IB applies FM to in-batch sampled data, while GraphFM-OB applies FM to out-of-batch data that are 1-hop neighborhood of in-batch data. paragraphs: Large-scale graph neural network training must obtain useful node representations without expanding computation over an unmanageably large neighborhood. This tension is especially relevant to node classification, where information from surrounding nodes helps determine a node’s prediction. The paper introduces feature momentum as a way to use previously computed embeddings when updating current representations.

The authors develop two variants that apply this idea to different data. GraphFM-IB incorporates historical embeddings for sampled nodes inside the current batch. GraphFM-OB applies feature momentum to nodes outside the batch that are one-hop neighbors of nodes inside it. Both use representation history, but they differ in which part of the graph receives the update.

The paper provides a convergence analysis for GraphFM-IB and theoretical insight for GraphFM-OB. Empirically, GraphFM-IB alleviates the neighborhood explosion problem encountered by existing methods, while GraphFM-OB shows promising performance on several large graph datasets. These findings support reusing historical representations as a practical training technique, while keeping the distinct theoretical and empirical support for the two variants clear.
summary.tldr: GraphFM incorporates historical node embeddings through momentum updates to improve large-scale graph neural network training.

title: GraphFM: Improving Large-Scale GNN Training via Feature Momentum

abstract: We show that running gradient descent with variable learning rate guarantees loss $f(x) ≤ 1.1 \cdot f(x^*)+\epsilon$ for the logistic regression objective, where the error $\epsilon$ decays exponentially with the number of iterations and polynomially with the magnitude of the entries of an arbitrary fixed solution $x$. This is in contrast to the common intuition that the absence of strong convexity precludes linear convergence of first-order methods, and highlights the importance of variable learning rates for gradient descent. We also apply our ideas to sparse logistic regression, where they lead to an exponential improvement of the sparsity-error tradeoff.

This is in contrast to the common intuition that the absence of strong convexity precludes linear convergence of first-order methods, and highlights the importance of variable learning rates for gradient descent. We also apply our ideas to sparse logistic regression, where they lead to an exponential improvement of the sparsity-error tradeoff.

paragraphs: This paper examines how quickly gradient descent can reduce the logistic regression objective in the separable-data setting. Its central ingredient is a learning rate that varies across iterations. The result challenges the intuition that first-order optimization cannot have linear convergence when strong convexity is absent, highlighting the role of the learning-rate schedule in such guarantees.

The stated guarantee bounds the achieved loss by 1.1 times the comparison loss plus an additive error. That additive error decreases exponentially with the number of iterations, with an additional polynomial dependence described in terms of the magnitude of entries of a fixed comparison solution. Thus, the precise claim concerns rapid reduction of an additive error within a multiplicative-comparison guarantee.

This distinction matters when interpreting the title: the result specifies the loss target and the way accuracy improves, rather than simply asserting unrestricted convergence to an exact optimum. The authors also apply their ideas to sparse logistic regression, obtaining an exponential improvement in the sparsity-error tradeoff. Together, the results show how variable learning rates can strengthen both optimization guarantees and sparse approximation.
summary.tldr: Variable learning rates give gradient descent an exponentially decaying additive loss error for logistic regression and improve the sparsity-error tradeoff.

title: Gradient Descent Converges Linearly for Logistic Regression on Separable Data

abstract: Graph Transformer (GT) recently has emerged as a new paradigm of graph learning algorithms, outperforming the previously popular Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) on multiple benchmarks. Previous work shows that with proper position embedding, GT can approximate MPNN arbitrarily well, implying that GT is at least as powerful as MPNN. In this paper, we study the inverse connection and show that MPNN with virtual node (VN), a commonly used heuristic with little theoretical understanding, is powerful enough to arbitrarily approximate the self-attention layer of GT. In particular, we first show that if we consider one type of linear transformer, the so-called Performer/Linear Transformer, then MPNN + VN with only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ depth and $\mathcal{O}(1)$ width can approximate a self-attention layer in Performer/Linear Transformer. Next, via a connection between MPNN + VN and DeepSets, we prove the MPNN + VN with $\mathcal{O}(n^d)$ width and $\mathcal{O}(1)$ depth can approximate the self-attention layer arbitrarily well, where $d$ is the input feature dimension. Lastly, under some assumptions, we provide an explicit construction of MPNN + VN with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ width and $\mathcal{O}(n)$ depth approximating the self-attention layer in GT arbitrarily well. On the empirical side, we demonstrate that 1) MPNN + VN is a surprisingly strong baseline, outperforming GT on the recently proposed Long Range Graph Benchmark (LRGB) dataset, 2) our MPNN + VN improves over early implementation on a wide range of OGB datasets and 3) MPNN + VN outperforms Linear Transformer and MPNN on the climate modeling task.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers and message-passing neural networks are often treated as distinct approaches to graph learning. Earlier theory showed that suitably equipped Transformers can approximate message-passing networks. This paper studies the reverse direction, showing that adding a virtual node gives a message-passing network enough expressive power to approximate Transformer self-attention.

The required network size depends on the attention mechanism and construction. A Performer or Linear Transformer attention layer can be approximated with constant depth and width. For general self-attention, one construction uses constant depth and width growing as O(n^d), where d is the feature dimension. Another, under additional assumptions, uses constant width and depth growing as O(n).

Experiments also establish the virtual-node model as a strong practical baseline. It outperforms Graph Transformers on the reported Long Range Graph Benchmark evaluation, improves on an earlier implementation across OGB datasets, and beats Linear Transformer and ordinary message passing on a climate task. The findings connect representational capability with empirical competitiveness while preserving the differing resource requirements of the theoretical constructions.
summary.tldr: Message-passing networks with a virtual node can approximate Transformer attention and perform strongly in the reported graph-learning experiments.

title: On the Connection Between MPNN and Graph Transformer

abstract: In zero-shot learning (ZSL), generative methods synthesize class-related sample features based on predefined semantic prototypes. They advance the ZSL performance by synthesizing unseen class sample features for better training the classifier. We observe that each class’s predefined semantic prototype (also referred to as semantic embedding or condition) does not accurately match its real semantic prototype. So the synthesized visual sample features do not faithfully represent the real sample features, limiting the classifier training and existing ZSL performance. In this paper, we formulate this mismatch phenomenon as the visual-semantic domain shift problem. We propose a dynamic semantic prototype evolving (DSP) method to align the empirically predefined semantic prototypes and the real prototypes for class-related feature synthesis. The alignment is learned by refining sample features and semantic prototypes in a unified framework and making the synthesized visual sample features approach real sample features. After alignment, synthesized sample features from unseen classes are closer to the real sample features and benefit DSP to improve existing generative ZSL methods by 8.5%, 8.0%, and 9.7% on the standard CUB, SUN AWA2 datasets, the significant performance improvement indicates that evolving semantic prototype explores a virgin field in ZSL.

paragraphs: Generative zero-shot learning creates feature examples for unseen classes using semantic descriptions of those classes. These synthetic features then help train a classifier. The paper identifies a mismatch between the predefined semantic prototype for a class and its real prototype, which can cause generated features to misrepresent real examples.

The authors describe this mismatch as visual-semantic domain shift and propose dynamic semantic prototype evolving, or DSP. Rather than treating the semantic prototypes as fixed, DSP refines them together with sample features in a unified framework. The alignment process encourages synthesized visual features to approach real sample features, improving the information available for classifier training.

The reported findings indicate that this alignment brings generated unseen-class features closer to their real counterparts. DSP improves existing generative zero-shot methods by 8.5%, 8.0%, and 9.7% on CUB, SUN, and AWA2, respectively. These results support revising the semantic conditions used for generation as a productive way to improve zero-shot classification.
summary.tldr: DSP jointly refines semantic prototypes and features to reduce visual-semantic mismatch and improve generative zero-shot learning.

title: Evolving Semantic Prototype Improves Generative Zero-Shot Learning

abstract: Data augmentation is a crucial component in unsupervised contrastive learning (CL). It determines how positive samples are defined and, ultimately, the quality of the learned representation. In this work, we open the door to new perspectives for CL by integrating prior knowledge, given either by generative models - viewed as prior representations - or weak attributes in the positive and negative sampling. To this end, we use kernel theory to propose a novel loss, called decoupled uniformity, that i) allows the integration of prior knowledge and ii) removes the positive-negative coupling in the original InfoNCE loss. We draw a connection between contrastive learning and the conditional mean embedding theory to derive tight bounds on the downstream classification loss. In an unsupervised setting, we empirically demonstrate that CL benefits from generative models to improve its representation both on natural and medical images. In a weakly supervised scenario, our framework outperforms other unconditional and conditional CL approaches.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning depends on which examples are treated as positive and negative pairs. Data augmentation usually plays a central role in making that choice. This paper broadens the available guidance by incorporating prior knowledge from generative-model representations or weak attributes into the sampling of both kinds of examples.

The authors use kernel theory to construct a loss called decoupled uniformity. It supports the use of prior information and removes the coupling between positive and negative terms present in the original InfoNCE loss. They also connect contrastive learning to conditional mean embeddings, using that connection to derive tight bounds on downstream classification loss.

In unsupervised experiments, knowledge supplied by generative models improves learned representations for both natural and medical images. In the weakly supervised setting, the framework outperforms the unconditional and conditional contrastive approaches considered. These findings support treating prior knowledge as part of the learning objective and sampling process, giving contrastive learning a source of structure beyond the choices encoded by augmentation alone.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based contrastive loss incorporates prior knowledge into sampling and improves representations in unsupervised and weakly supervised experiments.

title: Integrating Prior Knowledge in Contrastive Learning with Kernel

abstract: We propose a novel parameterized skill-learning algorithm that aims to learn transferable parameterized skills and synthesize them into a new action space that supports efficient learning in long-horizon tasks. We propose to leverage off-policy Meta-RL combined with a trajectory-centric smoothness term to learn a set of parameterized skills. Our agent can use these learned skills to construct a three-level hierarchical framework that models a Temporally-extended Parameterized Action Markov Decision Process. We empirically demonstrate that the proposed algorithms enable an agent to solve a set of highly difficult long-horizon (obstacle-course and robot manipulation) tasks.

paragraphs: Long-horizon tasks require an agent to coordinate behavior across many steps. This paper proposes learning transferable, parameterized skills and using them to create a new action space. A parameterized skill provides an adjustable unit of behavior, allowing the agent to work with skills that extend over time when learning a larger task.

The learning algorithm combines off-policy meta-reinforcement learning with a smoothness term defined around trajectories. These components are used to learn the skill set that supports the later hierarchy. The agent then constructs a three-level framework representing a Temporally-extended Parameterized Action Markov Decision Process, bringing both skill parameters and temporal extension into the decision structure.

Experiments show that the proposed algorithms enable agents to solve difficult long-horizon obstacle-course and robot-manipulation tasks. The result supports the practical feasibility of building a useful higher-level action space from learned parameterized skills. The contribution lies in connecting the skill-learning procedure to a hierarchical framework that can use those skills for extended tasks, with the reported evidence coming from those evaluations.
summary.tldr: Off-policy meta-learning produces parameterized skills that support a three-level hierarchy for difficult long-horizon control tasks.

title: Meta-learning Parameterized Skills

abstract: Sequential decision making algorithms often struggle to leverage different sources of unstructured offline interaction data. Imitation learning (IL) methods based on supervised learning are robust, but require optimal demonstrations, which are hard to collect. Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms promise to learn from sub-optimal data, but face optimization challenges especially with high-dimensional data. To bridge the gap between IL and RL, we introduce Distance Weighted Supervised Learning or DWSL, a supervised method for learning goal-conditioned policies from offline data. DWSL models the entire distribution of time-steps between states in offline data with only supervised learning, and uses this distribution to approximate shortest path distances. To extract a policy, we weight actions by their reduction in distance estimates. Theoretically, DWSL converges to an optimal policy constrained to the data distribution, an attractive property for offline learning, without any bootstrapping. Across all datasets we test, DWSL empirically maintains behavior cloning as a lower bound while still exhibiting policy improvement. In high-dimensional image domains, DWSL surpasses the performance of both prior goal-conditioned IL and RL algorithms. Visualizations and code can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/dwsl/home.

paragraphs: Learning actions from recorded interactions presents a tradeoff. Supervised imitation methods are robust but rely on optimal demonstrations, while offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning can use imperfect behavior but faces optimization difficulties. Distance Weighted Supervised Learning, or DWSL, seeks to combine supervised training with the ability to improve on the behavior present in offline data.

DWSL learns the full distribution of how many time steps separate states in the recorded data. It uses that distribution to approximate shortest-path distances, then weights actions according to how much they reduce the estimated distance to a goal. Both learning the distance information and extracting a policy use supervised learning, without bootstrapping.

The theoretical result establishes convergence to an optimal policy constrained to the data distribution. That qualification matters: optimality is tied to the available offline data. Empirically, DWSL at least matches behavior cloning across every tested dataset while also showing policy improvement. In image-based domains, it exceeds the performance of the prior goal-conditioned imitation and reinforcement learning methods considered.
summary.tldr: DWSL learns goal-reaching policies from offline data by supervising distance distributions and favoring actions that reduce estimated distance.

title: Distance Weighted Supervised Learning for Offline Interaction Data

abstract: Recently, contrastive learning has found impressive success in advancing the state of the art in solving various machine learning tasks. However, the existing generalization analysis is very limited or even not meaningful. In particular, the existing generalization error bounds depend linearly on the number $k$ of negative examples while it was widely shown in practice that choosing a large $k$ is necessary to guarantee good generalization of contrastive learning in downstream tasks. In this paper, we establish novel generalization bounds for contrastive learning which do not depend on $k$, up to logarithmic terms. Our analysis uses structural results on empirical covering numbers and Rademacher complexities to exploit the Lipschitz continuity of loss functions. For self-bounding Lipschitz loss functions, we further improve our results by developing optimistic bounds which imply fast rates in a low noise condition. We apply our results to learning with both linear representation and nonlinear representation by deep neural networks, for both of which we derive Rademacher complexity bounds to get improved generalization bounds.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning uses negative examples when learning representations, and practical success often involves using many of them. Existing generalization bounds create a tension with that practice: they grow linearly with the number of negatives, making the theoretical guarantee worse as that number increases. This paper develops bounds that largely remove that dependence.

The new guarantees depend on the number of negative examples only through logarithmic terms. The analysis combines empirical covering numbers and Rademacher complexities, mathematical tools for controlling the richness of a learning system, with the Lipschitz continuity of its loss. These ingredients allow a sharper account of how the training objective relates to generalization.

For self-bounding Lipschitz losses, the authors derive stronger, optimistic bounds that yield fast rates under a low-noise condition. They also specialize the analysis to linear representations and deep neural network representations. The contribution is a more informative theoretical explanation of contrastive learning, including conditional improvements that distinguish favorable learning settings from the general case.
summary.tldr: New contrastive-learning generalization bounds remove linear dependence on the number of negatives and give faster rates under additional favorable conditions.

title: Generalization Analysis for Contrastive Representation Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has made significant strides in various complex domains. However, identifying an effective policy via RL often necessitates extensive exploration. Imitation learning aims to mitigate this issue by using expert demonstrations to guide exploration. In real-world scenarios, one often has access to multiple suboptimal black-box experts, rather than a single optimal oracle. These experts do not universally outperform each other across all states, presenting a challenge in actively deciding which oracle to use and in which state. We introduce MAPS and MAPS-SE, a class of policy improvement algorithms that perform imitation learning from multiple suboptimal oracles. In particular, MAPS actively selects which of the oracles to imitate and improve their value function estimates, and MAPS-SE additionally leverages an active state exploration criterion to determine which states one should explore. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis and demonstrate that MAPS and MAPS-SE enjoy sample efficiency advantage over the state-of-the-art policy improvement algorithms. Empirical results show that MAPS-SE significantly accelerates policy optimization via state-wise imitation learning from multiple oracles across a broad spectrum of control tasks in the DeepMind Control Suite.

paragraphs: Learning an effective policy through reinforcement learning can require extensive exploration. Expert demonstrations can help, but the available experts may all be imperfect. When different experts perform best in different states, choosing a single teacher leaves useful guidance unused. This paper studies how a learner can actively decide whose advice to follow and where to seek it.

The authors introduce MAPS and MAPS-SE, algorithms for policy improvement using multiple black-box oracles. MAPS actively chooses which oracle to imitate and improves estimates of the oracles’ value functions. MAPS-SE adds a second decision: it uses an active exploration criterion to select states worth exploring. Together, these choices address both the source and the location of useful guidance.

The paper provides theoretical analysis supporting a sample efficiency advantage over existing policy improvement algorithms. Experiments across control tasks in the DeepMind Control Suite show that MAPS-SE accelerates policy optimization. The stated benefit comes from making imitation sensitive to the current state and the relative strengths of available experts.
summary.tldr: MAPS and MAPS-SE improve learning from imperfect experts by actively choosing which expert to imitate and, for MAPS-SE, which states to explore.

title: Active Policy Improvement from Multiple Black-box Oracles

abstract: Network binarization emerges as one of the most promising compression approaches offering extraordinary computation and memory savings by minimizing the bit-width. However, recent research has shown that applying existing binarization algorithms to diverse tasks, architectures, and hardware in realistic scenarios is still not straightforward. Common challenges of binarization, such as accuracy degradation and efficiency limitation, suggest that its attributes are not fully understood. To close this gap, we present BiBench, a rigorously designed benchmark with in-depth analysis for network binarization. We first carefully scrutinize the requirements of binarization in the actual production and define evaluation tracks and metrics for a comprehensive and fair investigation. Then, we evaluate and analyze a series of milestone binarization algorithms that function at the operator level and with extensive influence. Our benchmark reveals that 1) the binarized operator has a crucial impact on the performance and deployability of binarized networks; 2) the accuracy of binarization varies significantly across different learning tasks and neural architectures; 3) binarization has demonstrated promising efficiency potential on edge devices despite the limited hardware support. The results and analysis also lead to a promising paradigm for accurate and efficient binarization. We believe that BiBench will contribute to the broader adoption of binarization and serve as a foundation for future research. The code for our BiBench is released https://github.com/htqin/BiBench .

paragraphs: Network binarization reduces numerical bit-width to save computation and memory. Those savings make it attractive for deployment, but applying a binarization algorithm across different tasks, architectures, and hardware can produce uneven results. BiBench investigates this gap between the promise of compression and the practical combination of accuracy, efficiency, and deployability.

The authors first examine production requirements and use them to define evaluation tracks and metrics. They then benchmark influential algorithms that operate at the level of individual network operations. This organization connects the behavior of binarized operators to the performance of complete networks, rather than treating every compressed model as equivalent simply because it uses fewer bits.

The results show that operator design strongly affects performance and deployment, while accuracy varies substantially with the task and architecture. They also identify promising efficiency potential on edge devices despite limited hardware support. The analysis points toward a promising approach to accurate, efficient binarization and provides a structured basis for comparing future methods under practical conditions.
summary.tldr: BiBench shows how operator design, task, architecture, and hardware shape the practical accuracy and efficiency of binarized networks.

title: BiBench: Benchmarking and Analyzing Network Binarization

abstract: We study the learning dynamics of self-predictive learning for reinforcement learning, a family of algorithms that learn representations by minimizing the prediction error of their own future latent representations. Despite its recent empirical success, such algorithms have an apparent defect: trivial representations (such as constants) minimize the prediction error, yet it is obviously undesirable to converge to such solutions. Our central insight is that careful designs of the optimization dynamics are critical to learning meaningful representations. We identify that a faster paced optimization of the predictor and semi-gradient updates on the representation, are crucial to preventing the representation collapse. Then in an idealized setup, we show self-predictive learning dynamics carries out spectral decomposition on the state transition matrix, effectively capturing information of the transition dynamics. Building on the theoretical insights, we propose bidirectional self-predictive learning, a novel self-predictive algorithm that learns two representations simultaneously. We examine the robustness of our theoretical insights with a number of small-scale experiments and showcase the promise of the novel representation learning algorithm with large-scale experiments.

paragraphs: Self-predictive learning builds representations by predicting their own future values. This creates a troubling possibility: a constant representation can be perfectly predictable while carrying no useful information. The paper studies why successful learning can avoid that collapse, focusing on how the optimization process shapes representations rather than only on the prediction objective.

The authors identify two crucial design choices: optimizing the predictor at a faster pace and using semi-gradient updates for the representation. In an idealized setting, they show that the resulting dynamics perform a spectral decomposition of the state transition matrix. This explains how self-prediction can capture information about environmental transitions.

Those insights motivate bidirectional self-predictive learning, which learns two representations simultaneously. Small-scale experiments examine the robustness of the theoretical insights, and large-scale experiments demonstrate the new algorithm's promise. The spectral explanation is explicitly tied to the idealized setup, while the empirical work explores the usefulness of the underlying optimization choices and the proposed learning method.
summary.tldr: Carefully designed optimization helps self-predictive representations avoid collapse and motivates a bidirectional reinforcement learning representation method.

title: Understanding Self-Predictive Learning for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We present a fully Bayesian autoencoder model that treats both local latent variables and global decoder parameters in a Bayesian fashion. This approach allows for flexible priors and posterior approximations while keeping the inference costs low. To achieve this, we introduce an amortized MCMC approach by utilizing an implicit stochastic network to learn sampling from the posterior over local latent variables. Furthermore, we extend the model by incorporating a Sparse Gaussian Process prior over the latent space, allowing for a fully Bayesian treatment of inducing points and kernel hyperparameters and leading to improved scalability. Additionally, we enable Deep Gaussian Process priors on the latent space and the handling of missing data. We evaluate our model on a range of experiments focusing on dynamic representation learning and generative modeling, demonstrating the strong performance of our approach in comparison to existing methods that combine Gaussian Processes and autoencoders.

paragraphs: This paper develops an autoencoder that treats both the latent variables associated with individual examples and the decoder’s shared parameters probabilistically. The aim is to support flexible prior distributions and posterior approximations while keeping inference costs low. This extends Bayesian treatment across both local representations and global model parameters.

The inference method uses amortized Markov chain Monte Carlo: an implicit stochastic network learns to generate samples from the posterior over local latent variables. The authors then place a sparse Gaussian process prior over the latent space. They also treat its inducing points and kernel hyperparameters in a fully Bayesian way, and report that this extension improves scalability.

The framework additionally accommodates deep Gaussian process priors and missing data. Experiments examine dynamic representation learning and generative modeling, with strong reported performance against existing methods combining Gaussian processes and autoencoders. The contribution brings together flexible latent structure and learned posterior sampling, while extending probabilistic treatment to quantities that govern the Gaussian process itself.
summary.tldr: A fully Bayesian autoencoder combines learned posterior sampling with sparse Gaussian process latent priors for scalable representation learning and generation.

title: Fully Bayesian Autoencoders with Latent Sparse Gaussian Processes

abstract: DARTS search space (DSS) has become a canonical benchmark for NAS whereas some emerging works pointed out the issue of narrow accuracy range and claimed it would hurt the method ranking. We observe some recent studies already suffer from this issue that overshadows the meaning of scores. In this work, we first propose and orchestrate a suite of improvements to frame a larger and harder DSS, termed LHD, while retaining high efficiency in search. We step forward to renovate a LHD-based new benchmark, taking care of both discernibility and accessibility. Specifically, we re-implement twelve baselines and evaluate them across twelve conditions by combining two underexpolored influential factors: transductive robustness and discretization policy, to reasonably construct a benchmark upon multi-condition evaluation. Considering that the tabular benchmarks are always insufficient to adequately evaluate the methods of neural architecture search (NAS), our work can serve as a crucial basis for the future progress of NAS.

In this work, we first propose and orchestrate a suite of improvements to frame a larger and harder DSS, termed LHD, while retaining high efficiency in search. We step forward to renovate a LHD-based new benchmark, taking care of both discernibility and accessibility. Specifically, we re-implement twelve baselines and evaluate them across twelve conditions by combining two underexpolored influential factors: transductive robustness and discretization policy, to reasonably construct a benchmark upon multi-condition evaluation. Considering that the tabular benchmarks are always insufficient to adequately evaluate the methods of neural architecture search (NAS), our work can serve as a crucial basis for the future progress of NAS.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search methods are often compared using the DARTS search space. This paper examines a weakness of that benchmark: its architectures can occupy a narrow accuracy range, making method rankings less informative. The authors observe that this issue already affects some studies and reduces the meaning of their reported scores.

They introduce LHD, a larger and harder search space assembled through a suite of improvements while retaining efficient search. The benchmark built around it aims to make differences between methods easier to distinguish without making evaluation inaccessible. This connects benchmark design to the practical question of whether scores reveal meaningful differences in search quality.

The authors reimplement twelve baselines and evaluate them across twelve conditions combining transductive robustness and discretization policy, two influential factors they identify as underexplored. The resulting comparison examines methods under multiple conditions rather than relying on a single score. The contribution is an expanded evaluation foundation intended to support future architecture-search research and address shortcomings the authors identify in tabular benchmarks.
summary.tldr: LHD expands the DARTS search space and evaluates twelve baselines across twelve conditions to make architecture-search comparisons more informative.

title: Rethink DARTS Search Space and Renovate a New Benchmark

abstract: We refine and generalize what is known about coresets for classification problems via the sensitivity sampling framework. Such coresets seek the smallest possible subsets of input data, so one can optimize a loss function on the coreset and ensure approximation guarantees with respect to the original data. Our analysis provides the first no dimensional coresets, so the size does not depend on the dimension. Moreover, our results are general, apply for distributional input and can use iid samples, so provide sample complexity bounds, and work for a variety of loss functions. A key tool we develop is a Radamacher complexity version of the main sensitivity sampling approach, which can be of independent interest.

paragraphs: A classification coreset is a small subset of data that supports optimization while preserving an approximation guarantee for the original dataset’s loss. Its usefulness depends on how small that subset can be without losing the guarantee. This paper refines sensitivity sampling analysis to obtain coreset sizes that do not depend on the input dimension.

The central technical tool is a version of the sensitivity sampling framework based on Rademacher complexity. This changes the analysis used to establish the approximation guarantees and supports results across a variety of loss functions. The dimensional independence concerns the required coreset size, making the result relevant when each example has many features.

The framework also handles distributional inputs and can use independent, identically distributed samples. That extends the results beyond compressing a fixed dataset and yields sample-complexity bounds. The contribution is therefore both a classification result and an analytical tool: it establishes dimension-independent coresets while developing a sensitivity sampling approach that the authors identify as potentially useful on its own.
summary.tldr: A Rademacher-complexity analysis yields classification coresets whose size is independent of input dimension, with extensions to distributional sampling.

title: No Dimensional Sampling Coresets for Classification

abstract: Despite the remarkable capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) face deployment challenges due to their extensive size. Pruning methods drop a subset of weights to accelerate, but many of them require retraining, which is prohibitively expensive and computationally demanding. Recently, post-training pruning approaches introduced novel metrics, enabling the pruning of LLMs without retraining. However, these metrics require the involvement of human experts and tedious trial and error. To efficiently identify superior pruning metrics, we develop an automatic framework for searching symbolic pruning metrics using genetic programming. In particular, we devise an elaborate search space encompassing the existing pruning metrics to discover the potential symbolic pruning metric. We propose an opposing operation simplification strategy to increase the diversity of the population. In this way, Pruner-Zero allows auto-generation of symbolic pruning metrics. Based on the searched results, we explore the correlation between pruning metrics and performance after pruning and summarize some principles. Extensive experiments on LLaMA and LLaMA-2 on language modeling and zero-shot tasks demonstrate that our Pruner-Zero obtains superior performance than SOTA post-training pruning methods. Code at: https://github.com/pprp/Pruner-Zero.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a language model’s size by removing some of its weights. Post-training methods can do this without retraining, but their decisions depend on pruning metrics that often require expert design and repeated experimentation. Pruner-Zero automates the search for those metrics, targeting the rule used to decide which weights to remove.

The framework uses genetic programming to search over symbolic formulas. Its search space includes existing pruning metrics, allowing the procedure to explore alternatives within a broader family of expressions. An opposing-operation simplification strategy is introduced to increase population diversity during the search. The result is an automatically generated, explicit mathematical pruning metric.

Experiments on LLaMA and LLaMA-2 cover language modeling and zero-shot tasks. The authors report better performance than state-of-the-art post-training pruning methods in these evaluations. They also examine relationships between the discovered metrics and post-pruning performance, extracting principles from the search results. The approach thus serves both as a way to find effective pruning rules and as a tool for studying what makes such rules useful.
summary.tldr: Pruner-Zero automatically searches for symbolic pruning metrics and improves post-training pruning performance on the evaluated LLaMA models and tasks.

title: Pruner-Zero: Evolving Symbolic Pruning Metric From Scratch for Large Language Models

abstract: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning (MFRL), leveraging the policy gradient theorem, has demonstrated considerable success in continuous control tasks. However, these approaches are plagued by high gradient variance due to zeroth-order gradient estimation, resulting in suboptimal policies. Conversely, First-Order Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (FO-MBRL) methods employing differentiable simulation provide gradients with reduced variance but are susceptible to sampling error in scenarios involving stiff dynamics, such as physical contact. This paper investigates the source of this error and introduces Adaptive Horizon Actor-Critic (AHAC), an FO-MBRL algorithm that reduces gradient error by adapting the model-based horizon to avoid stiff dynamics. Empirical findings reveal that AHAC outperforms MFRL baselines, attaining 40% more reward across a set of locomotion tasks and efficiently scaling to high-dimensional control environments with improved wall-clock-time efficiency. adaptive-horizon-actor-critic.github.io

paragraphs: Differentiable simulators let reinforcement learning algorithms calculate how changes in actions affect simulated outcomes. These gradients can have lower variance than the estimates used by model-free approaches. Physical contact creates a difficulty, however: stiff dynamics can introduce sampling error into the gradients. The paper investigates this source of error in learning control policies.

The proposed Adaptive Horizon Actor-Critic, or AHAC, changes how far the algorithm follows the differentiable model when calculating its update. It adapts this model-based horizon to avoid stiff dynamics. The approach therefore makes the length of the gradient calculation responsive to the behavior of the simulation, reducing the gradient error associated with those difficult regions.

Across the reported locomotion tasks, AHAC achieves 40% more reward than the model-free reinforcement learning baselines. The authors also report improved efficiency in elapsed training time and effective scaling to high-dimensional control environments. These findings support adaptive horizons as a useful way to obtain the benefits of differentiable simulation in the contact-rich tasks studied.
summary.tldr: AHAC adapts the differentiable simulation horizon to reduce gradient errors around stiff dynamics and improve control learning.

title: Adaptive Horizon Actor-Critic for Policy Learning in Contact-Rich Differentiable Simulation

abstract: Generation of plausible but incorrect factual information, often termed hallucination, has attracted significant research interest. Retrieval-augmented language model (RALM)—which enhances models with up-to-date knowledge—emerges as a promising method to reduce hallucination. However, existing RALMs may instead exacerbate hallucination when retrieving lengthy contexts. To address this challenge, we propose COFT, a novel COarse-to-Fine highlighTing method to focus on different granularity-level key texts, thereby avoiding getting lost in lengthy contexts. Specifically, COFT consists of three components: recaller, scorer, and selector. First, recaller applies a knowledge graph to extract potential key entities in a given context. Second, scorer measures the importance of each entity by calculating its contextual weight. Finally, selector selects high contextual weight entities with a dynamic threshold algorithm and highlights the corresponding paragraphs, sentences, or words in a coarse-to-fine manner. Extensive experiments on knowledge hallucination benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of COFT, leading to a superior performance over 30% in F1 score metric. Moreover, COFT also exhibits remarkable versatility across various long-form tasks, such as reading comprehension and question answering.

paragraphs: Retrieving external knowledge can help language models answer factual questions, but long retrieved passages can also make hallucination worse. This paper addresses the problem of directing a model toward useful evidence within a lengthy context. Its method, COFT, highlights important text at several levels of detail.

COFT has three stages. A recaller uses a knowledge graph to identify potentially important entities in the context. A scorer assigns those entities contextual importance weights. A selector then applies a dynamic threshold and highlights the associated paragraphs, sentences, or individual words. The coarse-to-fine structure allows emphasis to range from broader passages down to specific pieces of text.

Experiments on a knowledge-hallucination benchmark report effectiveness, including an F1 improvement described as exceeding 30%. The authors also report applicability to long-form reading comprehension and question answering. The central finding is that retrieving knowledge and making relevant knowledge salient are distinct parts of the task: organizing emphasis within retrieved material can improve how a model uses that material.
summary.tldr: COFT reduces factual hallucination by identifying important entities and highlighting relevant evidence from paragraphs down to individual words.

title: Coarse-to-Fine Highlighting: Reducing Knowledge Hallucination in Large Language Models

abstract: We consider the hybrid reinforcement learning setting where the agent has access to both offline data and online interactive access. While RL research typically assumes offline data contains complete action, reward and transition information, datasets with only state information (also known as observation-only datasets) are more general, abundant and practical. This motivates our study of the hybrid RL with observation-only offline dataset framework. While the task of competing with the best policy “covered” by the offline data can be solved if a reset model of the environment is provided (i.e., one that can be reset to any state), we show evidence of hardness of competing when only given the weaker trace model (i.e., one can only reset to the initial states and must produce full traces through the environment), without further assumption of admissibility of the offline data. Under the admissibility assumptions– that the offline data could actually be produced by the policy class we consider– we propose the first algorithm in the trace model setting that provably matches the performance of algorithms that leverage a reset model. We also perform proof-of-concept experiments that suggest the effectiveness of our algorithm in practice.

This motivates our study of the hybrid RL with observation-only offline dataset framework. While the task of competing with the best policy “covered” by the offline data can be solved if a reset model of the environment is provided (i.e., one that can be reset to any state), we show evidence of hardness of competing when only given the weaker trace model (i.e., one can only reset to the initial states and must produce full traces through the environment), without further assumption of admissibility of the offline data. Under the admissibility assumptions– that the offline data could actually be produced by the policy class we consider– we propose the first algorithm in the trace model setting that provably matches the performance of algorithms that leverage a reset model. paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning that combines an existing dataset with new interaction in an environment. The offline dataset contains only states, without the actions or rewards usually assumed available. The goal is to compete with the best policy covered by that data while using online experience to support learning.

The authors distinguish two forms of access to the environment. A reset model can restart from any state, while a trace model can restart only from initial states and must generate full trajectories. They provide evidence that competing with the covered policy is hard under trace access without an additional condition on the offline data.

That condition, admissibility, requires that the offline data could have been produced by the policy class under consideration. Under these assumptions, the proposed algorithm provably matches the performance of algorithms using the stronger reset model. Proof-of-concept experiments suggest practical effectiveness. The key contribution is therefore conditional: observation-only data can support strong hybrid learning under trace access when it is compatible with the policy class.
summary.tldr: Under admissibility assumptions, observation-only offline data enables a trace-access RL algorithm to match the performance of algorithms with stronger reset access.

title: Hybrid Reinforcement Learning from Offline Observation Alone

abstract: Visual Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) promises to encapsulate agent’s knowledge about the underlying dynamics of the environment, enabling learning a world model as a useful planner. However, top MBRL agents such as Dreamer often struggle with visual pixel-based inputs in the presence of exogenous or irrelevant noise in the observation space, due to failure to capture task-specific features while filtering out irrelevant spatio-temporal details. To tackle this problem, we apply a spatio-temporal masking strategy, a bisimulation principle, combined with latent reconstruction, to capture endogenous task-specific aspects of the environment for world models, effectively eliminating non-essential information. Joint training of representations, dynamics, and policy often leads to instabilities. To further address this issue, we develop a Hybrid Recurrent State-Space Model (HRSSM) structure, enhancing state representation robustness for effective policy learning. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates significant performance improvements over existing methods in a range of visually complex control tasks such as Maniskill with exogenous distractors from the Matterport environment. Our code is avaliable at https://github.com/bit1029public/HRSSM.

paragraphs: Visual model-based reinforcement learning uses observations to learn a world model that supports decision-making. Irrelevant visual changes can interfere with this process: the model may represent distracting details instead of the aspects of the environment needed for the task. The paper targets this problem in visually complex control settings.

The approach combines masking across space and time, a bisimulation principle, and reconstruction in the latent representation. These components aim to preserve task-specific aspects of the environment while removing nonessential information. The authors also address instability that can arise when representations, environment dynamics, and the policy are trained together, introducing a Hybrid Recurrent State-Space Model to improve representation robustness.

The empirical evaluation reports significant improvements over existing methods on several visually complex control tasks. These include Maniskill tasks with external distractors from the Matterport environment. The findings support the value of learning a world representation that resists irrelevant observation changes. The contribution combines a strategy for selecting task-relevant information with a model structure intended to make policy learning more stable.
summary.tldr: Masking, bisimulation, latent reconstruction, and a hybrid state-space model improve world-model learning in visually distracting control environments.

title: Learning Latent Dynamic Robust Representations for World Models

abstract: The learning to defer (L2D) framework allows models to defer their decisions to human experts. For L2D, the Bayes optimality is the basic requirement of theoretical guarantees for the design of consistent surrogate loss functions, which requires the minimizer (i.e., learned classifier) by the surrogate loss to be the Bayes optimality. However, we find that the original form of Bayes optimality fails to consider the dependence between the model and the expert, and such a dependence could be further exploited to design a better consistent loss for L2D. In this paper, we provide a new formulation for the Bayes optimality called dependent Bayes optimality, which reveals the dependence pattern in determining whether to defer. Based on the dependent Bayes optimality, we further present a deferral principle for L2D. Following the guidance of the deferral principle, we propose a novel consistent surrogate loss. Comprehensive experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Learning to defer lets a model hand decisions to a human expert. Training such a system requires a rule for deciding when the model should answer and when the expert should take over. The paper argues that the usual formulation of Bayes optimality overlooks dependence between the model and the expert.

The authors introduce dependent Bayes optimality, a formulation that makes this relationship part of the deferral decision. This matters because the usefulness of handing off a decision depends on the model and expert together. Their dependence can contain information relevant to choosing who should decide, beyond what the original formulation captures.

From this formulation, the researchers derive a deferral principle and use it to construct a consistent surrogate loss. Consistency connects the training objective to the desired optimal decision rule. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show advantages for the proposed method. The contribution thus links a revised theoretical target to a trainable objective and empirical improvements in human–AI decision allocation.
summary.tldr: Accounting for dependence between a model and a human expert yields a new optimality formulation and improved learning-to-defer objective.

title: Exploiting Human-AI Dependence for Learning to Defer

abstract: We present Junk DNA Hypothesis by adopting a novel task-centric angle for the pre-trained weights of large language models (LLMs). It has been believed that weights in LLMs contain significant redundancy, leading to the conception that a considerable chunk of the parameters can be removed by pruning without compromising performance. Contrary to this belief, this paper presents a counter-argument: small-magnitude weights of pre-trained model weights encode vital knowledge essential for tackling difficult downstream tasks - manifested as the monotonic relationship between the performance drop of downstream tasks across the difficulty spectrum, as we prune more pre-trained weights by magnitude. Moreover, we reveal that these seemingly inconsequential weights can result in irreparable loss of knowledge and performance degradation in difficult tasks, even when downstream continual training is allowed. Interestingly, our evaluations show that the other popular compression, namely quantization fail to exhibit similar “monotonic" effect and does not as convincingly disentangle this task-difficulty information. To study formally, we introduce several quantifiable metrics to gauge the downstream task difficulty: (a) within the same task category, and (b) across different task categories. Our extensive experiments substantiate the Junk DNA Hypothesis across a diverse range of model sizes, tasks, datasets, and even pruning methods. Codes are available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/Junk_DNA_Hypothesis.git.

paragraphs: Small pretrained weights in language models are often treated as candidates for removal because their magnitudes suggest limited importance. This paper examines that assumption through downstream task difficulty. Its Junk DNA Hypothesis proposes that apparently minor weights can contain knowledge needed for difficult tasks.

The authors introduce metrics for comparing difficulty within a task category and across categories. Their experiments find a monotonic pattern of downstream performance degradation as more pretrained weights are removed by magnitude, revealing a relationship with task difficulty. They also report that losses on difficult tasks can remain irreparable even when downstream continual training is allowed.

The study spans different model sizes, tasks, datasets, and pruning methods. Quantization does not display the same clear monotonic effect in their evaluations, so the observed pattern does not extend equally to every compression approach. The findings challenge assessments of redundancy that ignore which tasks a model must support: weights that appear expendable under some evaluations can carry information that matters for harder downstream use.
summary.tldr: Experiments suggest small pretrained weights carry knowledge for difficult tasks that magnitude pruning can irreversibly damage.

title: Junk DNA Hypothesis: Pruning Small Pre-Trained Weights $\textitIrreversibly$ and $\textitMonotonically$ Impairs “Difficult" Downstream Tasks in LLMs

abstract: We introduce a novel semi-supervised learning approach, named Teacher-Student Bayesian Optimization ($\texttt{TSBO}$), integrating the teacher-student paradigm into BO to minimize expensive labeled data queries for the first time. $\texttt{TSBO}$ incorporates a teacher model, an unlabeled data sampler, and a student model. The student is trained on unlabeled data locations generated by the sampler, with pseudo labels predicted by the teacher. The interplay between these three components implements a unique selective regularization to the teacher in the form of student feedback. This scheme enables the teacher to predict high-quality pseudo labels, enhancing the generalization of the GP surrogate model in the search space. To fully exploit $\texttt{TSBO}$, we propose two optimized unlabeled data samplers to construct effective student feedback that well aligns with the objective of Bayesian optimization. Furthermore, we quantify and leverage the uncertainty of the teacher-student model for the provision of reliable feedback to the teacher in the presence of risky pseudo-label predictions. $\texttt{TSBO}$ demonstrates significantly improved sample-efficiency in several global optimization tasks under tight labeled data budgets. The implementation is available at https://github.com/reminiscenty/TSBO-Official.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good solutions when evaluating the objective is expensive. Teacher-Student Bayesian Optimization, or TSBO, aims to reduce the number of these costly labeled queries by using semi-supervised learning. It combines a teacher model, a student model, and a sampler that chooses unlabeled locations in the search space.

The teacher supplies predicted labels for the sampled locations, and the student learns from them. Feedback from the student selectively regularizes the teacher, helping it produce better pseudo labels. This interaction improves the generalization of the Gaussian-process surrogate used to guide the search.

The authors introduce two optimized sampling methods so that student feedback aligns with the optimization objective. They also use teacher-student uncertainty to make feedback more reliable when pseudo-label predictions are risky. Across several global optimization tasks with tight labeled-data budgets, TSBO substantially improves sample efficiency. Its central contribution is coordinating where synthetic supervision is produced, how it is learned, and how its uncertainty influences the teacher.
summary.tldr: TSBO combines optimized unlabeled sampling, teacher-generated labels, and uncertainty-aware student feedback to improve Bayesian optimization under tight evaluation budgets.

title: High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization via Semi-Supervised Learning with Optimized Unlabeled Data Sampling

abstract: In healthcare analytics, addressing binary diagnosis or prognosis tasks presents unique challenges due to the inherent asymmetry between positive and negative samples. While positive samples, indicating patients with a disease, are defined based on stringent medical criteria, negative samples are defined in an open-ended manner and remain underexplored in prior research. To bridge this gap, we propose an innovative approach to facilitate cohort discovery within negative samples, leveraging a Shapley-based exploration of interrelationships between these samples, which holds promise for uncovering valuable insights concerning the studied disease, and related comorbidity and complications. We quantify each sample’s contribution using data Shapley values, subsequently constructing the Negative Sample Shapley Field to model the distribution of all negative samples. Next, we transform this field through manifold learning, preserving the essential data structure information while imposing an isotropy constraint in data Shapley values. Within this transformed space, we pinpoint cohorts of medical interest via density-based clustering. We empirically evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on the real-world electronic medical records from National University Hospital in Singapore, yielding clinically valuable insights aligned with existing knowledge, and benefiting medical research and clinical decision-making.

paragraphs: In binary healthcare prediction, positive cases are often defined by specific medical criteria, while the negative category is more open-ended. The paper treats that negative category as a source of potentially meaningful patient groups. Its aim is to discover cohorts that could reveal information about the studied disease, related comorbidities, or complications.

The approach first assigns each sample a data Shapley value to quantify its contribution. It then constructs a Negative Sample Shapley Field describing the negative samples and their relationships. Manifold learning transforms this field while preserving essential structure and imposing an isotropy constraint on the Shapley values. Density-based clustering in the transformed space identifies candidate cohorts of medical interest.

The authors evaluate the approach using electronic medical records from Singapore's National University Hospital. They report clinically valuable insights consistent with existing knowledge. The result supports examining structure within negative cases rather than treating their shared label as the end of the analysis, with potential value for research and clinical decision-making.
summary.tldr: The method combines data Shapley values, manifold learning, and clustering to uncover medically meaningful cohorts among negatively labeled patients.

title: Exploiting Negative Samples: A Catalyst for Cohort Discovery in Healthcare Analytics

abstract: Inference with Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) on long sequences is both costly and slow due to the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism. We introduce Star Attention, a two-phase block-sparse approximation that improves computational efficiency by sharding attention across multiple hosts while minimizing communication overhead. In the first phase, the context is processed using blockwise-local attention across hosts, in parallel. In the second phase, query and response tokens attend to all prior cached tokens through sequence-global attention. originalAbstract: Inference with Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) on long sequences is both costly and slow due to the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism. We introduce Star Attention, a two-phase block-sparse approximation that improves computational efficiency by sharding attention across multiple hosts while minimizing communication overhead. In the first phase, the context is processed using blockwise-local attention across hosts, in parallel. In the second phase, query and response tokens attend to all prior cached tokens through sequence-global attention. Star Attention integrates seamlessly with most Transformer-based LLMs trained with global attention, reducing memory requirements and inference time by up to 11x while preserving 97-100% of accuracy.

paragraphs: Long sequences make transformer inference expensive because self-attention has quadratic complexity. Star Attention addresses this cost with a block-sparse approximation distributed across multiple hosts. Its design uses two phases so that context processing can happen in parallel while later query and response tokens retain access to the preceding sequence.

In the first phase, hosts process blocks of context with local attention. In the second, query and response tokens use global attention over all previously cached tokens. This division is the central mechanism: the initial context is handled with restricted interactions, followed by sequence-wide access during query and response processing. The method also aims to keep communication between hosts low.

The authors report reductions in memory requirements and inference time of up to elevenfold while preserving 97–100% of accuracy. Star Attention is designed to integrate with most transformer language models trained using global attention. These findings support a substantial efficiency benefit from the approximation in the evaluated settings, with the reported accuracy retention describing the empirical trade-off rather than an exact equivalence to full attention.
summary.tldr: Star Attention combines parallel local context processing with global query attention, reporting up to elevenfold efficiency gains while retaining 97–100% of accuracy.

title: Star Attention: Efficient LLM Inference over Long Sequences

abstract: Representation learning plays a crucial role in reinforcement learning, especially in complex environments with high-dimensional and unstructured states. Effective representations can enhance the efficiency of learning algorithms by improving sample efficiency and generalization across tasks. This paper considers the Laplacian-based framework for representation learning, where the eigenvectors of the Laplacian matrix of the underlying transition graph are leveraged to encode meaningful features from raw sensory observations of the states. Despite the promising algorithmic advances in this framework, it remains an open question whether the Laplacian-based representations can be learned online and with theoretical guarantees along with policy learning. We address this by formulating an online optimization approach using the Asymmetric Graph Drawing Objective (AGDO) and analyzing its convergence via online projected gradient descent under mild assumptions. Our extensive simulation studies empirically validate the convergence guarantees to the true Laplacian representation. Furthermore, we provide insights into the compatibility of different reinforcement learning algorithms with online representation learning.

Laplacian-based methods derive features from the graph describing transitions between states. Specifically, they use eigenvectors of its Laplacian matrix to encode structure that can support learning and transfer across tasks.

This paper asks whether those representations can be learned online alongside policy learning, with theoretical guarantees. The authors formulate the task as online optimization using the Asymmetric Graph Drawing Objective. They analyze online projected gradient descent and establish convergence under assumptions described as mild. The guarantee therefore depends on the conditions of that analysis rather than applying to every possible learning process.

Simulation studies empirically support convergence to the true Laplacian representation. The paper also investigates how different reinforcement-learning algorithms fit with online representation learning. This matters because an agent's representation and policy can develop together during interaction, making their compatibility part of the design problem. The contribution combines an online learning formulation, a conditional convergence analysis, and empirical evidence about the resulting representation.
summary.tldr: The paper develops online Laplacian representation learning alongside policy learning and proves convergence under stated assumptions.

title: Online Laplacian-Based Representation Learning in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Visual tokenization via auto-encoding empowers state-of-the-art image and video generative models by compressing pixels into a latent space. However, questions remain about how auto-encoder design impacts reconstruction and downstream generative performance. This work explores scaling in auto-encoders for reconstruction and generation by replacing the convolutional backbone with an enhanced Vision Transformer for Tokenization (ViTok). We find scaling the auto-encoder bottleneck correlates with reconstruction but exhibits a nuanced relationship with generation. Separately, encoder scaling yields no gains, while decoder scaling improves reconstruction with minimal impact on generation. As a result, we determine that scaling the current paradigm of auto-encoders is not effective for improving generation performance. Coupled with Diffusion Transformers, ViTok achieves competitive image reconstruction and generation performance on 256p and 512p ImageNet-1K. In videos, ViTok achieves SOTA reconstruction and generation performance on 16-frame 128p UCF-101.

paragraphs: Visual auto-encoders compress images or videos into latent representations that generative models can use. A natural question is whether improving that compression-and-reconstruction system also improves the quality of newly generated content. This paper investigates the relationship using ViTok, which replaces a convolutional backbone with an enhanced Vision Transformer for tokenization.

The authors separately examine scaling the bottleneck, encoder, and decoder. Bottleneck scaling correlates with reconstruction quality, but has a more nuanced relationship with generation. Increasing encoder scale yields no gains in their study, while increasing decoder scale improves reconstruction with little effect on generation. These results show that reconstruction improvements do not reliably translate into downstream generative improvements.

Based on these findings, the authors conclude that scaling the current auto-encoder paradigm is ineffective for improving generation performance. ViTok nevertheless delivers competitive image reconstruction and generation when paired with Diffusion Transformers on 256p and 512p ImageNet-1K. For 16-frame, 128p UCF-101 video, it achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction and generation results. The study separates a capable tokenizer design from the broader question of which scaling choices actually help generation.
summary.tldr: ViTok's scaling study finds that better auto-encoder reconstruction does not reliably improve downstream generation, despite strong image and video results.

title: Learnings from Scaling Visual Tokenizers for Reconstruction and Generation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in handling natural language processing (NLP) tasks and beyond. LLMs usually can be categorized as transformer decoder-only models (DOMs), utilizing Next-Token-Prediction (NTP) as their pre-training methodology. Despite their tremendous empirical successes, the theoretical understanding of how NTP pre-training affects the model’s generalization behavior is lacking. To fill this gap, we establish the fine-grained generalization analysis for NTP pre-training based on Rademacher complexity, where the dependence between tokens is also addressed. Technically, a novel decomposition of Rademacher complexity is developed to study DOMs from the representation learner and the token predictor, respectively. Furthermore, the upper bounds of covering number are established for multi-layer and multi-head transformer-decoder models under the Frobenius norm, which theoretically pioneers the incorporation of mask matrix within the self-attention mechanism. Our results reveal that the generalization ability of NTP pre-training is affected quantitively by the number of token sequences $N$, the maximum length of sequence $m$, and the count of parameters in the transformer model $\Theta$. Additionally, experiments on public datasets verify our theoretical findings.
