In this low-data setting, Neural-HSS learns from elliptic-PDE data more effectively than the compared baselines. Further demonstrations cover PDE data from electromagnetism, fluid dynamics, and biology. The findings show how incorporating relevant operator structure into a model can help reduce its dependence on large training datasets while retaining applicability across several scientific domains.
summary.tldr: Neural-HSS uses hierarchical matrix structure to learn PDE solutions efficiently from limited data, supported by theory and scientific-domain experiments.

title: Neural-HSS: Hierarchical Semi-Separable Neural PDE Solver

abstract: With the advance of federated learning (FL) in privacy-sensitive domains, the need for efficient and robust training becomes increasingly urgent. Communication bottlenecks, heterogeneous client distributions, and fairness requirements make it essential to select the “right” data and features for model training. Yet existing FL research often addresses feature selection and data selection separately, ignoring their interplay in real-world high-dimensional and noisy datasets, leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose a unified framework for data and feature selection by formulating the problem as a generalized CUR decomposition problem. We introduce FedGCUR, a practical framework that integrates a federated column-pivoted QR (FedCPQR) decomposition routine with per-silo row selection. We prove that FedCPQR produces exactly the same decomposition results as centralized CPQR and establish an upper bound of the reconstruction error of FedGCUR. Experiments on tabular tasks and vision benchmarks show strong downstream accuracy and absolute CUR reconstruction quality compared with representative data and feature selection baselines.

paragraphs: Federated learning must choose useful training examples and features while data remains distributed across clients. Communication limits, differing client distributions, and fairness requirements make those choices consequential. This paper argues that selecting examples and features separately overlooks their interaction, especially in noisy data with many dimensions.

FedGCUR formulates both choices through generalized CUR decomposition, connecting the selection of rows and columns in a data matrix. Its federated column-pivoted QR routine, FedCPQR, handles the feature side, while individual silos select rows. This gives the two selection tasks a shared mathematical framework instead of treating each as an independent preprocessing decision.

The authors prove that FedCPQR returns exactly the same decomposition as centralized column-pivoted QR and establish an upper bound on FedGCUR’s reconstruction error. Experiments on tabular and vision tasks show strong downstream accuracy and CUR reconstruction quality against representative selection baselines. The theoretical and empirical results connect distributed selection to both faithful data reconstruction and useful model training.
summary.tldr: FedGCUR jointly selects data and features in federated learning, with centralized-equivalent QR decomposition and a reconstruction-error bound.

title: Federated Data and Feature Selection by Generalized CUR Decomposition

abstract: Noisy evolution strategies under fixed evaluation budgets face a depth–fidelity trade-off: spending evaluations to denoise intra-generation rankings reduces the number of distribution updates the optimizer can execute. We argue for depth over fidelity and propose probabilistic elite membership (PEM), which replaces hard rank-based weights in evolution strategies with conditional expected rank weights that integrate over ranking uncertainty. PEM preserves the conditional mean update while reducing conditional update dispersion—a Rao–Blackwellization of the noisy rank-based step. We instantiate PEM via residual bootstrapping (RB-PEM) with capped per-generation overhead, complemented by an adaptive probe-and-switch mechanism for low-noise regimes. Across the COCO bbob-noisy suite and external tasks including RL policy search and hyperparameter optimization, RB-PEM achieves consistent gains in high-misranking, budget-constrained settings.

paragraphs: Evolution strategies improve a search distribution by evaluating candidate solutions and favoring better performers. When evaluations are noisy, candidate rankings can be wrong. Under a fixed budget, spending more evaluations to clarify each ranking leaves fewer opportunities to update the search distribution. This paper investigates that trade-off between ranking reliability and optimization depth.

Probabilistic elite membership replaces weights based on a single noisy ranking with expected rank weights that account for ranking uncertainty. The authors show that this preserves the conditional mean of the update while reducing its conditional dispersion, a statistical averaging operation known as Rao–Blackwellization. Their practical version, RB-PEM, uses residual bootstrapping with capped overhead and adds an adaptive probe-and-switch mechanism for low-noise settings.

Experiments cover the COCO bbob-noisy suite, reinforcement-learning policy search, and hyperparameter optimization. RB-PEM shows consistent gains where misranking is substantial and evaluation budgets are constrained. The finding supports handling uncertainty within the update rule so that more of the available budget can support successive optimization steps.
summary.tldr: RB-PEM accounts for uncertain candidate rankings to improve noisy evolution strategies when evaluation budgets are tight and misranking is substantial.

title: Depth over Fidelity in Fixed-Budget Noisy Evolution Strategies

abstract: Although Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning (RLFT) applied to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) substantially enhances multimodal reasoning capabilities, their prohibitive training cost limits broad adoption. Surprisingly, most existing methods simply port Large Language Model (LLM) RLFT techniques to VLMs, while ignoring a intrinsic property of multimodal models: their dynamic text–vision alignment. We ask a new question: Can this intrinsic alignment be turned into a training signal that makes VLM RLFT more efficient? We analyze how a VLM plans to attend, actually attends, and ideally should attend during reasoning, and derive two lightweight metrics from these patterns. Predictive View Accuracy (PVA) estimates sample difficulty, and Reasoning View Accuracy (RVA) reflects the quality of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. These alignment signals enable automated data curriculum and dense reasoning supervision. We introduce FOCUS-RL, a plug-and-play framework that can be seamlessly integrated into any VLM and dramatically boosts RLFT training efficiency. FOCUS-RL achieves 2.5 x – 4 x faster convergence over vanilla GRPO and consistent accuracy gains (+4.4 on average) across six different benchmarks and multiple VLM families.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can improve vision-language reasoning, but its training cost limits adoption. title: Seeing is Solving: Unlocking Efficient Multimodal RL via View Alignment

abstract: This paper studies the Minimal Embeddable Dimension (MED): the least dimension in which there exists a configuration of $m$ object vectors so that every subset of size at most $k$ is exactly retrieved by score comparison. Our result shows MED is $\Theta(k)$, independent of $m$, for inner product, Euclidean distance, and cosine similarity. We then consider Robust MED (RMED), where all vectors are unit normed and an $\epsilon$ gap of scores is required. We derive the $m$-dependent feasibility ceiling $\epsilon_\star(m,k)=m/\sqrt{k(m-1)(m-k)}$, which approaches $1/\sqrt{k}$ when $m\gg k$, and a Gaussian centroid construction gives a robust witness upper bound in the feasible margin regime. Numerical simulation on synthetic top-$2$ retrieval with cyclic polytope and centroid query optimization confirmed our theoretical claims. Experiments on LIMIT and LIMIT-small datasets also show that simple embedding-based retrieval baselines can overfit and outperform the reported single-vector LLM embedding baseline. Both theoretical and empirical findings rule out the lack of exact geometric capacity as the obstruction.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many embedding dimensions are needed to represent every possible retrieval target containing at most k objects from a collection of m. It defines the minimal embeddable dimension as the smallest dimension admitting such an object-vector configuration. For inner product, Euclidean distance, and cosine similarity, this dimension grows proportionally to k, independently of collection size.

Exact retrieval capacity differs from retrieval with a protective score margin. The authors therefore study a robust version requiring unit-length vectors and a gap ε between scores. They derive a collection-size-dependent ceiling on feasible margins, approaching 1/√k when m is much larger than k. A Gaussian centroid construction supplies an upper bound in the feasible-margin regime.

Synthetic top-two simulations support the theoretical claims. On LIMIT and LIMIT-small, simple embedding retrieval baselines can overfit and exceed the reported single-vector LLM embedding baseline. Together, these results rule out insufficient exact geometric capacity as the obstruction considered here. The robustness analysis separately shows why demanding score separation introduces constraints absent from exact representability alone.
summary.tldr: Exact top-k retrieval needs only dimension proportional to k, while robust retrieval with score margins faces additional feasibility constraints.

title: $\mathbbR^2k$ is Theoretically Large Enough for Embedding-based Top-$k$ Retrieval

abstract: We study a linear mixing model with dependent latent components, assuming multiple data domains. Most existing models assume that the components are independent or at least uncorrelated, in line with independent component analysis (ICA). Some recent work allows for dependent components, but then makes specific assumptions such as parametric forms of dependencies, multi-view settings, or interventions, or does not recover the individual components. In contrast, we consider a multi-domain setting in which domains differ through domain-specific scalings of the components, while the distribution of the underlying latent components is the same across domains. This approach can model data collected, for example, from different sensors measuring the same process, different laboratories conducting the same experiment, different experimental conditions, or different subjects that might differ in biological or physiological factors. We show that, under sufficient domain variability, latent variables and mixing functions can be identified from second-order statistics alone. We propose the Multi-Domain Covariance Matching (MuDo-CoM) algorithm that generalizes previous methods of joint diagonalization. MuDo-CoM is validated on simulated data and a real-world fMRI dataset.

paragraphs: Recovering hidden sources from mixed measurements is often approached by assuming the sources are independent or uncorrelated. This paper allows dependent latent components and instead draws information from multiple data domains. Its setting keeps the underlying latent distribution the same across domains while allowing each domain to scale the components differently.

Those changing scales provide the variation needed to separate the components. Under sufficient domain variability, the authors show that both latent variables and mixing functions can be identified using second-order statistics alone. The result makes the cross-domain structure central: dependence among sources is permitted, while the shared latent distribution and domain-specific scaling supply the identifying assumptions.

The proposed Multi-Domain Covariance Matching algorithm, MuDo-CoM, generalizes earlier joint-diagonalization methods and is validated on simulations and a real fMRI dataset. The formulation can represent measurements from different sensors, laboratories, experimental conditions, or subjects when they fit its assumptions. It provides a route to recovering individual dependent components by using structured changes across domains.
summary.tldr: MuDo-CoM uses domain-specific scaling differences to identify dependent latent components from covariance information under sufficient domain variability.

title: Identifying dependent components from multi-domain linear mixtures

abstract: Diagnosing rare diseases remains a persistent challenge, often hindered by cognitive anchoring: once clinicians settle on a common diagnosis, they often discount alternative explanations, including rare conditions. To address this, we propose a cognitive-aware counterfactual reasoning framework using a Denoising Masked AutoEncoder (DMAE) to simulate what-if diagnostic scenarios that probe clinicians’ initial assumptions. Our model jointly learns (1) the true distribution of diseases and symptoms, and (2) human diagnostic behavior, revealing critical gaps between medically possible and clinically considered diagnoses. By strategically perturbing latent patient representations, it generates contrastive counterfactuals that highlight rare yet plausible diseases that cognitive bias often obscures. Unlike traditional decision-support tools, our system suggests rare diseases not because they are statistically dominant, but because they are systematically under-considered relative to the observed evidence and learned diagnostic behavior. Across four public and three private rare-disease datasets, our approach outperforms standard machine learning classifiers in detecting rare conditions while maintaining strong performance on common diagnoses. Beyond boosting accuracy, the counterfactual evidence encourages hypothesis-driven reasoning and supports clinical learning.

This paper addresses that problem by modeling both disease–symptom relationships and human diagnostic behavior. summary.tldr: A counterfactual diagnostic model highlights plausible rare diseases that learned patterns of human diagnostic behavior suggest are being under-considered.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Latent Perturbations for Cognitive-Aware Diagnosis

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has shown promise for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) to follow instructions with various constraints. Despite the encouraging results, RL improvement inevitably relies on sampling successful, high-quality responses; however, the initial model often struggles to generate responses that satisfy all constraints due to its limited capabilities, yielding sparse or indistinguishable rewards that impede learning. In this work, we propose H*indsight instruction Replay (HiR), a novel sample-efficient RL framework for complex instruction following tasks, which employs a select-then-rewrite strategy to replay failed attempts as successes* based on the constraints that have been satisfied in hindsight. We perform RL on these replayed samples as well as the original ones, theoretically framing the objective as dual-preference learning at both the instruction- and response-level to enable efficient optimization using only a binary reward signal. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed HiR yields promising results across different instruction following tasks, while requiring less computational budget. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/sastpg/HIR.

paragraphs: An instruction can impose several constraints that an initially weak model rarely satisfies together. Reinforcement learning then receives few successful examples, and failure rewards may offer little distinction between responses. Hindsight Instruction Replay, or HiR, seeks useful training signals inside these failed attempts by considering which constraints they actually satisfied.

The framework first selects attempts and then rewrites instructions so that the selected responses count as successes under the satisfied constraints. Training uses these replayed samples alongside the original ones. This preserves learning from the original task while adding examples whose success becomes visible through hindsight.

The authors formulate the objective as preference learning at both the instruction and response levels, enabling optimization with a binary reward signal. Experiments across different instruction-following tasks report promising results with a smaller computational budget. The contribution is a way to reuse partial achievement as training evidence, reducing dependence on repeatedly sampling responses that meet every original constraint before useful learning can occur.
summary.tldr: HiR rewrites instructions around constraints that failed responses did satisfy, creating additional successful training examples for efficient reinforcement learning.

title: Replay Failures as Successes: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Instruction Following

abstract: LLM-as-a-judge ensembles are the standard paradigm for scalable evaluation, but their aggregation mechanisms suffer from a fundamental flaw: they implicitly assume that judges provide independent estimates of true quality. However, in practice, LLM judges exhibit correlated errors caused by shared latent confounders—such as verbosity, stylistic preferences, or training artifacts—causing standard aggregation rules like majority vote or averaging to provide little gain or even amplify systematic mistakes. To address this, we introduce CARE, a confounder-aware aggregation framework that explicitly models LLM judge scores as arising from both a latent true-quality signal and shared confounding factors. Rather than heuristically re-weighting judges, CARE separates quality from confounders without access to ground-truth labels. We provide theoretical guarantees for identifiability and finite-sample recovery under shared confounders, and we quantify the systematic bias incurred when aggregation models omit confounding latent factors. Across 12 public benchmarks spanning continuous scoring, binary classification, and pairwise preference settings, CARE improves aggregation accuracy, reducing error by up to 26.8%.

To address this, we introduce CARE, a confounder-aware aggregation framework that explicitly models LLM judge scores as arising from both a latent true-quality signal and shared confounding factors. Rather than heuristically re-weighting judges, CARE separates quality from confounders without access to ground-truth labels. We provide theoretical guarantees for identifiability and finite-sample recovery under shared confounders, and we quantify the systematic bias incurred when aggregation models omit confounding latent factors. Across 12 public benchmarks spanning continuous scoring, binary classification, and pairwise preference settings, CARE improves aggregation accuracy, reducing error by up to 26.8%.

paragraphs: Combining several language-model judges can seem like a straightforward way to obtain more reliable evaluations. But judges may share preferences for verbosity or style, or inherit similar training artifacts. Their mistakes can therefore be correlated, allowing averaging or majority voting to preserve or amplify the same systematic error.

CARE models each judge's score as a mixture of an underlying quality signal and shared confounding factors. It aims to separate those components without ground-truth labels, rather than simply adjusting how much weight each judge receives. This directly addresses the possibility that agreement among judges reflects a common bias instead of agreement about true quality.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for identifying and recovering the modeled signals under shared confounders, along with an analysis of bias when aggregation omits those factors. Across 12 public benchmarks covering numerical scores, binary decisions, and pairwise preferences, CARE improves aggregation accuracy and reduces error by up to 26.8%. The findings show the value of modeling why judges agree when combining their assessments.
summary.tldr: CARE separates shared judge biases from latent quality signals, improving LLM evaluation aggregation without ground-truth labels.

title: CARE: Confounder-Aware Aggregation for Reliable LLM Evaluation

abstract: Embodied agents operating in decentralized and partially observable environments have attracted growing attention in recent years. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based agents often exhibit behaviors that are misaligned with their partners or inconsistent with the environment state, leading to inefficient cooperation and poor task success. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework, Learning Laws of Cooperation (LLawCo), that enables embodied agents to autonomously align with both their partners and task objectives. Our framework allows agents to reflect on past failures to extract misaligned behavioral patterns, which are used to derive high-level behavioral laws, such as “Talk when necessary” and “Wait for partner.” These laws are explicitly incorporated into the agents’ chains of thought via supervised fine-tuning, aligning their reasoning with task requirements and the behavior of other agents. To evaluate our approach, we introduce PARTNR-Dialog, a large-scale multi-agent communicative and cooperative planning benchmark built on the PARTNR environment. Experiments on existing tasks and our new benchmark demonstrate significant improvements in cooperative efficiency and task success rates. Across four backbone LLMs, our method achieves average success rate improvements of 4.5% on the PARTNR-Dialog benchmark and 6.8% on the TDW-MAT benchmark over state-of-the-art open-source communicative agent frameworks. Code and benchmark resources are publicly available at https://www.merl.com/research/highlights/LLawCo.

abstract: Invariant learning can fail even when the invariant structure is statistically identifiable. We show a conditional computational barrier: under a black-box samplable supervised sparse recovery primitive motivated by average-case sparse-recovery reductions, there exist samplable multi-environment instances with a one-dimensional predictive invariant subspace ($k=1$) that are learnable with polynomial samples by exhaustive search, while any polynomial-time constant-accuracy recovery algorithm would contradict the primitive. We further quantify environment diversity by a separation parameter $\gamma$, which controls identifiability and the curvature of invariance objectives. Under sufficient diversity and local Gaussian regularity, the minimax risk is $\mathbb{E}[dist(\hat{V},V_{\mathrm{inv}})^2]=\Theta(k(d-k)/(n|\mathcal{E}|))$, and under label-induced shifts a phase transition occurs at $n^*\propto k(d-k)/(|\mathcal{E}|\gamma^2)$ with refined estimation error scaling proportional to $1/\gamma^2$. Synthetic and real datasets illustrate the predicted gaps and transitions and motivate simple diversity diagnostics.

paragraphs: Learning an invariant predictor means finding predictive structure that remains useful across environments. This paper distinguishes having enough data to identify that structure from being able to recover it efficiently. It establishes a conditional computational barrier based on an assumed black-box, samplable supervised sparse-recovery primitive.

Under that assumption, the authors construct samplable problems with only a one-dimensional predictive invariant subspace. Exhaustive search can learn these problems with polynomially many samples, but a polynomial-time algorithm achieving constant recovery accuracy would contradict the assumed primitive. The difficulty therefore persists even when the invariant representation is small and statistically identifiable.

The paper also quantifies environment diversity through a separation parameter, gamma. With sufficient diversity and local Gaussian regularity, it derives an optimal risk rate governed by subspace dimensions and the number of samples and environments. Under label-induced shifts, it identifies a sample threshold and refined error scaling involving inverse squared gamma. Synthetic and real-data results illustrate these gaps and transitions, motivating diagnostics for whether environments provide enough distinguishing information.
summary.tldr: Invariant prediction can be statistically learnable yet computationally hard under a stated assumption, with environment diversity also governing recovery.

title: Is Spurious Correlation Removal Always Learnable?

abstract: Pursuing training-free open-vocabulary semantic segmentation in an efficient and generalizable manner remains challenging due to the deep-seated spatial bias in CLIP. To overcome the limitations of existing solutions, this work moves beyond the CLIP-based paradigm and harnesses the recent spatially-aware dino.txt framework to facilitate more efficient and high-quality dense prediction. While dino.txt exhibits robust spatial awareness, we find that the semantic ambiguity of text queries gives rise to severe mismatch within its dense cross-modal interactions. To address this, we introduce VIsual-guided Prompt evolution (VIP) to rectify the semantic expressiveness of text queries in dino.txt, unleashing its potential for fine-grained object perception. Towards this end, VIP integrates alias expansion with a visual-guided distillation mechanism to mine valuable semantic cues, which are robustly aggregated in a saliency-aware manner to yield a high-fidelity prediction. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that VIP: I) surpasses the top-leading methods by 1.4% 8.4% average mIoU, II) generalizes well to diverse challenging domains, and III) requires marginal inference time and memory overhead.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation assigns labels throughout an image using text queries. This paper pursues an efficient, training-free approach with the spatially aware dino.txt framework. Although dino.txt captures spatial information well, the authors find that ambiguous text queries can still produce serious mismatches between language and local visual content.

Visual-guided Prompt Evolution, or VIP, improves how those queries express meaning. It combines alias expansion with visually guided distillation to extract useful semantic cues. A saliency-aware aggregation process then combines the cues into the final prediction. The method therefore uses information from the image to improve the language guidance involved in fine-grained object perception.

Evaluations report improvements in average mIoU over leading methods, generalization across challenging domains, and only marginal additional inference time and memory use. These findings indicate that stronger spatial features alone do not resolve every cross-modal mismatch: the wording and interpretation of category queries also matter. VIP contributes a way to refine that semantic interface while retaining the efficiency sought in training-free dense prediction.
summary.tldr: VIP refines dino.txt text queries using visual guidance to improve training-free segmentation with little additional inference cost.

title: VIP: Visual-guided Prompt Evolution for Efficient Dense Vision-Language Inference

abstract: Personalization underpins the modern digital economy. Today, personalization is largely implemented through provider-managed infrastructure that infers user preferences from behavioral data, with limited portability or user control. However, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to perform tasks on users’ behalf. The age of LLMs for the first time provides a path to a more controllable and interpretable personalization paradigm, grounded in user-expressed natural language preferences and context. In this position paper, we argue that to provide robust and user-centric personalization, we need a new Human Context Protocol (HCP) to represent and share personal preferences across AI systems. HCP treats preferences as a portable, user-governed layer in the personalization stack, enabling interoperability, scoped access, and revocation. Along with a working prototype to ground discussion, we consider counterarguments along adoption dynamics and market incentives, high-stakes use cases, and outline novel paths via the HCP towards trustworthy personalization in the human-AI economy.

paragraphs: Personalization usually relies on providers inferring preferences from behavioral data, leaving users with limited control or ability to move those preferences elsewhere. This paper argues that LLMs create an opportunity for a different arrangement. People can express preferences and relevant context in natural language as AI systems increasingly perform tasks on their behalf.

The proposed Human Context Protocol would represent and share that information across AI systems. It treats preferences as a portable layer governed by the user. Interoperability would allow that layer to work across systems, while scoped access and revocation would support control over which systems can use it and when that access ends.

The authors include a working prototype to make the proposal concrete and examine counterarguments involving adoption, market incentives, and high-stakes applications. They argue that this shared infrastructure is needed for robust, user-centered personalization. The contribution combines a protocol proposal with discussion of the conditions affecting its uptake, outlining a route toward personalization that users can more directly interpret and control.
summary.tldr: A Human Context Protocol would make expressed preferences portable across AI systems while giving users control over access and revocation.

abstract: This paper aims to conduct a comprehensive study on the listwise approach to learning to rank. The listwise approach learns a ranking function by taking individual lists as instances and minimizing a loss function defined on two lists (one is predicted result and the other ground truth). Existing work on the approach mainly focused on the development of new algorithms; methods such as RankCosine and ListNet have been proposed and better performances by them have also been observed. Unfortunately, the underlying theory was not sufficiently studied as far. To amend the problem, this paper proposes conducting theoretical analysis of learning to rank algorithms through investigation on the properties of the loss functions, including consistency, soundness, continuity, differentiability, convexity, and efficiency. A sufficient condition on consistency for ranking is given, which seems to be the first such result obtained in related research. The paper then conducts analysis on three loss functions: likelihood loss, cosine loss, and cross entropy loss. The latter two were used in RankCosine and ListNet respectively. The use of likelihood loss leads to the development of a new listwise method called ListMLE, whose loss function offers better properties. Experimental results have also verified the correctness of the theoretical results obtained in the paper.

paragraphs: Listwise learning to rank treats an entire list as a training instance. A ranking function is learned by minimizing a loss that compares its predicted ordering with the ground-truth ordering. This paper investigates the theoretical foundations of that approach, addressing a gap left by earlier work that emphasized new algorithms and observed performance gains.

The analysis examines loss functions through properties including consistency, soundness, continuity, differentiability, convexity, and computational efficiency. The authors provide a sufficient condition for ranking consistency. Such a condition identifies circumstances under which consistency follows; it does not establish that the condition is required for every consistent ranking method.

The paper studies likelihood, cosine, and cross-entropy losses, with the latter two corresponding to RankCosine and ListNet. Using likelihood loss leads to a new method, ListMLE, whose loss offers better properties according to the analysis. Experiments support the theoretical results. The contribution is therefore both a way to assess ranking objectives and a new algorithm motivated by that assessment.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes listwise ranking losses, gives a sufficient consistency condition, and introduces the likelihood-based ListMLE method.

title: Listwise approach to learning to rank: theory and algorithm

abstract: Most models of utility elicitation in decision support and interactive optimization assume a predefined set of "catalog" features over which user preferences are expressed. However, users may differ in the features over which they are most comfortable expressing their preferences. In this work we consider the problem of feature elicitation: a user's utility function is expressed using features whose definition (in terms of "catalog" features) is unknown. We cast this as a problem of concept learning, but whose goal is to identify only enough about the concept to enable a good decision to be recommended. We describe computational procedures for identifying optimal alternatives w.r.t. minimax regret in the presence of concept uncertainty; and describe several heuristic query strategies that focus on reduction of relevant concept uncertainty.

paragraphs: Interactive decision systems often assume that users describe preferences using a predefined catalog of features. This paper considers users who prefer to express themselves through different features, whose definitions in terms of the catalog are unknown. The system must therefore learn something about what the user's features mean while helping make a decision.

The authors formulate feature elicitation as concept learning. The objective is to identify enough about the unknown concepts to recommend a good alternative. This makes the information needed for the current decision central to learning, rather than requiring a complete definition of every user feature before a recommendation can be made.

The paper gives computational procedures for selecting alternatives according to minimax regret while concept uncertainty remains. This criterion addresses the worst-case shortfall associated with a choice under the remaining uncertainty. It also introduces heuristic query strategies aimed at reducing uncertainty that matters for the decision. Together, these components connect questions about feature meaning to the practical task of choosing an alternative.
summary.tldr: The paper learns enough about users' unfamiliar preference features to recommend alternatives using minimax regret.

title: Online feature elicitation in interactive optimization

abstract: Markov logic networks (MLNs) combine logic and probability by attaching weights to first-order clauses, and viewing these as templates for fea- tures of Markov networks. Learning MLN struc- ture from a relational database involves learn- ing the clauses and weights. The state-of-the-art MLN structure learners all involve some element of greedily generating candidate clauses, and are susceptible to local optima. To address this prob- lem, we present an approach that directly utilizes the data in constructing candidates. A relational database can be viewed as a hypergraph with con- stants as nodes and relations as hyperedges. We find paths of true ground atoms in the hyper- graph that are connected via their arguments. To make this tractable (there are exponentially many paths in the hypergraph), we lift the hypergraph by jointly clustering the constants to form higher- level concepts, and find paths in it. We variabilize the ground atoms in each path, and use them to form clauses, which are evaluated using a pseudo- likelihood measure. In our experiments on three real-world datasets, we find that our algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.

The proposed method uses the data itself to guide candidate construction.

The database is represented as a hypergraph: constants become nodes and relations become hyperedges. Paths through true ground atoms expose connections through shared arguments. The contribution links relational pattern discovery with clause generation, while using abstraction to manage the otherwise excessive number of paths.
summary.tldr: Clustering a relational hypergraph makes data-guided path search tractable for generating Markov logic network clauses.

title: Learning Markov logic network structure via hypergraph lifting

abstract: We consider the problem of extracting informative exemplars from a data stream. Examples of this problem include exemplar-based clustering and nonparametric inference such as Gaussian process regression on massive data sets. We show that these problems require maximization of a submodular function that captures the informativeness of a set of exemplars, over a data stream. We develop an efficient algorithm, Stream Greedy, which is guaranteed to obtain a constant fraction of the value achieved by the optimal solution to this NP-hard optimization problem. We extensively evaluate our algorithm on large real- world data sets.

We develop an efficient algorithm, Stream Greedy, which is guaranteed to obtain a constant fraction of the value achieved by the optimal solution to this NP-hard optimization problem. paragraphs: When data arrive as a stream, a learning system may need to retain a limited set of informative examples. This paper studies that selection problem for applications including exemplar-based clustering and nonparametric inference, such as Gaussian process regression on massive datasets. The goal is to choose a useful collection of exemplars within a budget.

The authors express these tasks as maximizing a submodular function that measures the informativeness of an exemplar set. This formulation evaluates the collection as a whole and provides a common optimization framework for the applications considered. Finding the optimal solution is NP-hard, motivating an efficient approximation that operates over a stream.

The proposed Stream Greedy algorithm has a guarantee: it obtains a constant fraction of the objective value achieved by the optimal solution. That guarantee concerns the informativeness objective used in the formulation. The authors also evaluate the method extensively on large real-world datasets. The contribution combines a shared mathematical description of exemplar selection with a streaming algorithm offering a provable approximation.
summary.tldr: Stream Greedy selects informative exemplars from data streams with a guaranteed constant-factor approximation to the optimal objective value.

title: Budgeted Nonparametric Learning from Data Streams

abstract: Many real-world applications involve multi-label classification, in which the labels are organized in the form of a tree or directed acyclic graph (DAG). However, current research efforts typically ignore the label dependencies or can only exploit the dependencies in tree-structured hierarchies. In this paper, we present a novel hierarchical multi-label classification algorithm which can be used on both tree- and DAG-structured hierarchies. The key idea is to formulate the search for the optimal consistent multi-label as the finding of the best subgraph in a tree/DAG. Using a simple greedy strategy, the proposed algorithm is computationally efficient, easy to implement, does not suffer from the problem of insufficient/skewed training data in classifier training, and can be readily used on large hierarchies. Theoretical results guarantee the optimality of the obtained solution. Experiments are performed on a large number of functional genomics data sets. The proposed method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art method on both tree- and DAG-structured hierarchies.

paragraphs: The paper addresses prediction problems in which an example can receive several labels and those labels belong to a hierarchy. The hierarchy may be a tree or a directed acyclic graph. The authors aim to exploit these dependencies while producing a label combination that is consistent with the hierarchy’s structure.

Their key step is to express the search for the best consistent label combination as a search for the best subgraph. A simple greedy strategy solves the resulting problem, and theoretical results guarantee optimality for the proposed formulation. The method supports both hierarchy types, extending beyond approaches that use only tree-structured dependencies.

The authors describe the algorithm as efficient, easy to implement, suitable for large hierarchies, and free of the identified insufficient or skewed training-data problem in classifier training. Across numerous functional-genomics datasets, it consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art method on both trees and directed acyclic graphs. These results support the practical value of the subgraph formulation in the evaluated classification setting.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical multi-label prediction becomes a best-subgraph problem, enabling efficient greedy inference with an optimality guarantee for trees and DAGs.

title: MultiLabel Classification on Tree- and DAG-Structured Hierarchies

abstract: Data streams are ubiquitous and have in the last two decades become an important research topic. For their predictive non-parametric analysis, Hoeffding-based trees are often a method of choice, offering a possibility of any-time predictions. However, one of their main problems is the delay in learning progress due to the existence of equally discriminative attributes. Options are a natural way to deal with this problem. Option trees build upon regular trees by adding splitting options in the internal nodes. As such they are known to improve accuracy, stability and reduce ambiguity. In this paper, we present on-line option trees for faster learning on numerical data streams. Our results show that options improve the any-time performance of ordinary on-line regression trees, while preserving the interpretable structure of trees and without significantly increasing the computational complexity of the algorithm.

paragraphs: Hoeffding-based trees support prediction while learning from a continuing stream of data. One difficulty is that learning can stall when several attributes are equally useful for splitting the data. The paper addresses this delay for numerical streams, where the aim is to improve regression predictions throughout the learning process.

The proposed approach uses online option trees. These extend ordinary trees by allowing splitting options at internal nodes, accommodating alternatives when the choice of split is ambiguous. The motivation is that competing attributes need not prevent useful learning progress. Options are also associated with improvements in accuracy and stability and with reduced ambiguity.

The reported results show improved anytime performance over ordinary online regression trees, meaning better performance while learning is still underway. The method preserves an interpretable tree structure and does not significantly increase computational complexity in the reported assessment. Its contribution is a way to handle split ambiguity that improves ongoing predictive performance while retaining the practical appeal of tree-based models.
summary.tldr: Online option trees improve regression learning from numerical streams by handling competing split choices without significantly increasing computational complexity.

title: Speeding-Up Hoeffding-Based Regression Trees With Options

abstract: Variational methods are widely used for approximate posterior inference. However, their use is typically limited to families of distributions that enjoy particular conjugacy properties. To circumvent this limitation, we propose a family of variational approximations inspired by nonparametric kernel density estimation. The locations of these kernels and their bandwidth are treated as variational parameters and optimized to improve an approximate lower bound on the marginal likelihood of the data. Using multiple kernels allows the approximation to capture multiple modes of the posterior, unlike most other variational approximations. We demonstrate the efficacy of the nonparametric approximation with a hierarchical logistic regression model and a nonlinear matrix factorization model. We obtain predictive performance as good as or better than more specialized variational methods and sample-based approximations. The method is easy to apply to more general graphical models for which standard variational methods are difficult to derive.

Using multiple kernels allows the approximation to capture multiple modes of the posterior, unlike most other variational approximations. We demonstrate the efficacy of the nonparametric approximation with a hierarchical logistic regression model and a nonlinear matrix factorization model. We obtain predictive performance as good as or better than more specialized variational methods and sample-based approximations. The method is easy to apply to more general graphical models for which standard variational methods are difficult to derive.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution through optimization, but standard methods often depend on convenient conjugacy relationships within the model. Those requirements can make an approximation difficult to derive for more general graphical models. This paper proposes a flexible approximation family inspired by nonparametric kernel density estimation.

The approximation uses multiple kernels whose locations and bandwidth are adjustable variational parameters. Optimization moves and reshapes these components to improve an approximate lower bound on the data's marginal likelihood. Having several kernels allows the approximation to represent multiple posterior modes, so it can capture several separated concentrations of probability.

The authors demonstrate the method on hierarchical logistic regression and nonlinear matrix factorization. Predictive performance matches or exceeds that of more specialized variational methods and sample-based approximations in these evaluations. The stated appeal is both representational flexibility and ease of application to models for which standard variational derivations are difficult. The results support this approach as a practical alternative without requiring the posterior approximation to concentrate around only one mode.
summary.tldr: Optimized kernel-based variational approximations capture multiple posterior modes and work in models where standard conjugate approaches are difficult to derive.

title: Nonparametric variational inference

abstract: We consider the challenge of building feature detectors for high-level concepts from only unlabeled data. For example, we would like to understand if it is possible to learn a face detector using only unlabeled images downloaded from the Internet. To answer this question, we trained a 9-layered locally connected sparse autoencoder with pooling and local contrast normalization on a large dataset of images (which has 10 million images, each image has 200x200 pixels). On contrary to what appears to be a widely-held negative belief, our experimental results reveal that it is possible to achieve a face detector via only unlabeled data. Control experiments show that the feature detector is robust not only to translation but also to scaling and 3D rotation. Also via recognition and visualization, we find that the same network is sensitive to other high-level concepts such as cat faces and human bodies.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether a learning system can discover detectors for meaningful visual concepts using images without labels. Faces provide the central example: can a network become sensitive to faces without being told which training images contain them? This makes the emergence of recognizable concepts from unlabeled data the main research question.

The authors train a nine-layer locally connected sparse autoencoder on ten million images, each measuring 200 by 200 pixels. The network includes pooling and local contrast normalization. This setup allows them to test the question at a large scale using a layered representation learned from the images themselves, without supplying face labels during training.

The experiments show that a face detector can emerge in this setting. Control experiments find robustness to translation, scaling, and three-dimensional rotation. Recognition tests and visualizations also reveal sensitivity to cat faces and human bodies. These findings demonstrate the possibility of learning high-level visual features from unlabeled data in the evaluated system, extending beyond a detector tied to one exact appearance or position.
summary.tldr: A large autoencoder trained on unlabeled images develops sensitivity to faces, cat faces, and human bodies.

title: Building high-level features using large scale unsupervised learning

abstract: As datasets continue to grow, neural network (NN) applications are becoming increasingly limited by both the amount of available computational power and the ease of developing high-performance applications. Researchers often must have expert systems knowledge to make their algorithms run efficiently. Although available computing power approximately doubles every two years, algorithm efficiency is not able to keep pace due to the use of general purpose compilers, which are not able to fully optimize specialized application domains. Within the domain of NNs, we have the added knowledge that network architecture remains constant during training, meaning the architecture's data structure can be statically optimized by a compiler. In this paper, we present SONNC, a compiler for NNs that utilizes static analysis to generate optimized parallel code. We show that SONNC's use of static optimizations make it able to outperform optimized MATLAB code by up to 242X. Additionally, we show that use of SONNC significantly reduces code complexity when using structurally sparse networks.

Within the domain of NNs, we have the added knowledge that network architecture remains constant during training, meaning the architecture's data structure can be statically optimized by a compiler. We show that SONNC's use of static optimizations make it able to outperform optimized MATLAB code by up to 242X. paragraphs: Efficient neural-network applications can require substantial systems expertise, especially as datasets grow. This paper argues that general-purpose compilers miss optimization opportunities available from knowledge of neural networks. It focuses on a specific property: when a network's architecture remains fixed during training, its underlying data structure can be optimized ahead of time.

The authors introduce SONNC, a neural-network compiler that uses static analysis to generate optimized parallel code. The compiler uses architectural information that is already known before training to specialize the implementation. This places some of the burden of producing efficient code in the compilation process rather than requiring researchers to manage every optimization themselves.

The reported experiments show speedups of up to 242 times over optimized MATLAB code. SONNC also significantly reduces code complexity for structurally sparse networks. The speedup is a reported maximum, not a uniform improvement across all applications. Together, the findings demonstrate the potential of architecture-aware compilation to improve execution speed and simplify the implementation of sparse neural networks.
summary.tldr: SONNC uses fixed network architecture to generate optimized parallel code, reporting up to 242-fold speedups over optimized MATLAB.

title: Utilizing Static Analysis and Code Generation to Accelerate Neural Networks
